A telecom company runs an Amazon Lex V2 bot in its contact center. The bot's intents for bill checks and plan changes call a legacy billing system through an AWS Lambda function. Customers also ask about roaming rules and contract terms. None of the intents covers these questions, so the bot says that it did not understand. The answers are in policy documents in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and the documents change every week. The security team manages the bot's IAM role, and the bot must keep that role. The team must not change the existing intents and will not write new code.
Which combination of steps should the team take?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A telecom company runs an Amazon Lex V2 bot in its contact center. The bot's intents for bill checks and plan changes call a legacy billing system through an AWS Lambda function. Customers also ask about roaming rules and contract terms. None of the intents covers these questions, so the bot says that it did not understand. The answers are in policy documents in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and the documents change every week. The security team manages the bot's IAM role, and the bot must keep that role. The team must not change the existing intents and will not write new code.
Which combination of steps should the team take?
Select TWO.

options.text: Add the built-in AMAZON.QnAIntent to the bot locale, choose the knowledge base as its store, and choose generated responses from an Amazon Bedrock model.
Add permissions to the bot's IAM role that allow the bot to invoke the chosen Amazon Bedrock model and to query the knowledge base.
Turn on assisted NLU for the bot locale, so a model in Amazon Bedrock helps Amazon Lex match each question to one of the bot's intents.
Add a Lambda code hook to AMAZON.FallbackIntent that calls RetrieveAndGenerate on the knowledge base and returns the generated answer to the customer.
Switch the bot to the service-linked role that Amazon Lex creates, so the console adds the Amazon Bedrock and knowledge base permissions by itself.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add the built-in AMAZON.QnAIntent to the bot locale, choose the knowledge base as its store, and choose generated responses from an Amazon Bedrock model.
AMAZON.QnAIntent is a built-in intent that answers customer questions with an Amazon Bedrock model and a knowledge store, such as an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Amazon Lex activates it only when an utterance does not match any other intent in the bot. So the bill check and plan change intents keep working as before, with no change, and the roaming and contract questions now reach the knowledge base. With generated responses, the model writes each answer from the documents that it retrieves, so a weekly change to the documents reaches the answers after the next sync. The bot locale needs its generative AI features turned on, and the team writes no code.

CORRECT: Add permissions to the bot's IAM role that allow the bot to invoke the chosen Amazon Bedrock model and to query the knowledge base.
To use AMAZON.QnAIntent, the bot's IAM role needs permission to call bedrock:InvokeModel and permission to access the knowledge base that the intent uses. When a team turns on the feature in the Amazon Lex console, the console adds these policies by itself, but only when the bot uses the service-linked role that Amazon Lex created. Here the security team manages the bot's IAM role, and the bot must keep that role, so the console does not add the policies. The team adds them to that role. Without them, the new intent cannot reach the model or the knowledge base.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.1: "Create enterprise connectivity solutions to seamlessly incorporate FM capabilities into existing enterprise environments"
Example: "API-based integrations with legacy systems"

Sources:

  • AMAZON.QnAIntent

  • Permissions for the AMAZON.QnAIntent

  • Improve intent classification and slot resolution in Lex V2 with assisted NLU

INCORRECT: Turn on assisted NLU for the bot locale, so a model in Amazon Bedrock helps Amazon Lex match each question to one of the bot's intents.
Assisted NLU uses a large language model to improve how Amazon Lex classifies utterances into intents and resolves slots. It helps a bot whose customers phrase requests in unusual ways that the bot matches to the wrong intent. It stays within the intents and slots that the bot already has, and it creates no content. Here none of the intents covers roaming or contract questions, so better classification still has no intent to send them to.

INCORRECT: Add a Lambda code hook to AMAZON.FallbackIntent that calls RetrieveAndGenerate on the knowledge base and returns the generated answer to the customer.
AMAZON.FallbackIntent can call a Lambda function when the bot cannot match the customer's input. A function that calls RetrieveAndGenerate on the knowledge base is a working design for a team that wants full control over the request and the reply. But the team will not write new code, and this design needs a new function that the team must write, test and maintain.

INCORRECT: Switch the bot to the service-linked role that Amazon Lex creates, so the console adds the Amazon Bedrock and knowledge base permissions by itself.
Amazon Lex can create a service-linked role for a bot. When a bot uses that role and the team turns on AMAZON.QnAIntent in the Amazon Lex console, the console adds the model and knowledge base permissions to the role by itself. This fits a team that lets Amazon Lex manage the bot's role. Here the security team manages the bot's role, and the bot must keep that role. So the team adds the permissions to the existing role instead.

questions.promptHtml:
A financial services firm is preparing to ingest 50 TB of historical PDF loan applications into an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base for a RAG application. Before the ingestion pipeline runs, the compliance team requires a comprehensive audit of the source Amazon S3 bucket to identify any files containing unencrypted Credit Card Numbers (CCN) or Social Security Numbers (SSN).
Which solution provides the most operationally efficient way to discover and report this sensitive data at scale?
questions.promptText:
A financial services firm is preparing to ingest 50 TB of historical PDF loan applications into an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base for a RAG application. Before the ingestion pipeline runs, the compliance team requires a comprehensive audit of the source Amazon S3 bucket to identify any files containing unencrypted Credit Card Numbers (CCN) or Social Security Numbers (SSN).
Which solution provides the most operationally efficient way to discover and report this sensitive data at scale?

options.text: Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the bucket with a sampling depth of 100 percent, select the managed data identifiers for credit card and Social Security numbers, and review its findings.

Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the bucket with a sampling depth of 20 percent, select the managed data identifiers for credit card and Social Security numbers, and review its findings.

Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the bucket with a sampling depth of 100 percent, add custom data identifiers with regular expressions for card and Social Security numbers, and review its findings.

Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the bucket with a sampling depth of 20 percent, add custom data identifiers with regular expressions for card and Social Security numbers, and review its findings.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the bucket with a sampling depth of 100 percent, select the managed data identifiers for credit card and Social Security numbers, and review its findings.
A sensitive data discovery job analyzes the S3 objects in its scope. Sampling depth sets the share of eligible objects that the job analyzes, and at 100 percent the job analyzes every eligible object in the bucket instead of a random share. Macie already maintains managed data identifiers for both data types: credit card numbers sit in the Financial information category, and Social Security numbers sit in Personal information: PII. The team writes no detection rules. The job's findings name each object that holds these numbers, which gives the compliance team its report before the ingestion runs.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.2: "Develop privacy-preserving systems to protect sensitive information during FM interactions"
Example: "Amazon Comprehend and Amazon Macie to detect personally identifiable information [PII]"

Sources:

  • Scope options for sensitive data discovery jobs
  • Building custom data identifiers
  • Creating a sensitive data discovery job

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the bucket with a sampling depth of 20 percent, select the managed data identifiers for credit card and Social Security numbers, and review its findings.
With a sampling depth below 100 percent, Macie picks that share of the eligible objects at random and analyzes only those. A low depth gives a fast, lower-cost estimate of what a very large bucket holds. The compliance team must identify any file with these numbers. At 20 percent, about four out of five objects are never analyzed, so the job can miss files that hold card or Social Security numbers.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the bucket with a sampling depth of 100 percent, add custom data identifiers with regular expressions for card and Social Security numbers, and review its findings.
A custom data identifier finds text that matches a regular expression, with optional keywords near the match. It fits data that no managed identifier covers, such as employee IDs or internal account numbers. Macie already has managed identifiers for credit card numbers and Social Security numbers. Writing and testing regular expressions for them adds work, and the question asks for the most operationally efficient way.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the bucket with a sampling depth of 20 percent, add custom data identifiers with regular expressions for card and Social Security numbers, and review its findings.
This option fails in two ways. At 20 percent, the job analyzes only about one in five eligible objects, picked at random, so it can miss files that hold card or Social Security numbers. The compliance team must identify any such file. Custom regular expressions for these two data types also add work, because Macie already has managed data identifiers for both.

questions.promptHtml:
A healthcare organization is building a generative AI application on Amazon EC2 instances located in a private subnet. The application processes highly sensitive patient data and uses Amazon Bedrock models for summarization. The compliance team enforces the following strict network security requirements:
1. All traffic between the EC2 instances and Amazon Bedrock must remain entirely within the AWS global network and must never traverse the public internet.
2. The connectivity solution must strictly enforce that only the specific IAM role associated with the EC2 application is permitted to invoke models through this network path.
Which architecture implementation meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A healthcare organization is building a generative AI application on Amazon EC2 instances located in a private subnet. The application processes highly sensitive patient data and uses Amazon Bedrock models for summarization. The compliance team enforces the following strict network security requirements:
1. All traffic between the EC2 instances and Amazon Bedrock must remain entirely within the AWS global network and must never traverse the public internet.
2. The connectivity solution must strictly enforce that only the specific IAM role associated with the EC2 application is permitted to invoke models through this network path.
Which architecture implementation meets these requirements?

options.text: Provision an Interface VPC Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for bedrock-runtime. Attach a VPC Endpoint Policy to this endpoint that explicitly allows the bedrock:InvokeModel action only for the Principal of the EC2 instance profile's IAM role.

Provision an Interface VPC Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for bedrock-runtime. Attach a Security Group to the endpoint network interface that restricts inbound access to only the security group associated with the EC2 application instances. Do not configure a VPC Endpoint Policy.

Provision an Interface VPC Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for bedrock-runtime. Attach a VPC Endpoint Policy that allows bedrock:InvokeModel with Principal: "*" and a Condition block using aws:SourceVpc to restrict access to the application VPC's ID.

Provision an Interface VPC Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for bedrock instead of bedrock-runtime. Attach a VPC Endpoint Policy restricting the bedrock:InvokeModel action to the EC2 instance profile's IAM role. Update the application to route inference calls through the endpoint's private DNS hostname.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Provision an Interface VPC Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for bedrock-runtime. Attach a VPC Endpoint Policy to this endpoint that explicitly allows the bedrock:InvokeModel action only for the Principal of the EC2 instance profile's IAM role.
This solution addresses both requirements. The Interface VPC Endpoint for bedrock-runtime routes all inference traffic over the AWS private network via PrivateLink, ensuring it never traverses the public internet. The VPC Endpoint Policy is a resource-based IAM policy attached directly to the endpoint. It enforces identity-based access control at the network boundary by specifying the EC2 instance profile's IAM role as the only permitted Principal. Any request arriving through this endpoint from a different IAM principal is denied, regardless of that principal's IAM identity policies. This combination of private routing and endpoint-level principal enforcement satisfies both network isolation and IAM restriction requirements.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.1: "Develop protected AI environments to ensure comprehensive security for FM deployments"
Example: "VPC endpoints to isolate networks"

Sources:

  • Use interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) to create a private connection between your VPC and Amazon Bedrock

  • Control access to VPC endpoints using endpoint policies

INCORRECT: Provision an Interface VPC Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for bedrock-runtime. Attach a Security Group to the endpoint network interface that restricts inbound access to only the security group associated with the EC2 application instances. Do not configure a VPC Endpoint Policy.
This option correctly provisions the Interface VPC Endpoint for bedrock-runtime, ensuring all traffic remains within the AWS private network and satisfying requirement one. The failure is in how it enforces requirement two. Security Groups are stateful network-layer controls that filter traffic based on IP addresses, ports, and protocols, or by referencing other security groups. They have no awareness of IAM identity. Restricting the endpoint's security group to the EC2 instances' security group ensures only those instances can reach the endpoint network interface at the network layer, but it does not enforce which IAM role is making the API call. The endpoint accepts calls from any principal that can reach it, including other roles on those same instances, so this network path does not limit model invocation to the one application role.

INCORRECT: Provision an Interface VPC Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for bedrock-runtime. Attach a VPC Endpoint Policy that allows bedrock:InvokeModel with Principal: "*" and a Condition block using aws:SourceVpc to restrict access to the application VPC's ID.
This option correctly provisions the Interface VPC Endpoint for bedrock-runtime and uses a VPC Endpoint Policy to restrict access, satisfying requirement one. The failure is in the specificity of the restriction. Setting Principal: "*" with an aws:SourceVpc condition enforces that requests must originate from within the specified VPC, but any IAM principal in that VPC, whether a role, a user, or a service, can invoke models through this endpoint. Requirement two mandates that only the specific EC2 instance profile's IAM role is permitted. The VPC Endpoint Policy's Principal field must be set to the specific IAM role ARN to enforce identity-level restriction at the endpoint boundary.

INCORRECT: Provision an Interface VPC Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for bedrock instead of bedrock-runtime. Attach a VPC Endpoint Policy restricting the bedrock:InvokeModel action to the EC2 instance profile's IAM role. Update the application to route inference calls through the endpoint's private DNS hostname.
This option correctly uses PrivateLink to keep traffic off the public internet and correctly applies a VPC Endpoint Policy scoped to the EC2 role, satisfying the intent of both requirements. The failure is in the endpoint service name. Amazon Bedrock has several interface endpoint service names. com.amazonaws.region.bedrock covers the control plane API used for managing models and configuration, while com.amazonaws.region.bedrock-runtime covers the data plane API that handles model inference calls, including InvokeModel. Routing InvokeModel requests through the bedrock control plane endpoint will result in failed API calls. The correct endpoint for application inference traffic is bedrock-runtime.

questions.promptHtml:
A development team at an aerospace company builds a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) application with an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Mechanics ask the application about thousands of maintenance manuals, which are PDF files in an Amazon S3 bucket. The manuals form one dataset for each aircraft type. Aviation rules set three requirements. Each answer must cite the ID and the version number of the manual that the answer comes from. Every dataset must have an entry in one central catalog, and the catalog must keep each earlier version of an entry when the team changes the entry. Every read of a manual file in the S3 bucket must be logged for audits.

Which solution meets all three requirements?
questions.promptText:
A development team at an aerospace company builds a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) application with an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Mechanics ask the application about thousands of maintenance manuals, which are PDF files in an Amazon S3 bucket. The manuals form one dataset for each aircraft type. Aviation rules set three requirements. Each answer must cite the ID and the version number of the manual that the answer comes from. Every dataset must have an entry in one central catalog, and the catalog must keep each earlier version of an entry when the team changes the entry. Every read of a manual file in the S3 bucket must be logged for audits.
Which solution meets all three requirements?

options.text: Register the manual datasets in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, store the manual ID and version number as metadata on each chunk so answers cite them, and turn on CloudTrail data events for the bucket.

Register the manual datasets in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, store the manual ID and version number as metadata on each chunk so answers cite them, and create a CloudTrail trail that logs management events.
Turn on S3 Versioning for the manual bucket, store the manual ID and version number as metadata on each chunk so answers cite them, and turn on CloudTrail data events for the bucket.
Turn on S3 Versioning for the manual bucket, store the manual ID and version number as metadata on each chunk so answers cite them, and create a CloudTrail trail that logs management events.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Register the manual datasets in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, store the manual ID and version number as metadata on each chunk so answers cite them, and turn on CloudTrail data events for the bucket.
Each part of this option meets one requirement. The AWS Glue Data Catalog is a central repository of metadata about datasets, and each aircraft dataset becomes one table entry in the catalog. When the team updates a table entry, AWS Glue keeps the earlier version of that entry by default. Metadata on each chunk comes back with the chunk at retrieval, so each answer can cite the manual ID and version number. A read of a manual file is a GetObject call, and CloudTrail records GetObject as an S3 data event. CloudTrail does not log data events by default, so the team turns them on for the bucket.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.2: "Implement data source tracking to maintain traceability in GenAI applications"
Example: "AWS Glue Data Catalog to register data sources"

Sources:

  • Amazon S3 CloudTrail events

  • Data discovery and cataloging in AWS Glue

  • UpdateTable (AWS Glue Web API Reference)

INCORRECT: Register the manual datasets in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, store the manual ID and version number as metadata on each chunk so answers cite them, and create a CloudTrail trail that logs management events.
Management events record control plane actions in Amazon S3, such as creating a bucket or changing a bucket policy. A trail that logs management events fits an audit of who changed the setup. In this option, the catalog and the chunk metadata meet the first two requirements. A read of a manual file is a GetObject call, which is a data event, not a management event. So this trail records none of the reads, and the option fails the third requirement.

INCORRECT: Turn on S3 Versioning for the manual bucket, store the manual ID and version number as metadata on each chunk so answers cite them, and turn on CloudTrail data events for the bucket.
S3 Versioning keeps every version of every object in a bucket, so a team can restore a manual file that someone overwrote or deleted. In this option, the chunk metadata and the data events meet the citation and the logging requirements. The catalog requirement asks for one entry for each dataset in a central catalog, together with the earlier versions of each entry. Versioning keeps old copies of files inside one bucket. It gives the team no catalog entry for a dataset, and no history of such an entry.

INCORRECT: Turn on S3 Versioning for the manual bucket, store the manual ID and version number as metadata on each chunk so answers cite them, and create a CloudTrail trail that logs management events.
This option fails two requirements. S3 Versioning keeps old copies of files in the bucket, but it is not a central catalog of datasets. A trail that logs management events records changes to the setup, but not the GetObject calls that read the manual files. The option meets only the citation requirement.

questions.promptHtml:
A pharmaceutical company is fine-tuning Foundation Models (FMs) on Amazon SageMaker AI to assist with clinical trial documentation. To comply with strict regulatory audit requirements, the MLOps team must implement a traceability system that allows auditors to traverse the entire history of a deployed model.
Specifically, the system must allow auditors to query a relationship graph to identify exactly which version of the raw training data in Amazon S3 was used by a specific training job to produce a specific model version currently running on a SageMaker AI endpoint. Each version of the raw training data sits at its own S3 prefix. The team will write no lineage code.
Which solution meets these governance requirements using AWS native tools?
questions.promptText:
A pharmaceutical company is fine-tuning Foundation Models (FMs) on Amazon SageMaker AI to assist with clinical trial documentation. To comply with strict regulatory audit requirements, the MLOps team must implement a traceability system that allows auditors to traverse the entire history of a deployed model.
Specifically, the system must allow auditors to query a relationship graph to identify exactly which version of the raw training data in Amazon S3 was used by a specific training job to produce a specific model version currently running on a SageMaker AI endpoint. Each version of the raw training data sits at its own S3 prefix. The team will write no lineage code.
Which solution meets these governance requirements using AWS native tools?

options.text: Use SageMaker AI ML Lineage Tracking, and query the lineage graph from the endpoint back through the model and the training job to the S3 dataset artifact of the job.
Turn on CloudTrail data events for the training data bucket, and use Amazon Athena to match GetObject calls by the training role with the time each model version was created.
Register each model version in SageMaker Model Registry, and store the S3 prefix of its training data version in the customer metadata properties of the model package.
Use data lineage in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, and follow the lineage graph from the S3 dataset through the AWS Glue job that prepared it for training.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use SageMaker AI ML Lineage Tracking, and query the lineage graph from the endpoint back through the model and the training job to the S3 dataset artifact of the job.
SageMaker AI ML Lineage Tracking stores a graph of entities and the associations between them. SageMaker AI creates these entities by itself for training jobs, models, model packages and endpoints, so the team writes no lineage code of its own. For a training job, the S3 URI of each input channel becomes a dataset artifact that is linked to the job. Lineage tracks S3 data by that URI, not by the version of each file, so the separate S3 prefix for each data version is what makes the answer exact. A lineage query that starts at the endpoint and moves up the graph returns the datasets behind the deployed model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.2: "Implement data source tracking to maintain traceability in GenAI applications"

Sources:

  • Amazon SageMaker AI-Created Tracking Entities

  • Lineage Tracking Entities

  • Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking

INCORRECT: Turn on CloudTrail data events for the training data bucket, and use Amazon Athena to match GetObject calls by the training role with the time each model version was created.
CloudTrail data events record each GetObject call with the caller and the time. With Athena, a team can find who read a file and when, which fits an access audit. Matching read times with model creation times is a guess, not a recorded link, because the same role can read data for other jobs. The auditors need a relationship graph that links the data, the job and the model.

INCORRECT: Register each model version in SageMaker Model Registry, and store the S3 prefix of its training data version in the customer metadata properties of the model package.
Customer metadata properties are key and value pairs that a team stores on a model package version, for example the ID of an approval ticket. They fit short notes that reviewers read. Here someone must write the S3 prefix into every model package, and the team will write no lineage code. The property is also one note on one model package, not a link in a graph. Model Registry does show a lineage view of each registered model, but that view is for visualization only. The auditors must query the graph from the endpoint back to the data.

INCORRECT: Use data lineage in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, and follow the lineage graph from the S3 dataset through the AWS Glue job that prepared it for training.
Data lineage in SageMaker Unified Studio captures lineage automatically from ETL tools, such as AWS Glue jobs. It fits a data team that follows its data through ETL jobs in the catalog. Its automatic capture does not include SageMaker AI training jobs or endpoints, so the graph stops at the prepared dataset. To add those steps, the team would have to send custom lineage events, and the team will write no lineage code.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A legal technology firm uses a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application on Amazon Bedrock to summarize case law. The retrieval process currently fetches the top 30 chunks from an Amazon OpenSearch Service vector index to ensure comprehensive coverage. However, this approach fills the prompt context window with irrelevant information, leading to excessive input token costs and high inference latency.
Which solution should the developer implement to dynamically prune the context and optimize costs while strictly maintaining retrieval relevance?
questions.promptText:
A legal technology firm uses a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application on Amazon Bedrock to summarize case law. The retrieval process currently fetches the top 30 chunks from an Amazon OpenSearch Service vector index to ensure comprehensive coverage. However, this approach fills the prompt context window with irrelevant information, leading to excessive input token costs and high inference latency.
Which solution should the developer implement to dynamically prune the context and optimize costs while strictly maintaining retrieval relevance?

options.text: Implement a reranking step using an Amazon Bedrock reranking model. Configure the application to rescore the initial retrieved chunks and discard any chunks that fall below a specific relevance score threshold before prompt construction.

Update the retrieval logic to summarize each of the 30 retrieved chunks using a smaller, lower-cost Amazon Bedrock model in a Map-Reduce pattern, then pass the consolidated summaries as the final context to the main generation model.

Reduce the vector database top-k retrieval parameter from 30 to 5 to limit the number of chunks passed to the generation model, and implement a sliding window strategy that only sends the most recent document segments to the model.

Configure Provisioned Throughput for the Amazon Bedrock generation model to reserve dedicated inference capacity, increase the available tokens-per-minute quota, and reduce per-token processing latency when handling the full 30-chunk context.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Implement a reranking step using an Amazon Bedrock reranking model. Configure the application to rescore the initial retrieved chunks and discard any chunks that fall below a specific relevance score threshold before prompt construction.
A reranker model in Amazon Bedrock calculates how relevant each chunk is to the query. The Rerank operation takes the query and the documents that the application sends, from any source, and returns a relevance score for each document. The application keeps the wide search of 30 chunks, sends them to the reranker, and drops every chunk with a score under its threshold before it builds the prompt. Only chunks that match the question reach the generation model, so the prompt holds fewer input tokens, costs less and returns sooner. Because the first search still covers 30 chunks, a relevant chunk that the vector search ranked low can still reach the prompt.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.1: "Develop token efficiency systems to reduce FM costs while maintaining effectiveness"
Example: "context pruning"

Sources:

  • Improve the relevance of query responses with a reranker model in Amazon Bedrock

  • Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Update the retrieval logic to summarize each of the 30 retrieved chunks using a smaller, lower-cost Amazon Bedrock model in a Map-Reduce pattern, then pass the consolidated summaries as the final context to the main generation model.
A Map-Reduce pattern summarizes each chunk with a model and then combines the summaries. It fits long documents where every part must be read, for example a summary of a full contract. Here the question asks to remove the chunks that do not help the answer. The summaries keep a short form of every chunk, including the irrelevant ones, so the noise stays in the prompt. The pattern also adds a model call for each of the 30 chunks before the main call, which adds cost and latency.

INCORRECT: Reduce the vector database top-k retrieval parameter from 30 to 5 to limit the number of chunks passed to the generation model, and implement a sliding window strategy that only sends the most recent document segments to the model.
A smaller top-k value returns fewer chunks from the vector search, which cuts input tokens with no extra step. It fits an index where the best matches reliably sit at the top of the results. The firm chose 30 chunks to cover case law fully, and the question requires the team to keep retrieval relevance. A fixed limit of 5 can drop a relevant case that the vector search ranked sixth. A sliding window that sends the most recent segments chooses text by its date, not by how well it matches the question.

INCORRECT: Configure Provisioned Throughput for the Amazon Bedrock generation model to reserve dedicated inference capacity, increase the available tokens-per-minute quota, and reduce per-token processing latency when handling the full 30-chunk context.
Provisioned Throughput reserves model units for a model. Each model unit processes a set number of input and output tokens per minute, and the capacity is billed by the hour. It fits steady, heavy traffic that needs capacity without throttling. It does not change what goes into a request. Each prompt still holds all 30 chunks, so the irrelevant text and its input tokens stay in every call.

A company serves text generation from two Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints, one with a small model and one with a larger model. Mobile and web clients call POST /generate on a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. The method uses an AWS service integration with the SageMaker AI runtime, and today it always calls the small model's endpoint. Each client sends an x-plan header with the value basic or premium. Premium requests must reach the larger model on every call, and basic requests the small model. The clients keep the same URL and request format, the endpoints keep their current names, and the team will run no new compute.
Which change should the team make to the API?
questions.promptText:
A company serves text generation from two Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints, one with a small model and one with a larger model. Mobile and web clients call POST /generate on a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. The method uses an AWS service integration with the SageMaker AI runtime, and today it always calls the small model's endpoint. Each client sends an x-plan header with the value basic or premium. Premium requests must reach the larger model on every call, and basic requests the small model. The clients keep the same URL and request format, the endpoints keep their current names, and the team will run no new compute.
Which change should the team make to the API?

options.text: On the POST /generate integration, set the path override to endpoints/{endpoint}/invocations, and add a mapping template that picks the endpoint name for each x-plan value.
On the POST /generate integration, set the path override to endpoints/{endpoint}/invocations, and map the endpoint path parameter from the x-plan header with parameter mapping.
On the POST /generate integration, set the path override to endpoints/{endpoint}/invocations, map the endpoint path parameter from a stage variable, and deploy one stage for each plan.
On the POST /generate integration, keep the fixed endpoint name, and host both models on that endpoint as production variants with traffic weights that match the premium share.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: On the POST /generate integration, set the path override to endpoints/{endpoint}/invocations, and add a mapping template that picks the endpoint name for each x-plan value.
An AWS service integration lets API Gateway call the SageMaker AI runtime directly, with no Lambda function in between. The InvokeEndpoint call uses the path endpoints/EndpointName/invocations, so the path override endpoints/{endpoint}/invocations makes the endpoint name a URL path parameter of the integration request. In the request mapping template, $input.params reads the x-plan header, an #if statement picks the larger model's endpoint name for premium and the small model's name for basic, and $context.requestOverride.path.endpoint sets the path parameter to that name. The template also passes the request on with $input.body. Every request reaches the endpoint for its plan, and the clients change nothing.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.4: "Develop intelligent model routing systems to optimize model selection"
Example: "API Gateway with request transformations for routing logic"

Sources:

  • Creating a machine learning-powered REST API with Amazon API Gateway mapping templates and Amazon SageMaker

  • Variables for data transformations for API Gateway

  • Parameter mapping source reference for REST APIs in API Gateway

INCORRECT: On the POST /generate integration, set the path override to endpoints/{endpoint}/invocations, and map the endpoint path parameter from the x-plan header with parameter mapping.
Parameter mapping fills an integration request parameter from one source, such as a method request header, a stage variable or a static value. It fits a client that already sends the exact value that the backend needs, for example the endpoint name itself. Here the header holds basic or premium, and the endpoints keep their current names. The mapping passes the header value as it is, so the path would name an endpoint called basic or premium, and no endpoint has that name.

INCORRECT: On the POST /generate integration, set the path override to endpoints/{endpoint}/invocations, map the endpoint path parameter from a stage variable, and deploy one stage for each plan.
A stage variable is a valid source for parameter mapping, so each stage of the API can call a different endpoint. This fits separate environments, such as test and production, where each group of clients uses its own stage. The stage name is part of the base URL of a REST API. Premium clients would need the URL of a new stage, and the clients must keep the same URL.

INCORRECT: On the POST /generate integration, keep the fixed endpoint name, and host both models on that endpoint as production variants with traffic weights that match the premium share.
Production variants put several models behind one endpoint, and the traffic weights send each variant a share of the requests in proportion to its weight. This fits a test that compares two models on live traffic. Weights split the requests by share, not by the plan that each request carries. Some premium requests would reach the small model, and premium requests must reach the larger model on every call.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A compliance team runs an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that uses Amazon Neptune Analytics for GraphRAG. The contract PDFs are in an Amazon S3 bucket. The team chose hierarchical chunking, because auditors want each cited passage to show more of the section around the matching text. For multi-hop questions that connect parties across separate contracts, the knowledge base returns the correct relationships. These questions must keep working. However, each cited passage is a short fragment that shows little of its section.

What should the team do so that each cited passage shows more of its section?
questions.promptText:
A compliance team runs an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that uses Amazon Neptune Analytics for GraphRAG. The contract PDFs are in an Amazon S3 bucket. The team chose hierarchical chunking, because auditors want each cited passage to show more of the section around the matching text. For multi-hop questions that connect parties across separate contracts, the knowledge base returns the correct relationships. These questions must keep working. However, each cited passage is a short fragment that shows little of its section.
What should the team do so that each cited passage shows more of its section?

options.text: Replace the data source with one that uses fixed-size chunking at a higher maximum token count, then sync it so each chunk can contain more of the section.
Re-create the data source with hierarchical chunking and a larger parent chunk size, so the search returns a larger parent chunk for each matching child chunk.
Raise the number of results in the retrieval configuration of the knowledge base, so each response draws on more of the chunks that match the question.
Move the documents to a new knowledge base with an OpenSearch Serverless vector store and hierarchical chunking, so the search returns the parent chunk for each matching child chunk.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Replace the data source with one that uses fixed-size chunking at a higher maximum token count, then sync it so each chunk can contain more of the section.
With GraphRAG on Amazon Neptune Analytics, a knowledge base that uses hierarchical chunking retrieves only the child chunks. The knowledge base does not replace the child chunks with their parent chunks, so each cited passage is a short child chunk. Fixed-size chunking sets the maximum number of tokens in a chunk. A higher maximum allows larger chunks, so a chunk can contain more of the section around the matching text. The chunking settings of an existing data source cannot be changed, so the team creates a new data source with the new settings and syncs it. The knowledge base keeps Neptune Analytics and GraphRAG, so the multi-hop questions still work.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.1: "Develop effective document segmentation approaches to optimize retrieval performance for FM context augmentation"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock chunking capabilities"

Sources:

  • Build a knowledge base with Amazon Neptune Analytics graphs

  • Modify a data source for your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base

  • How content chunking works for knowledge bases

INCORRECT: Re-create the data source with hierarchical chunking and a larger parent chunk size, so the search returns a larger parent chunk for each matching child chunk.
In standard vector retrieval, hierarchical chunking matches small child chunks and then returns their larger parent chunks, so a bigger parent gives more context. That fits a knowledge base with a vector store such as Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. With GraphRAG, the knowledge base returns only the child chunks and never swaps them for their parents. A larger parent is never returned, and the cited passages stay short.

INCORRECT: Raise the number of results in the retrieval configuration of the knowledge base, so each response draws on more of the chunks that match the question.
A higher number of results returns more chunks for each query. This setting fits a problem where the answer is spread over more chunks than the knowledge base returns. Here the problem is the size of each passage. More results bring more short child chunks, and each cited passage still shows little of its section. Every prompt also grows with extra tokens.

INCORRECT: Move the documents to a new knowledge base with an OpenSearch Serverless vector store and hierarchical chunking, so the search returns the parent chunk for each matching child chunk.
A knowledge base with an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store and hierarchical chunking returns the parent chunk for each matching child chunk. The cited passages would then show the wider section. This design fits document search that needs broad context. But the move drops the Neptune Analytics graph, and the graph is what links parties across separate contracts. The multi-hop questions must keep working, so the team cannot leave GraphRAG.

questions.promptHtml:
A finance team built an agent that answers questions about expense data. The team used Strands Agents. Analysts upload CSV files and Excel workbooks with thousands of rows, and each question asks for a different calculation, such as a total by region or a growth rate between two months. The columns also differ from file to file. The agent often gives totals that are wrong by small amounts, even after the team told the model to work through each sum step by step. Company policy says that an uploaded file may stay only in an isolated environment for one session. The file must not be available after the session ends.

What should the team add to the agent?
questions.promptText:
A finance team built an agent that answers questions about expense data. The team used Strands Agents. Analysts upload CSV files and Excel workbooks with thousands of rows, and each question asks for a different calculation, such as a total by region or a growth rate between two months. The columns also differ from file to file. The agent often gives totals that are wrong by small amounts, even after the team told the model to work through each sum step by step. Company policy says that an uploaded file may stay only in an isolated environment for one session. The file must not be available after the session ends.
What should the team add to the agent?

options.text: Add AgentCore Code Interpreter as a tool, so the model writes Python code that reads the uploaded file and runs each calculation in an isolated sandbox.
Add an AWS Lambda function as a tool that reads the uploaded file and returns a fixed set of totals, averages and growth rates for each numeric column.
Add a tool that loads each uploaded file into an Amazon Athena table in Amazon S3, and runs the SQL query that the model writes for each question.
Add the uploaded files to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and give the agent a tool that retrieves the rows that best match each question.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add AgentCore Code Interpreter as a tool, so the model writes Python code that reads the uploaded file and runs each calculation in an isolated sandbox.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter lets an agent write code and run it in a sandbox. Each session runs in its own microVM, with isolated CPU, memory, and file system. The agent writes the uploaded file into a Code Interpreter session, and the model writes Python for the calculation that the analyst asked for. The step-by-step instruction did not help, because the model still did the arithmetic itself. Now the code does the arithmetic, and code can read new columns and run a new calculation for every question. Files and data created during a session are available for the whole life of the session. When the session ends, Code Interpreter cleans up the session's data. Agents built with Strands Agents can use Code Interpreter as a tool.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.6: "Implement intelligent tool integrations to extend FM capabilities and to ensure reliable tool operations"

Sources:

  • Execute code and analyze data using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter

  • Session management (Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter)

  • Introducing the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter

INCORRECT: Add an AWS Lambda function as a tool that reads the uploaded file and returns a fixed set of totals, averages and growth rates for each numeric column.
A Lambda function tool with fixed calculations gives exact results that repeat every time. It fits a report whose metrics and columns never change. Here each question asks for a different calculation, and the columns differ from file to file. A function that returns a fixed set of results cannot answer a growth rate between two months that the analyst chooses, or a total by a column that the function does not know.

INCORRECT: Add a tool that loads each uploaded file into an Amazon Athena table in Amazon S3, and runs the SQL query that the model writes for each question.
Amazon Athena runs standard SQL on data in Amazon S3, and a SQL query computes exact totals. It fits large datasets that are already stored in S3. To query an upload, this tool must first store the file in an S3 bucket. The file stays in the bucket after the session ends, so the policy does not allow it.

INCORRECT: Add the uploaded files to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and give the agent a tool that retrieves the rows that best match each question.
A knowledge base splits documents into chunks, stores them in a vector store, and returns the chunks that best match a question. It fits questions whose answer is in a few passages. A total over thousands of rows needs every row, but retrieval returns only a limited number of matching chunks, and the model must still add the numbers itself. The chunks also stay in the vector store after the session ends, which the policy does not allow.

questions.promptHtml:
A hospital network is building a generative AI application that summarizes patient medical records for its emergency room dashboard. Because of strict data residency rules, Protected Health Information (PHI) must never leave the hospital's physical data center. The rules cover names and IDs, and also symptoms, test results and every other medical detail in a record. The dashboard also needs fast answers, so no request may make a network round trip to an AWS Region.
Which architecture meets the residency rules and the dashboard's need for speed?
questions.promptText:
A hospital network is building a generative AI application that summarizes patient medical records for its emergency room dashboard. Because of strict data residency rules, Protected Health Information (PHI) must never leave the hospital's physical data center. The rules cover names and IDs, and also symptoms, test results and every other medical detail in a record. The dashboard also needs fast answers, so no request may make a network round trip to an AWS Region.
Which architecture meets the residency rules and the dashboard's need for speed?

options.text: Run an open-source model in a container on Amazon ECS on an AWS Outposts rack inside the hospital's data center, and send each dashboard request to it.
Deploy an open-source model on Amazon EC2 instances in an AWS Wavelength Zone near the hospital, and send each dashboard request to it over the carrier network.
Run the application in a VPC in the nearest AWS Region, and have it call a model in Amazon Bedrock through an AWS PrivateLink interface endpoint.
Remove patient names and IDs in the data center, and have an application in the nearest AWS Region send the rest to a model in Amazon Bedrock through an AWS PrivateLink interface endpoint.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run an open-source model in a container on Amazon ECS on an AWS Outposts rack inside the hospital's data center, and send each dashboard request to it.
AWS Outposts puts AWS infrastructure inside the customer's own building. On an Outposts rack, Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon ECS clusters run locally, next to the hospital's own systems. The model runs in a container on that rack, so every record stays in the hospital's data center while the model reads it. The dashboard sends each request to this local endpoint, not to a Region, so no request makes the network round trip that the dashboard cannot wait for. Amazon SageMaker AI is not on the list of services that run on an Outposts rack, so the model runs in a container on ECS.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.4: "Develop cross-environment AI solutions to ensure data compliance across jurisdictions while enabling FM access"
Example: "AWS Outposts for on-premises data integration"

Sources:

  • What is AWS Outposts?
  • What is AWS Wavelength?
  • Use interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) to create a private connection between your VPC and Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Deploy an open-source model on Amazon EC2 instances in an AWS Wavelength Zone near the hospital, and send each dashboard request to it over the carrier network.
AWS Wavelength places AWS compute in the data centers of telecom providers, at the edge of their 5G networks. It suits applications that need fast answers on mobile devices, for example an app that paramedics use in an ambulance. But a Wavelength Zone sits in the carrier's building, not in the hospital. Every record would travel over the carrier network to that zone, and PHI must never leave the hospital's data center.

INCORRECT: Run the application in a VPC in the nearest AWS Region, and have it call a model in Amazon Bedrock through an AWS PrivateLink interface endpoint.
An interface VPC endpoint lets an application in a VPC reach Amazon Bedrock over a private connection, with no internet gateway and no NAT device. This is a good design when data may go to an AWS Region but must stay off the public internet. Here the full record leaves the data center and reaches a model in the Region. That breaks the residency rules. Each request also makes the round trip to a Region that the dashboard cannot accept.

INCORRECT: Remove patient names and IDs in the data center, and have an application in the nearest AWS Region send the rest to a model in Amazon Bedrock through an AWS PrivateLink interface endpoint.
Removing names and IDs before data leaves a site is a common privacy step. It fits rules that protect only the fields that identify a person. Here the rules also cover symptoms, test results and every other medical detail. The text that goes to Amazon Bedrock still holds those details, so PHI leaves the data center, and every request still goes to a Region.

questions.promptHtml:
A smart-home device manufacturer wants to use a large language model (LLM) in Amazon Bedrock to find usage trends in millions of daily device logs. Each log holds a Device ID, the user's exact GPS coordinates and a timestamped list of voice commands. An application reads the prepared logs from Amazon S3 and sends them to the model.
The model must count usage per device and find regional patterns, such as heating use in Northern Europe. Privacy rules say the model must never receive a real Device ID or an exact location. The privacy team wants no key or lookup table anywhere that turns a prepared ID back into a Device ID.
Which data preparation step meets these rules?
questions.promptText:
A smart-home device manufacturer wants to use a large language model (LLM) in Amazon Bedrock to find usage trends in millions of daily device logs. Each log holds a Device ID, the user's exact GPS coordinates and a timestamped list of voice commands. An application reads the prepared logs from Amazon S3 and sends them to the model.
The model must count usage per device and find regional patterns, such as heating use in Northern Europe. Privacy rules say the model must never receive a real Device ID or an exact location. The privacy team wants no key or lookup table anywhere that turns a prepared ID back into a Device ID.
Which data preparation step meets these rules?

options.text: In an AWS Lambda function, replace each Device ID with a hash of the ID, and replace each pair of GPS coordinates with the name of its region.
In an AWS Lambda function, replace each Device ID with a random token that an Amazon DynamoDB table maps to the ID, and replace the GPS coordinates with a region name.
In an AWS Lambda function, replace each Device ID with a hash of the ID, and keep the exact GPS coordinates so that the model can find each region itself.
In an AWS Lambda function, replace each Device ID with a random token that an Amazon DynamoDB table maps to the ID, and keep the exact GPS coordinates.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: In an AWS Lambda function, replace each Device ID with a hash of the ID, and replace each pair of GPS coordinates with the name of its region.
A hash function turns a value into a fixed-length string. It has no key, and it always gives the same output for the same input. So the model still sees one stable value for each device and can count usage per device, but it never sees the real Device ID. No key or lookup table exists, so the privacy team has nothing that turns a hash value back into a Device ID. A region name is a general form of the location. It keeps the regional patterns that the model needs and removes the exact location that the rules ban.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.3: "Create privacy-focused AI systems to protect user privacy while maintaining FM utility and effectiveness"
Example: "anonymization strategies for sensitive information"

Sources:

  • What is Cryptography?
  • What is Data Masking?
  • Pseudonymization

INCORRECT: In an AWS Lambda function, replace each Device ID with a random token that an Amazon DynamoDB table maps to the ID, and replace the GPS coordinates with a region name.
Tokenization replaces each Device ID with a random token and keeps the original value in a separate, secure store, here a DynamoDB table. It is the right choice when an authorized team must find the real device later, for example to follow up on a fault. The model would still get one token for each device and a region name. But the DynamoDB table is a lookup table that turns a token back into a Device ID, and the privacy team wants no such table anywhere.

INCORRECT: In an AWS Lambda function, replace each Device ID with a hash of the ID, and keep the exact GPS coordinates so that the model can find each region itself.
The hash hides the Device ID and needs no key or table. Keeping exact coordinates is fine when the rules allow them, for example for a map of where devices fail. Here the privacy rules say the model must never receive an exact location. If the model has to find each region itself, it still receives the exact coordinates.

INCORRECT: In an AWS Lambda function, replace each Device ID with a random token that an Amazon DynamoDB table maps to the ID, and keep the exact GPS coordinates.
This step keeps two things that the rules ban. The DynamoDB table maps each token back to a Device ID, and the privacy team wants no lookup table anywhere. The model also receives exact GPS coordinates, which the privacy rules forbid. Each part fits a company that must find devices again later and may share exact locations, but this company can do neither.

questions.promptHtml:
A media production company uses an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow to run a long generative AI video pipeline. The pipeline transcribes audio with Amazon Transcribe, writes summaries with a model in Amazon Bedrock and translates subtitles. Each new video file that arrives in a specific Amazon S3 bucket must start its own workflow run as soon as the upload completes. The team wants no new code between the bucket and the workflow. The company also does not want to pay for extra logging of bucket activity.
Which trigger design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A media production company uses an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow to run a long generative AI video pipeline. The pipeline transcribes audio with Amazon Transcribe, writes summaries with a model in Amazon Bedrock and translates subtitles. Each new video file that arrives in a specific Amazon S3 bucket must start its own workflow run as soon as the upload completes. The team wants no new code between the bucket and the workflow. The company also does not want to pay for extra logging of bucket activity.
Which trigger design meets these requirements?

options.text: Turn on Amazon EventBridge notifications for the bucket, and create a rule on the default event bus that matches Object Created events and targets the state machine.
Log the bucket's S3 data events in an AWS CloudTrail trail, and create a rule on the default event bus that matches PutObject calls and targets the state machine.
Send S3 event notifications for new objects to an AWS Lambda function, and have the function call the Step Functions StartExecution API for each new video.
Create an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule that starts the state machine every 10 minutes, and have the workflow process each video added since the last run.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on Amazon EventBridge notifications for the bucket, and create a rule on the default event bus that matches Object Created events and targets the state machine.
Amazon S3 can send its events to Amazon EventBridge after you turn this on in the bucket's properties. A rule on the default event bus matches the Object Created event and names the state machine as its target. EventBridge then starts one execution for each new file, soon after the upload completes. The design needs one bucket setting and one rule, with no code and no extra logging service.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.2: "Develop integrated AI capabilities to enhance existing applications with GenAI functionality"
Example: "Amazon EventBridge to implement event-driven integrations"

Sources:

  • Starting a Step Functions workflow in response to events
  • Event notification types and destinations
  • Amazon EventBridge event bus (default and Classic)

INCORRECT: Log the bucket's S3 data events in an AWS CloudTrail trail, and create a rule on the default event bus that matches PutObject calls and targets the state machine.
When a trail records S3 data events, EventBridge receives those API calls on the default event bus, and a rule can match PutObject. This path fits a team that also needs the details CloudTrail records, such as the identity that made each call. But CloudTrail charges for the data events that a trail delivers. The company does not want to pay for extra logging of bucket activity, and the bucket's own EventBridge notifications give the same start signal with no trail.

INCORRECT: Send S3 event notifications for new objects to an AWS Lambda function, and have the function call the Step Functions StartExecution API for each new video.
S3 event notifications can invoke a Lambda function, and the function can start the workflow with StartExecution. Teams use this when they need their own logic first, for example to check the file type or to add details to the workflow input. Here the team wants no new code between the bucket and the workflow. This design needs a function that the team writes and maintains.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule that starts the state machine every 10 minutes, and have the workflow process each video added since the last run.
EventBridge Scheduler can start a state machine at fixed times. A schedule fits batch work, such as a nightly report over all the files of one day. Here each video must start its own run as soon as the upload completes. A schedule waits for its next run time, and one run handles several videos together.

questions.promptHtml:
A company hosts a fine-tuned open-source model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for its customer support chat. For the next two weeks, a new version that the data science team trained must answer about 10 percent of live chat requests on the same endpoint. Users must see those answers, because the team wants real user reactions. The current version must keep the other 90 percent until the team decides. Before all traffic moves to one version, the team must compare two figures for each version on this live traffic. These figures are how long the model takes to respond and the share of requests that fail with a server error.

Which TWO actions meet these requirements?

Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company hosts a fine-tuned open-source model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for its customer support chat. For the next two weeks, a new version that the data science team trained must answer about 10 percent of live chat requests on the same endpoint. Users must see those answers, because the team wants real user reactions. The current version must keep the other 90 percent until the team decides. Before all traffic moves to one version, the team must compare two figures for each version on this live traffic. These figures are how long the model takes to respond and the share of requests that fail with a server error.
Which TWO actions meet these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Create an endpoint configuration with two production variants, one for each model version, with weights of 9 and 1, and update the endpoint to use it.
Create an endpoint configuration with the current version as the production variant and the new version as a shadow variant, and update the endpoint to use it.
Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that uses canary traffic shifting, and send 10 percent of the traffic to the new version during the baking period.
Compare the ModelLatency and Invocation5XXErrors metrics in Amazon CloudWatch for each production variant, using the VariantName dimension of the endpoint invocation metrics, over the two weeks.
Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model on saved responses from each version, and compare the scores of the two evaluation jobs.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an endpoint configuration with two production variants, one for each model version, with weights of 9 and 1, and update the endpoint to use it.
One endpoint can hold several production variants, each with its own model and a weight. SageMaker AI splits the requests by those weights, so weights of 9 and 1 send about 10 percent of requests to the new version. Users see the answer of the variant that serves them, and the chat application keeps calling the same endpoint. When the team decides, it can change the traffic split with UpdateEndpointWeightsAndCapacities, with no new endpoint configuration.

CORRECT: Compare the ModelLatency and Invocation5XXErrors metrics in Amazon CloudWatch for each production variant, using the VariantName dimension of the endpoint invocation metrics, over the two weeks.
The team must compare how long the model takes to respond and the share of requests that fail with a server error. SageMaker AI sends both figures to Amazon CloudWatch as endpoint invocation metrics. ModelLatency is the time that the model takes to respond to a request. Invocation5XXErrors records 1 for each request where the model returned a 5xx HTTP response code, which is a server error, and 0 for every other request. So the Average statistic of Invocation5XXErrors is the share of requests that fail with a server error. The VariantName dimension shows each metric for one production variant. The new version serves far fewer requests, so the team compares shares, not counts.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.2: "Create systematic model evaluation systems to identify optimal configurations"
Example: "A/B testing and canary testing of FMs"

Sources:

  • Testing models with production variants

  • Amazon SageMaker AI metrics in Amazon CloudWatch

  • Shadow tests

INCORRECT: Create an endpoint configuration with the current version as the production variant and the new version as a shadow variant, and update the endpoint to use it.
A shadow variant receives a copy of the requests that go to the production variant. Only the production variant's answers go back to the application, and the team can log the shadow answers for an offline comparison. This is a safe way to test a new version on live requests while users do not see its answers. Here users must see the new version's answers, because the team wants real user reactions.

INCORRECT: Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that uses canary traffic shifting, and send 10 percent of the traffic to the new version during the baking period.
Canary traffic shifting sends part of the traffic to the new fleet while CloudWatch alarms watch it during a baking period. If no alarm goes off, all traffic moves to the new fleet, and SageMaker AI then removes the old fleet. This fits a release that should go ahead unless errors appear. Here the current version must keep 90 percent of the traffic until the team decides after two weeks.

INCORRECT: Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model on saved responses from each version, and compare the scores of the two evaluation jobs.
Amazon Bedrock can run an evaluation job in which a judge model scores the answers of another model. The judge rates the quality of each answer, for example whether the answer is correct, so the judge can find wrong answers. The job can also score saved answers from a model outside Amazon Bedrock. In this test, the team compares how long the model takes to respond and the share of requests that fail with a server error. A judge job measures neither figure. It scores a set of saved answers once, while this comparison runs on live traffic for two weeks.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A telemedicine platform is building a pipeline that turns audio recordings of doctor and patient consultations into SOAP notes. Amazon Transcribe creates the transcript, and a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock writes the note. The model often gives the doctor's advice to the patient and the patient's symptoms to the doctor. Each consultation is recorded as a single mono track from one microphone in the room. The transcripts spell every medical term correctly.
Which approach fixes the mixed-up roles in the notes?
questions.promptText:
A telemedicine platform is building a pipeline that turns audio recordings of doctor and patient consultations into SOAP notes. Amazon Transcribe creates the transcript, and a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock writes the note. The model often gives the doctor's advice to the patient and the patient's symptoms to the doctor. Each consultation is recorded as a single mono track from one microphone in the room. The transcripts spell every medical term correctly.
Which approach fixes the mixed-up roles in the notes?

options.text: Turn on speaker diarization in the Transcribe job, and put each speaker label in front of that speaker's lines in the prompt, so the model can tell the two voices apart.
Turn on channel identification in the Transcribe job, and put each channel label in front of that channel's lines in the prompt, so the model can tell the two voices apart.
Turn on channel identification in the Transcribe job, and replace the ch_0 label with Doctor and the ch_1 label with Patient in the prompt before the model writes the note.
Add a custom vocabulary table with the clinic's medical terms to the Transcribe job, and pass the improved transcript to the model with no other change to the prompt.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on speaker diarization in the Transcribe job, and put each speaker label in front of that speaker's lines in the prompt, so the model can tell the two voices apart.
Speaker diarization finds the different speakers in one audio track and labels each one, from spk_0 upward. You turn it on with ShowSpeakerLabels and set MaxSpeakerLabels to 2 for the two people in the room. The labels sit in a separate speaker_labels section of the output, not in the plain transcript text. So the pipeline builds the prompt from that section, with the label in front of each line. The model then sees which lines come from one person and which come from the other, and it can work out each role from what that person says.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.2: "Create data processing workflows to handle complex data types including text, image, audio, and tabular data with specialized processing requirements for FM consumption"
Example: "AWS Transcribe"

Sources:

  • Partitioning speakers (diarization)
  • Transcribing multi-channel audio
  • Custom vocabularies

INCORRECT: Turn on channel identification in the Transcribe job, and put each channel label in front of that channel's lines in the prompt, so the model can tell the two voices apart.
Channel identification transcribes each channel of a two-channel recording on its own, with the labels ch_0 and ch_1. It is the right tool when each person speaks on a separate channel, for example a phone call with the caller on one channel and the agent on the other. Here the audio is a single mono track from one microphone, so there is no second channel to separate.

INCORRECT: Turn on channel identification in the Transcribe job, and replace the ch_0 label with Doctor and the ch_1 label with Patient in the prompt before the model writes the note.
In a two-channel recording where the doctor always uses the same channel, a fixed mapping from channel label to role works well. But channel identification is for audio with two channels. This consultation is a single mono track from one microphone, so the labels cannot follow the doctor and the patient.

INCORRECT: Add a custom vocabulary table with the clinic's medical terms to the Transcribe job, and pass the improved transcript to the model with no other change to the prompt.
A custom vocabulary improves how Transcribe writes specific words, such as drug names or other terms that it gets wrong. New vocabularies use the table format, with Phrase and DisplayAs columns. This helps when the transcript has wrong words. Here the transcripts already spell every medical term correctly. The problem is that nothing tells the model who said each line, and a custom vocabulary does not change that.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A logistics company is automating the weekly fine-tuning of a Foundation Model (FM) used to summarize driver delivery logs. The workflow must ingest the new logs from Amazon S3, fine-tune the model, evaluate its accuracy against a golden dataset, and ensure that only models meeting a specific quality threshold are preserved for potential production release. The weekly run happens at night, when no one on the team is at work. A person decides later which kept version goes to production.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: A SageMaker AI pipeline scores the model on the golden dataset in a Processing step. When a Condition step finds the score above the threshold, a Model step registers it in SageMaker Model Registry.
SageMaker Pipelines runs each step as a managed job and tracks the lineage of what each run creates. The Processing step runs the evaluation on the golden dataset and writes the score to a property file. The Condition step reads that score with JsonGet and compares it with the threshold, so the check needs no person during the night run. Only a version that passes reaches the Model step, which registers it in SageMaker Model Registry. AWS recommends the Model step for this job, because the older RegisterModel step is no longer actively supported. The team registers each version with the status PendingManualApproval, so it waits in the registry until a person decides whether it goes to production.

A Lambda step runs an AWS Lambda function inside the pipeline, and the function can update an endpoint. Teams use this for continuous deployment, where every version that passes the tests goes live at once. Here a person decides later which kept version goes to production. This design sends each passing version straight to users and keeps no version in a registry for that decision.

An outside process, such as a review app, answers with SendPipelineExecutionStepSuccess or SendPipelineExecutionStepFailure. This fits a gate where a person must approve each version before registration. Here the run happens at night with no one at work, and the threshold is a fixed value that a Condition step can check with no person.

INCORRECT: A SageMaker AI pipeline scores the model on the golden dataset in a Processing step. When a reviewer approves the score through a Callback step, a Lambda step moves the production endpoint to it.
This design has two problems. The Callback step waits for a reviewer, but the run happens at night when no one is at work. The Lambda step then sends the version to production, although a person must choose later which kept version goes live. Each part fits some other team: a manual gate suits a team that reviews every version, and a direct update suits a team that releases every passing version.

CORRECT: Compare the confidence score of every field in the Data Automation output with a threshold, send forms with a lower score to the review team, and pass the rest on.
A document blueprint in Amazon Bedrock Data Automation returns a confidence score with each field it extracts. The score is the percentage of certainty that Data Automation has that the extraction is right. The company sets a threshold. A form with any field under that score goes to the review team, and every other form goes straight to the claims system. This is a human augmentation pattern: people check only the uncertain results, so the small team spends its time where errors are likely. The score works for every field, including names and addresses, and the company keeps its project and blueprint.

Example: "human augmentation patterns"

  • Best Practices (Amazon Textract Developer Guide)

INCORRECT: Send every form with its Data Automation output to the review team, and pass each form to the claims system only after a reviewer approves its fields.
A person approving every result is the right design when a rule requires a human check on each item, for example before a large payment. Here the review team can check only a few forms each day, and the company wants every other form to go straight to the claims system. Sending all forms to review would build a long queue and delay every claim.

INCORRECT: Check each extracted field in an AWS Lambda function against format and total rules, send forms that fail any rule to the review team, and pass the rest on.
Validation rules in a Lambda function catch values that break a known pattern, such as a date in the wrong format or line amounts that do not add up to the total. They are a good check for fields that have such rules. Here many fields, such as names and street addresses, have no rule that a program can check. A wrong name passes every rule, so that form would skip review.

Amazon Textract queries return an answer and a confidence score for each question about a document. A minimum confidence threshold that flags results for human review is a sound design for a team that extracts fields with Textract. Here the company wants to keep its Data Automation project and blueprint, and this design replaces them with Textract.

The new images carry only generic tags, such as the collection name. The index already uses the model's largest vector size. The model does not represent this new art style well.
Which steps should the GenAI Developer take to fix these search results?
