options.text: Run a model customization job in Amazon Bedrock that fine-tunes Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 on the new images, each paired with a caption that describes it.
Embed every image in the catalog again with the fine-tuned model, rebuild the index, and embed each user query with the same fine-tuned model.
Embed every image in the catalog again with the base model at a larger output vector size, rebuild the index, and embed each query at that size.
Turn on hybrid search in OpenSearch Service, so that each query combines keyword matches on the image metadata with the vector similarity scores.
Raise the k value of each k-NN query, so that every search returns more nearest neighbors for the application to show to the user.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run a model customization job in Amazon Bedrock that fine-tunes Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 on the new images, each paired with a caption that describes it.
Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 supports fine-tuning in Amazon Bedrock, and its training data is image and text pairs. A customization job on the new images and their captions trains the model to place these images close to the words that describe them. The model does not represent the new style well, so the fix must change the model itself.

CORRECT: Embed every image in the catalog again with the fine-tuned model, rebuild the index, and embed each user query with the same fine-tuned model.
A query vector must come from the same embedding model that created the stored vectors. The fine-tuned model is a new model, so its vectors do not match the vectors that the base model created. The team embeds the whole catalog again, rebuilds the index, and embeds each user query with the fine-tuned model. Then all vectors in a search come from one model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.4: "Troubleshoot retrieval system issues to identify and resolve problems that affect information retrieval effectiveness for FM augmentation"
Example: "embedding quality diagnostics"

Sources:

  • Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 model
  • Supported regions and models for model customization
  • Querying vectors

INCORRECT: Embed every image in the catalog again with the base model at a larger output vector size, rebuild the index, and embed each query at that size.
Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 can return vectors of different sizes, and a larger size keeps more detail. Moving to a larger size can help an index that uses a small one. Here the index already uses the largest size that the model offers. The base model also does not represent the new style well, so new vectors from it keep the same problem.

INCORRECT: Turn on hybrid search in OpenSearch Service, so that each query combines keyword matches on the image metadata with the vector similarity scores.
Hybrid search combines a keyword score and a vector score in one query. It helps when the words that users type appear in the metadata, for example in detailed tags or product names. Here the new images carry only generic tags, such as the collection name, so the keyword part of the query finds nothing for "Viscous flow".

INCORRECT: Raise the k value of each k-NN query, so that every search returns more nearest neighbors for the application to show to the user.
The k value sets how many nearest neighbors a k-NN query returns. A larger k helps when the right items rank just below the cutoff. Here the new images do not appear even among the top 200 results. Their vectors sit far from the query vectors, so a longer list of results does not bring them up.

The application layer uses Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda to handle document ingestion, embedding generation, and semantic search queries. The platform must support two customer tiers:

Premium Tier: Consists of 20 large enterprise tenants who require strict data isolation and guaranteed query performance unaffected by other tenants' embedding search workloads ("noisy neighbor" protection).

Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A SaaS provider is building a multi-tenant RAG application using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Service managed domains as the vector database. Fine-grained access control (FGAC) is enabled. The application layer uses Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda to handle document ingestion, embedding generation, and semantic search queries. The platform must support two customer tiers:
Standard Tier: Consists of 5,000+ small tenants with sporadic usage patterns. The primary goal for this tier is cost minimization.
Premium Tier: Consists of 20 large enterprise tenants who require strict data isolation and guaranteed query performance unaffected by other tenants' embedding search workloads ("noisy neighbor" protection).
Which combination of data partitioning and access control strategies should the developer implement to meet these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Implement a Silo model for Premium Tier tenants at the domain level. Provision a dedicated OpenSearch Service domain per tenant, and have Lambda look up each tenant's domain endpoint in a mapping table.
Implement a Pool model for Standard Tier tenants. Store all tenant data in a shared index with a tenant_id field per document, and filter results by tenant with OpenSearch Document Level Security.
Implement a Silo model for Premium Tier tenants at the index level. Provision a dedicated index per tenant inside the shared domain, and have Lambda route each tenant's requests to its own index.

Implement a Silo model for Standard Tier tenants at the domain level. Provision a dedicated OpenSearch Service domain per tenant, and have Lambda look up each tenant's domain endpoint in a mapping table.

Implement a Pool model for Premium Tier tenants. Store all Premium tenant data in a shared index with a tenant_id field per document, and filter results by tenant with OpenSearch Document Level Security.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Implement a Silo model for Premium Tier tenants at the domain level. Provision a dedicated OpenSearch Service domain per tenant, and have Lambda look up each tenant's domain endpoint in a mapping table.
A dedicated domain gives each Premium tenant its own cluster nodes. Compute, memory, and disk are no longer shared, so one tenant's heavy vector search cannot slow another tenant's queries. Each tenant's data also sits in its own domain, apart from all other tenants, which meets the strict isolation requirement. The trade-off is cost and operational effort, because the team scales, patches, and monitors each domain separately. With only 20 Premium tenants, that effort is acceptable. Lambda looks up the tenant's domain endpoint in a mapping table, then sends the request there.

CORRECT: Implement a Pool model for Standard Tier tenants. Store all tenant data in a shared index with a tenant_id field per document, and filter results by tenant with OpenSearch Document Level Security.
A shared index keeps cost low for more than 5,000 small tenants with sporadic usage. One index per tenant does not work well at that scale. Each index adds shards, a domain can hold only a limited number of shards, and small tenants leave most of their shards idle. Here every document carries a tenant_id field, and each tenant's role has a Document Level Security query on that field. OpenSearch then returns only the documents that match the query, so each tenant sees only its own documents. This meets the cost goal and still keeps each tenant's data apart.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.1: "Develop protected AI environments to ensure comprehensive security for FM deployments"

Sources:

  • Fine-grained access control in Amazon OpenSearch Service

  • Storing Multi-Tenant SaaS Data with Amazon OpenSearch Service

INCORRECT: Implement a Silo model for Premium Tier tenants at the index level. Provision a dedicated index per tenant inside the shared domain, and have Lambda route each tenant's requests to its own index.
Index per tenant is a valid silo option, and it does prevent data commingling. However, it does not meet the performance requirement. All Premium indexes still sit on the same cluster nodes. They share CPU, JVM heap, and disk I/O. A large embedding search from one tenant can still degrade query latency for the others, so this does not deliver the noisy neighbor protection the tier demands. Only a dedicated domain gives each tenant separate compute resources.

INCORRECT: Implement a Silo model for Standard Tier tenants at the domain level. Provision a dedicated OpenSearch Service domain per tenant, and have Lambda look up each tenant's domain endpoint in a mapping table.
A domain per tenant gives each tenant its own cluster nodes. It fits large tenants that need strict isolation and steady performance, as the Premium Tier does here. The Standard Tier has more than 5,000 small tenants with sporadic usage, and its main goal is low cost. Each domain bills for its instance hours and storage for as long as it runs, even when its tenant sends no queries. The team would also scale, update, and monitor thousands of domains one by one, and create a new domain for every new tenant.

INCORRECT: Implement a Pool model for Premium Tier tenants. Store all Premium tenant data in a shared index with a tenant_id field per document, and filter results by tenant with OpenSearch Document Level Security.
A shared index with Document Level Security keeps each tenant's documents apart at a low cost. It fits many small tenants whose main goal is cost, as the Standard Tier does here. But all Premium tenants would then search the same index on the same nodes. When one large tenant runs heavy embedding searches, it uses the shared CPU, memory, and disk, and the queries of the other tenants slow down. The Premium Tier requires query performance that other tenants' workloads cannot affect, so a pooled index does not meet it.

A media company allows users to upload screenplays to an Amazon S3 bucket. A GenAI Developer needs to build a pipeline that automatically triggers an Amazon Bedrock summarization job, but only for files stored under the final/ prefix. The solution must decouple the upload process from the inference logic to prevent throttling during traffic bursts. Writers need each summary on the same day as the upload.
Which architectural pattern meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A media company allows users to upload screenplays to an Amazon S3 bucket. A GenAI Developer needs to build a pipeline that automatically triggers an Amazon Bedrock summarization job, but only for files stored under the final/ prefix. The solution must decouple the upload process from the inference logic to prevent throttling during traffic bursts. Writers need each summary on the same day as the upload.
Which architectural pattern meets these requirements?

options.text: Turn on Amazon EventBridge for the bucket, route final/ uploads through a rule on the default event bus to an SQS queue, and set maximum concurrency on the Lambda event source mapping.
Turn on Amazon EventBridge for the bucket, route final/ uploads through a rule on the default event bus to an SQS queue, and set a delivery delay on the queue for each message.
Turn on Amazon EventBridge for the bucket, route final/ uploads through a rule on the default event bus to an SQS queue, and raise the batch size and batch window on the event source mapping.
Turn on Amazon EventBridge for the bucket, route final/ uploads through a rule on the default event bus to an SQS queue, and have Lambda add them to a nightly Amazon Bedrock batch inference job.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on Amazon EventBridge for the bucket, route final/ uploads through a rule on the default event bus to an SQS queue, and set maximum concurrency on the Lambda event source mapping.
When EventBridge is turned on for the bucket, Amazon S3 sends its events to the default event bus. A rule with a prefix match on the object key picks only files under final/, so no filter code is needed. The SQS queue holds every matched event, so uploads never wait for the model. A queue alone does not limit the rate. While many messages wait, Lambda keeps adding concurrent invocations of the function, so the calls to Amazon Bedrock would still rise with the burst. Maximum concurrency on the event source mapping caps how many copies of the function the queue can invoke at the same time. Set it to a value that keeps the Bedrock calls within the quota. The other messages wait in the queue until a copy of the function is free.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.1: "Create enterprise connectivity solutions to seamlessly incorporate FM capabilities into existing enterprise environments"
Example: "event-driven architectures to implement loose coupling"

Sources:

  • Configuring scaling behavior for SQS event source mappings

  • Comparison operators for use in event patterns in Amazon EventBridge

  • Amazon SQS delay queues

INCORRECT: Turn on Amazon EventBridge for the bucket, route final/ uploads through a rule on the default event bus to an SQS queue, and set a delivery delay on the queue for each message.
A delivery delay keeps each new message hidden from consumers for a set time. It fits a consumer that needs extra time before it can process a message. Here the problem is a burst of uploads. Every message in the burst waits the same time, so the burst reaches Lambda a little later but still all at once, and Amazon Bedrock throttles the calls in the same way.

INCORRECT: Turn on Amazon EventBridge for the bucket, route final/ uploads through a rule on the default event bus to an SQS queue, and raise the batch size and batch window on the event source mapping.
A larger batch size and a batch window make Lambda pass more messages to each invocation. This cuts the number of invocations when many small messages arrive. It does not cap concurrency. During a burst, Lambda still adds concurrent invocations while messages wait, and each copy still calls Amazon Bedrock once for every screenplay in its batch, so the throttling continues.

INCORRECT: Turn on Amazon EventBridge for the bucket, route final/ uploads through a rule on the default event bus to an SQS queue, and have Lambda add them to a nightly Amazon Bedrock batch inference job.
Amazon Bedrock batch inference sends many prompts from files in Amazon S3 as one asynchronous job and writes the responses to S3. It fits large sets of documents when nobody waits for the results. A nightly job returns the summaries on the next day, and the writers need each summary on the same day as the upload.

options.text: Use a DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode with UserId as partition key and Timestamp as sort key, one item per turn. Query by UserId with ScanIndexForward set to false and Limit set to 20.
Use a DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode with UserId as partition key and Timestamp as sort key, one item per turn. Query by UserId with ScanIndexForward set to true and Limit set to 20.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use a DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode with UserId as partition key and Timestamp as sort key, one item per turn. Query by UserId with ScanIndexForward set to false and Limit set to 20.
The table stores each turn as its own item. UserId as the partition key keeps one customer's turns together, and Timestamp as the sort key keeps them in time order. Query reads only that customer's items. With ScanIndexForward set to false, DynamoDB reads the items from the newest to the oldest, and Limit stops the read after 20 items, so the agent gets exactly the 20 most recent turns. A new turn is a new small item, however long the history grows. On-demand capacity mode scales with traffic and needs no capacity planning, so holiday sales need no manual capacity work.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.2: "Build interactive AI systems to maintain context and improve user interactions with FMs"
Example: "DynamoDB for conversation history storage"

  • DynamoDB throughput capacity

INCORRECT: Use a DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode with UserId as partition key and Timestamp as sort key, one item per turn. Query by UserId with ScanIndexForward set to true and Limit set to 20.
With ScanIndexForward set to true, which is the default, Query returns the items in ascending sort key order. Limit then stops the read after the 20 oldest turns. That order fits a task that reads a conversation from its start, for example to replay it. Here the agent needs the 20 most recent turns, so it would load turns from the first weeks and miss what the customer said last.

INCORRECT: Use a DynamoDB table with fixed provisioned capacity, UserId as partition key and Timestamp as sort key, one item per turn. Query by UserId with ScanIndexForward set to false and Limit set to 20.
In provisioned capacity mode, the team sets how many reads and writes per second the table serves. It fits steady workloads that the team can forecast. The key design and the query are right. But holiday sales bring sudden high traffic, and with fixed capacity the team must raise the numbers by hand before each sale. The requirement asks for no manual capacity management.

INCORRECT: Use a DynamoDB table with fixed provisioned capacity, UserId as partition key and Timestamp as sort key, one item per turn. Query by UserId with ScanIndexForward set to true and Limit set to 20.
In provisioned capacity mode, the team sets how many reads and writes per second the table serves. With ScanIndexForward set to true, Query returns the items in ascending sort key order, so Limit stops the read after the 20 oldest turns. This pair fits a steady workload that reads each conversation from its start, for example to replay it. Here it fails twice. Holiday sales would need manual capacity work, which the requirements rule out, and the agent would load the first turns instead of the 20 most recent.

An insurance company runs a policy assistant on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store. The assistant calls the RetrieveAndGenerate API, and each answer shows numbered source links next to its sentences. Auditors found two problems. Some links open a passage that says nothing about the sentence beside it. Other answers state policy rules with no link at all. A review showed that the facts in the answers do appear in the retrieved passages, and that the retrieved passages match the questions. The team wants built-in scores only, with no judge prompt to write and maintain.
Which metrics should the team select in an Amazon Bedrock RAG evaluation job?
Select TWO.

options.text: In a retrieve-and-generate job, score each answer with the built-in Citation precision metric, which measures how many of the cited passages were cited correctly.
In a retrieve-and-generate job, score each answer with the built-in Citation coverage metric, which measures how well the cited passages support the answer and finds missing citations.
In a retrieve-and-generate job, score each answer with the built-in Faithfulness metric, which measures how well the answer avoids hallucination with respect to the retrieved passages.
In a retrieve-only job, score each question's results with the built-in Context relevance metric, which measures how relevant the retrieved passages are to the question.
In a retrieve-and-generate job, score each answer with a custom metric whose judge prompt asks whether each linked passage supports the sentence beside it.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: In a retrieve-and-generate job, score each answer with the built-in Citation precision metric, which measures how many of the cited passages were cited correctly.
A retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job scores the answers that the knowledge base and its response model produce. Citation precision is one of its built-in metrics. It checks the passages that an answer cites and measures how many of them were cited correctly. A link that opens a passage with nothing about the sentence beside it is a wrong citation, so it lowers the score. This matches the first problem the auditors found, and the team can see whether a fix raises the score.

CORRECT: In a retrieve-and-generate job, score each answer with the built-in Citation coverage metric, which measures how well the cited passages support the answer and finds missing citations.
Citation coverage measures the second problem. It checks how well the cited passages support the whole answer, and whether citations are missing. An answer that states a policy rule with no link at all scores low, even when the rule is true. Together, the two citation metrics measure both problems with built-in scores, so the team writes no judge prompt.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.5: "Develop comprehensive assessment systems to ensure thorough evaluation from multiple perspectives for FM outputs"
Example: "RAG evaluation"

Sources:

  • Use metrics to understand RAG system performance
  • Evaluate the performance of RAG sources using Amazon Bedrock evaluations
  • Amazon Bedrock RAG and Model Evaluations now support custom metrics

INCORRECT: In a retrieve-and-generate job, score each answer with the built-in Faithfulness metric, which measures how well the answer avoids hallucination with respect to the retrieved passages.
Faithfulness fits a team whose answers add facts that no retrieved passage holds. Here the review showed that the facts in the answers do appear in the retrieved passages. Faithfulness would score these answers high, because it does not check which passage each link points to, or whether a sentence has a link at all.

INCORRECT: In a retrieve-only job, score each question's results with the built-in Context relevance metric, which measures how relevant the retrieved passages are to the question.
A retrieve-only job tests only the retrieval step, with no generated answer. Context relevance finds retrieval that brings back text that does not fit the question. The review showed that the retrieved passages match the questions. The problems sit in the links of the generated answers, and a retrieve-only job never sees those answers.

INCORRECT: In a retrieve-and-generate job, score each answer with a custom metric whose judge prompt asks whether each linked passage supports the sentence beside it.
A custom metric lets a team write its own judge prompt and rating scale, and the evaluator model scores each answer with that prompt. It fits a quality check that no built-in metric covers. Here built-in metrics already measure both problems. The team wants built-in scores only, with no judge prompt to write and maintain.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company hosts an open-weight LLM on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for its contact center. A target tracking policy in Application Auto Scaling scales the endpoint, and the maximum instance count equals the usual daytime need. The center opens at 08:00 on weekdays, and traffic rises within minutes to four times the night level. The policy starts to add instances within two minutes, but each new instance needs several minutes to load the model, so agents wait every morning. At night, the company must not pay for daytime capacity. Campaigns sometimes push traffic above the daytime level at unknown times, and a short wait is accepted then.
Which changes should the team make to the endpoint's scaling?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company hosts an open-weight LLM on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for its contact center. A target tracking policy in Application Auto Scaling scales the endpoint, and the maximum instance count equals the usual daytime need. The center opens at 08:00 on weekdays, and traffic rises within minutes to four times the night level. The policy starts to add instances within two minutes, but each new instance needs several minutes to load the model, so agents wait every morning. At night, the company must not pay for daytime capacity. Campaigns sometimes push traffic above the daytime level at unknown times, and a short wait is accepted then.
Which changes should the team make to the endpoint's scaling?
Select TWO.

options.text: Add two recurring scheduled actions for the scalable target: one raises the minimum instance count before 08:00 on weekdays, and one lowers it after closing time.
Raise the maximum instance count of the scalable target above the usual daytime need, so the target tracking policy can add instances on campaign days.
Raise the minimum instance count of the scalable target to the usual daytime need for all hours, so loaded instances are ready before calls arrive.
Lower the target value of the target tracking policy, so the policy starts to add instances at a smaller number of invocations per instance.
Add a step scaling policy beside the target tracking policy, so the endpoint adds several instances at once when traffic passes the usual daytime need.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add two recurring scheduled actions for the scalable target: one raises the minimum instance count before 08:00 on weekdays, and one lowers it after closing time.
Scheduled scaling in Application Auto Scaling changes the capacity limits of a scalable target at set times, and a recurring schedule repeats on every weekday. When the minimum instance count rises before 08:00, the endpoint adds instances early, so they have time to load the model before the calls arrive. The second action lowers the minimum after closing time, so the endpoint can scale in again and the company does not pay for daytime capacity at night. The target tracking policy keeps working between the limits that the schedule sets.

CORRECT: Raise the maximum instance count of the scalable target above the usual daytime need, so the target tracking policy can add instances on campaign days.
The maximum instance count is the highest capacity that the scaling policy can reach. Today it equals the usual daytime need, so on a campaign day the policy cannot add any instance above that level. A higher maximum lets the target tracking policy react when a campaign pushes traffic higher at a time nobody knows in advance. The new instances still need minutes to load the model, and the question accepts a short wait on those days.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.5: "Create efficient resource allocation systems specifically for FM workloads"
Example: "auto-scaling configurations that are optimized for GenAI traffic patterns"

Sources:

  • Scheduled scaling for Application Auto Scaling

  • Auto scaling policy overview

  • Introducing Fast Model Loader in SageMaker Inference: Accelerate autoscaling for your Large Language Models (LLMs), part 1

INCORRECT: Raise the minimum instance count of the scalable target to the usual daytime need for all hours, so loaded instances are ready before calls arrive.
A higher minimum at all hours keeps loaded instances ready before any rise in traffic. It fits a service that is busy around the clock. Here few people call at night, and the company must not pay for daytime capacity then, so the extra instances would run for many hours with no need.

INCORRECT: Lower the target value of the target tracking policy, so the policy starts to add instances at a smaller number of invocations per instance.
A lower target value fits a policy that starts to scale out too late. Here the policy already starts within two minutes of the rise. The wait comes from the minutes that each new instance needs to load the model, and a lower target does not shorten that time. It would also keep extra instances running for the whole day.

INCORRECT: Add a step scaling policy beside the target tracking policy, so the endpoint adds several instances at once when traffic passes the usual daytime need.
Step scaling adds a set number of instances when a metric passes a threshold, so it fits traffic that jumps in large steps. But every scaling policy must keep the capacity between the minimum and the maximum instance count of the scalable target. The maximum equals the usual daytime need, so on a campaign day the step scaling policy could not add any instance above that level either.

A financial services firm is building an internal "Analyst Assistant" using a Generative AI agent. The agent uses Amazon Athena to query a data lake stored in Amazon S3 and registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. The dataset includes a Transaction_ID, Merchant, Date, and a highly sensitive Customer_PAN (Primary Account Number) column. The security team requires that the IAM role assumed by the agent must be technically blocked from retrieving any data from the Customer_PAN column, while maintaining full access to the rest of the dataset for analysis. The agent reads the data only through Athena.
Which solution should the developer implement to enforce this column-level restriction?
questions.promptText:
A financial services firm is building an internal "Analyst Assistant" using a Generative AI agent. The agent uses Amazon Athena to query a data lake stored in Amazon S3 and registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. The dataset includes a Transaction_ID, Merchant, Date, and a highly sensitive Customer_PAN (Primary Account Number) column. The security team requires that the IAM role assumed by the agent must be technically blocked from retrieving any data from the Customer_PAN column, while maintaining full access to the rest of the dataset for analysis. The agent reads the data only through Athena.
Which solution should the developer implement to enforce this column-level restriction?

options.text: Register the data lake location with AWS Lake Formation, create a data filter with all rows that excludes the Customer_PAN column, and grant SELECT with that filter to the agent's role.
Use AWS Lake Formation row-level security on the table, with the expression Customer_PAN IS NULL, so the agent's role can SELECT the rows that have no card number.
Apply an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the agent's model calls with a sensitive information filter that masks credit and debit card numbers in every answer.
Apply an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the agent's model calls with a sensitive information filter that blocks any answer with a credit or debit card number.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Register the data lake location with AWS Lake Formation, create a data filter with all rows that excludes the Customer_PAN column, and grant SELECT with that filter to the agent's role.
Lake Formation data filters give column-level security. A filter that includes all rows and excludes one column lets the role read every row and every other column. The filter takes effect when Lake Formation grants SELECT to the agent's role, and Athena applies it to each query. So the role can analyze transactions, merchants, and dates, but it has no permission on Customer_PAN. The agent reads the data only through Athena, so this grant covers every path the agent has to the data.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.1: "Develop protected AI environments to ensure comprehensive security for FM deployments"
Example: "AWS Lake Formation to provide granular data access"

Sources:

  • Data filters in Lake Formation

  • Data filtering and cell-level security in Lake Formation

  • Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters

INCORRECT: Use AWS Lake Formation row-level security on the table, with the expression Customer_PAN IS NULL, so the agent's role can SELECT the rows that have no card number.
A row filter expression chooses which rows a role can read, like a WHERE clause. It fits a rule such as showing each analyst only the rows of one region. Customer_PAN IS NULL keeps only the rows that have no card number. Almost every transaction has one, so the agent would lose most of the data, and the requirement asks for full access to the rest of the dataset. The filter also keeps the column itself visible.

INCORRECT: Apply an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the agent's model calls with a sensitive information filter that masks credit and debit card numbers in every answer.
A sensitive information filter in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails finds personal data, such as credit and debit card numbers, in model input and output, and it can mask them. It fits a chat application that must not show card numbers to its users. Here the rule is that the agent's role must be blocked from retrieving the column at all. With a guardrail, Athena still returns the card numbers to the agent, and the filter only hides them later in the answers.

INCORRECT: Apply an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the agent's model calls with a sensitive information filter that blocks any answer with a credit or debit card number.
The Block action of a sensitive information filter stops a whole response when it contains a card number. It fits a rule that no answer with a card number may reach users at all. Here the rule is about retrieval: the agent's role must be blocked from reading the column. With a guardrail, Athena still returns every card number to the agent, and the filter acts only on what the model writes. The block would also stop useful answers instead of only hiding one value.

A legal services company fine-tuned an open-weight model with Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs. The weights are stored in Amazon S3 in Hugging Face safetensors format, and Amazon Bedrock supports the model's architecture. The quality team approved exactly these weights. An internal drafting tool will use the model a few times a week, at times nobody can predict, and the model needs GPUs to answer in time. The platform team has no one to choose instance types, write scaling policies, or patch servers. The company wants no compute charges while nobody uses the tool. After a quiet period, a wait of a few minutes for the first answer is accepted.
Which deployment option meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A legal services company fine-tuned an open-weight model with Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs. The weights are stored in Amazon S3 in Hugging Face safetensors format, and Amazon Bedrock supports the model's architecture. The quality team approved exactly these weights. An internal drafting tool will use the model a few times a week, at times nobody can predict, and the model needs GPUs to answer in time. The platform team has no one to choose instance types, write scaling policies, or patch servers. The company wants no compute charges while nobody uses the tool. After a quiet period, a wait of a few minutes for the first answer is accepted.
Which deployment option meets these requirements?

options.text: Import the weights from Amazon S3 with Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, and have the tool call the imported model on demand with InvokeModel.
Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint, and set its memory size and maximum concurrency to fit the tool's traffic.
Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with inference components, and set up auto scaling that scales it to zero instances.
Run an Amazon Bedrock fine-tuning job on a supported base model with the same training data, and have the tool call the new custom model.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Import the weights from Amazon S3 with Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, and have the tool call the imported model on demand with InvokeModel.
Custom Model Import brings a model that was customized in another environment, such as SageMaker AI, into Amazon Bedrock. It reads the model files in Hugging Face safetensors format from Amazon S3, and the model's architecture must be one that Bedrock supports, which the question states. The tool then calls the model on demand with InvokeModel, and nobody chooses instances or writes scaling policies. Compute charges run only while a copy of the model is active, and Bedrock scales the copies to zero when no calls arrive for a short time. Bedrock still charges a monthly fee to store the imported model, but that is not a compute charge. After a quiet period, the next call can return ModelNotReadyException while Bedrock restores the model. By default, the SDK retries such calls with exponential backoff, so the first answer can take a few minutes, which the company accepts.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.2.1: "Deploy FMs based on specific application needs and performance requirements"

Sources:

  • Use Custom model import to import a customized open-source model into Amazon Bedrock
  • Invoke your imported model
  • Deploy models with Amazon SageMaker Serverless Inference

INCORRECT: Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint, and set its memory size and maximum concurrency to fit the tool's traffic.
Serverless Inference starts compute when requests arrive and scales down to zero when none arrive, so nobody chooses instance types. It fits a small model with rare or unpredictable traffic. It does not support GPUs, and this model needs GPUs to answer in time.

INCORRECT: Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with inference components, and set up auto scaling that scales it to zero instances.
A real-time endpoint that hosts inference components can scale to zero instances when it is idle, so compute charges stop. It fits a team that wants to control the hardware and the scaling. The team must choose the GPU instance type, and it must set up a step scaling policy and an alarm that start an instance again when requests arrive. The platform team has no one to do that work.

INCORRECT: Run an Amazon Bedrock fine-tuning job on a supported base model with the same training data, and have the tool call the new custom model.
Amazon Bedrock can fine-tune a supported base model with a company's own data and create a new custom model. This fits a team that has not trained its model yet. Here the model is already trained, and the quality team approved exactly those weights. A new fine-tuning job makes a different model that nobody has approved.

The business has outlined the following critical requirements:
1. Performance: The application must handle a steady stream of 500 requests per minute with guaranteed capacity and predictable, low latency during market hours.
2. Security: All network traffic between the application VPC and the AI model must remain entirely within the AWS network and never traverse the public internet. Calls must never go to a public Amazon Bedrock endpoint.
Which architectural design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A financial services firm is designing a generative AI application to analyze proprietary market data. The application requires access to a specific proprietary Foundation Model (FM) available only on Amazon Bedrock. The chosen model offers Provisioned Throughput.
The business has outlined the following critical requirements:
1. Performance: The application must handle a steady stream of 500 requests per minute with guaranteed capacity and predictable, low latency during market hours.
2. Security: All network traffic between the application VPC and the AI model must remain entirely within the AWS network and never traverse the public internet. Calls must never go to a public Amazon Bedrock endpoint.
Which architectural design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create Provisioned Throughput with model units for the model, and create an interface VPC endpoint for the Amazon Bedrock runtime with private DNS turned on.
Create Provisioned Throughput with model units for the model, and add a NAT gateway so the private subnets can reach the public Amazon Bedrock runtime endpoint.
Use the model in on-demand mode with no reserved capacity, and create an interface VPC endpoint for the Amazon Bedrock runtime with private DNS turned on.
Use the model in on-demand mode with no reserved capacity, and add a NAT gateway so the private subnets can reach the public Amazon Bedrock runtime endpoint.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create Provisioned Throughput with model units for the model, and create an interface VPC endpoint for the Amazon Bedrock runtime with private DNS turned on.
Provisioned Throughput sets aside model units for one model. Each model unit processes a set number of input and output tokens per minute, so the application has a fixed level of throughput for its steady stream of requests during market hours. An interface VPC endpoint gives the Amazon Bedrock runtime private IP addresses inside the VPC. With private DNS turned on, the application keeps calling the default Regional Bedrock name, and the calls go to the endpoint. Interface endpoints work through DNS, not through route table entries, and the application needs no internet gateway and no NAT device to reach Amazon Bedrock.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.2.1: "Deploy FMs based on specific application needs and performance requirements"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock provisioned throughput configurations"

Sources:

  • Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput in Amazon Bedrock
  • Use interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) to create a private connection between your VPC and Amazon Bedrock
  • Gateway endpoints

INCORRECT: Create Provisioned Throughput with model units for the model, and add a NAT gateway so the private subnets can reach the public Amazon Bedrock runtime endpoint.
A NAT gateway lets instances in a private subnet connect to services outside the VPC. It fits calls to a service that offers no VPC endpoint. Provisioned Throughput meets the capacity need, but the calls would go to the public Amazon Bedrock endpoint, and the requirements say calls must never go to a public Bedrock endpoint.

INCORRECT: Use the model in on-demand mode with no reserved capacity, and create an interface VPC endpoint for the Amazon Bedrock runtime with private DNS turned on.
In on-demand mode, the application calls the model without any model units. It fits traffic that changes a lot or stays low. The interface endpoint meets the security requirement. But on-demand mode sets aside no capacity for the model, and the application needs guaranteed capacity for a steady stream of requests during market hours.

INCORRECT: Use the model in on-demand mode with no reserved capacity, and add a NAT gateway so the private subnets can reach the public Amazon Bedrock runtime endpoint.
In on-demand mode, the application calls the model without any model units, and a NAT gateway lets instances in private subnets connect to services outside the VPC. This pair fits a small application with changing traffic that calls a service with no VPC endpoint. Here it fails both requirements. On-demand mode sets aside no capacity for the steady stream during market hours, and the calls would go to the public Amazon Bedrock endpoint, which the requirements forbid.

questions.promptHtml:
A legal technology company is building a generative AI application to draft contract clauses. The application must utilize a repository of 200,000 proprietary legal documents that is updated with new case files every night.
The Chief Legal Officer has set the following strict requirements:
1. Attribution: Every generated clause must include a direct citation to the specific case file it was derived from.
2. Freshness: The model must incorporate data from documents added to the repository within the last 24 hours.
3. Accuracy: The solution must minimize hallucinations and strictly adhere to the facts present in the proprietary documents.
Which architectural strategy should the GenAI engineer implement to meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A legal technology company is building a generative AI application to draft contract clauses. The application must utilize a repository of 200,000 proprietary legal documents that is updated with new case files every night.
The Chief Legal Officer has set the following strict requirements:
1. Attribution: Every generated clause must include a direct citation to the specific case file it was derived from.
2. Freshness: The model must incorporate data from documents added to the repository within the last 24 hours.
3. Accuracy: The solution must minimize hallucinations and strictly adhere to the facts present in the proprietary documents.
Which architectural strategy should the GenAI engineer implement to meet these requirements?

options.text: Use an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on the repository, start an ingestion job after each nightly update, and draft clauses with RetrieveAndGenerate, which returns citations to the source files.
Use an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on the repository, start an ingestion job once each weekend, and draft clauses with RetrieveAndGenerate, which returns citations to the source files.
Fine-tune an Amazon Nova Lite model on the full repository with Amazon Bedrock model customization, and draft clauses with the newest version of the custom model.
Send the full text of the whole repository in each request to a model with a long context window, and ask the model to name the source file of each clause.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on the repository, start an ingestion job after each nightly update, and draft clauses with RetrieveAndGenerate, which returns citations to the source files.
A knowledge base keeps the case files outside the model. For each request, it finds the chunks that match, and the model writes the clause from those chunks, so the answer comes from the company's own documents. This knowledge base does not pick up new files on its own. Each time the company adds, changes or removes files, it must sync the data source, for example with the StartIngestionJob operation. A job after each nightly update puts the new case files in the index within 24 hours. The sync is incremental, so each job processes only the files added, changed or deleted since the last sync. RetrieveAndGenerate returns citations with its answer. Each citation links a part of the generated text to the source chunks and their location, such as the S3 URI of the case file, so every clause can name the file it came from.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.3: "Develop accuracy verification systems to reduce hallucinations in FM responses"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base to ground responses and perform fact-checking"

Sources:

  • Sync your data with your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base
  • RetrieveAndGenerate

INCORRECT: Use an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on the repository, start an ingestion job once each weekend, and draft clauses with RetrieveAndGenerate, which returns citations to the source files.
This is the same design with a weekly sync. A weekly sync fits a repository that changes once a week or less. Here new case files arrive every night, and the Chief Legal Officer wants documents from the last 24 hours in the answers. A case file added on a Monday night would stay out of the index until the weekend.

INCORRECT: Fine-tune an Amazon Nova Lite model on the full repository with Amazon Bedrock model customization, and draft clauses with the newest version of the custom model.
Fine-tuning trains a model on example records so that it learns a task or a style, for example the wording and structure of the firm's clauses. The training changes the model's weights, and the weights do not record where a fact came from. The custom model cannot point to the case file that a clause came from, so it fails the attribution requirement. A model that writes from its weights can also state facts that are in no document.

INCORRECT: Send the full text of the whole repository in each request to a model with a long context window, and ask the model to name the source file of each clause.
Putting whole documents in the prompt works when a request needs only a few of them, such as one contract and its annexes. This repository holds 200,000 documents. They cannot fit in one context window, and sending them with every request would cost a great deal in input tokens. Even with fewer files, nothing would link the model's answer to a real source, so the file names it writes could be wrong.

How should the company add the title suggestions?

A retail company's web app and mobile app call an AWS AppSync GraphQL API. Users sign in through an Amazon Cognito user pool, and the API uses it for authorization.
The company wants a new query that returns a short product title suggestion from a model in Amazon Bedrock. Each title is a few words, and the model returns it in about two seconds. The model is available in the API's Region.
All client traffic must keep going through the existing GraphQL API. The team does not want to write or run any Lambda functions for this feature. Each suggestion must arrive in the response to the query that asked for it.
How should the company add the title suggestions?

options.text: Add an Amazon Bedrock runtime data source to the GraphQL API, and attach a JavaScript resolver to the new query that calls Converse and returns the title in the response.
Add an AWS Lambda data source to the GraphQL API, and attach it to the new query with a function that calls Converse and returns the title in the response.
Give each app temporary AWS credentials from an Amazon Cognito identity pool, and have the app call Converse with the AWS SDK and show the returned title.
Add an Amazon EventBridge data source to the GraphQL API that puts each request on the default event bus, where a rule starts a Step Functions workflow that calls InvokeModel.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add an Amazon Bedrock runtime data source to the GraphQL API, and attach a JavaScript resolver to the new query that calls Converse and returns the title in the response.
AWS AppSync can use the Amazon Bedrock runtime as a data source. A JavaScript resolver on the new query calls Converse or InvokeModel directly, with no Lambda function in between, and the model's answer goes back in the query response. The apps keep calling the same GraphQL API with the same Cognito sign-in. AppSync supports only short synchronous calls to Amazon Bedrock, and it cannot call the stream APIs. That fits here: each title is a few words, it arrives in about two seconds, and the app shows the whole title when it arrives. The resolver can call only models and inference profiles in the Region of the API, and the model is available there.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.1: "Create flexible model interaction systems"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock APIs to manage synchronous requests from various compute environments"

Sources:

  • AWS AppSync JavaScript resolver and function reference for Amazon Bedrock runtime
  • AWS AppSync launches AI gateway capabilities with new Amazon Bedrock integration in AppSync GraphQL
  • Invoke and customize Amazon Bedrock models with Step Functions

INCORRECT: Add an AWS Lambda data source to the GraphQL API, and attach it to the new query with a function that calls Converse and returns the title in the response.
A Lambda data source runs a function for the resolver. The function can call Amazon Bedrock and also run extra steps before or after the model call, such as reading data from other systems. This design would work, but the team does not want to write or run any Lambda functions for this feature.

INCORRECT: Give each app temporary AWS credentials from an Amazon Cognito identity pool, and have the app call Converse with the AWS SDK and show the returned title.
An identity pool gives each user temporary AWS credentials, and the app can use them to sign requests to AWS services with the SDK, including Converse. Mobile and web apps use this pattern to call AWS services directly. Here all client traffic must keep going through the existing GraphQL API. With this design, the apps would call Amazon Bedrock directly, and those calls would not pass through the GraphQL API.

INCORRECT: Add an Amazon EventBridge data source to the GraphQL API that puts each request on the default event bus, where a rule starts a Step Functions workflow that calls InvokeModel.
An EventBridge data source lets a resolver put events on an event bus. A rule on the default event bus can start a Step Functions workflow, and Step Functions can call InvokeModel through its optimized Amazon Bedrock integration. This fits long jobs where the client does not wait and reads the result later. Here each suggestion must arrive in the response to the query that asked for it. The event only starts the work, so the query returns before the model writes the title.

An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base in that Region answers staff questions. It uses an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region as its data source, and it syncs every morning. Answers must stop using a deleted policy by the next morning.

questions.promptText:
A company must keep its HR policy documents inside its home country, and its rules allow only an AWS Region in that country. The documents sit on an SMB file share in the company's data center. HR staff add, change and delete files there every day.
An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base in that Region answers staff questions. It uses an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region as its data source, and it syncs every morning. Answers must stop using a deleted policy by the next morning.
The company can add new servers in the data center, but it allows no new software or scheduled jobs on the file server itself.
Which combination of steps should the company take?
Select TWO.

options.text: Deploy an AWS DataSync agent as a virtual machine in the data center, and create an SMB location for the file share and an S3 location for the bucket.
Create a DataSync task between the two locations that runs every night, copies the files that changed since the last run, and removes files from the bucket that are gone from the share.
Create a DataSync task between the two locations that runs every night, copies the files that changed since the last run, and keeps files in the bucket that are gone from the share.
Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP server that stores files in the bucket, and add a nightly job on the file server that uploads new and changed files over SFTP.
Create a DataSync task between the two locations, run it once to copy the whole share, and start one knowledge base ingestion job when the copy finishes.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Deploy an AWS DataSync agent as a virtual machine in the data center, and create an SMB location for the file share and an S3 location for the bucket.
AWS DataSync reaches storage that a company runs itself, such as an on-premises SMB file server, through an agent. The agent is a virtual machine appliance that runs in the company's storage environment, and it connects to the file server over SMB. So the file server itself runs nothing new. An SMB location tells DataSync how to reach the share, and an S3 location names the bucket in the allowed Region, so the files go only to that Region.

CORRECT: Create a DataSync task between the two locations that runs every night, copies the files that changed since the last run, and removes files from the bucket that are gone from the share.
A DataSync task moves data from a source location to a destination location, and a schedule runs it at a set time, such as every night. When the task transfers only changed data, each run after the first copies just the files and metadata that differ between the share and the bucket. By default, DataSync keeps files in the destination that no longer exist at the source. This task removes them instead, so a policy that HR deletes also leaves the bucket that night. The knowledge base sync the next morning then removes it from the index, because each sync processes added, changed and deleted documents.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.4: "Develop cross-environment AI solutions to ensure data compliance across jurisdictions while enabling FM access"

Sources:

  • Configuring AWS DataSync transfers with an SMB file server

  • Configuring how to handle files, objects, and metadata

  • Scheduling when your AWS DataSync task runs

INCORRECT: Create a DataSync task between the two locations that runs every night, copies the files that changed since the last run, and keeps files in the bucket that are gone from the share.
This task matches the correct one in every setting except one: it keeps files in the bucket after they are deleted from the share. That is the DataSync default, and it fits a destination that must keep old files, such as a backup copy. Here a policy that HR deletes would stay in the bucket, and the knowledge base would keep using it, which breaks the rule for deleted policies.

INCORRECT: Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP server that stores files in the bucket, and add a nightly job on the file server that uploads new and changed files over SFTP.
AWS Transfer Family runs a managed SFTP server that saves the files that clients send into Amazon S3. It fits partners or teams that already send files with an SFTP client. Here a job on the file server would have to send the files each night, and the company allows no new software or scheduled jobs on the file server.

INCORRECT: Create a DataSync task between the two locations, run it once to copy the whole share, and start one knowledge base ingestion job when the copy finishes.
One DataSync run and one ingestion job fit a one-time move, for example when a company retires a file server and keeps only the copy in AWS. HR changes the files every day. After the first run, no new, changed or deleted file on the share would reach the bucket or the knowledge base.

questions.promptHtml:
A large company is scaling its use of generative AI. Each project runs in its own AWS account, and every team defines its infrastructure as code with the AWS CDK. All prompts and responses are short text. An internal audit finds that teams log model calls in different ways. Some teams write raw prompts with personally identifiable information (PII) to plain text logs, and other teams turned logging off. The company now sets one standard, based on the AWS Well-Architected Framework Generative AI Lens. Every project logs its prompts and responses, and the logs mask PII.

How can the lead GenAI developer give every team a ready-made setup that meets this standard, with the least extra work for developers?
questions.promptText:
A large company is scaling its use of generative AI. Each project runs in its own AWS account, and every team defines its infrastructure as code with the AWS CDK. All prompts and responses are short text. An internal audit finds that teams log model calls in different ways. Some teams write raw prompts with personally identifiable information (PII) to plain text logs, and other teams turned logging off. The company now sets one standard, based on the AWS Well-Architected Framework Generative AI Lens. Every project logs its prompts and responses, and the logs mask PII.
How can the lead GenAI developer give every team a ready-made setup that meets this standard, with the least extra work for developers?

options.text: Publish AWS CDK constructs to AWS CodeArtifact that turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to a CloudWatch Logs log group with a data protection policy that masks PII.
Create a custom lens in the AWS Well-Architected Tool with questions on PII masking and logging, and make each deployment pipeline wait until an architect approves the lens review of the workload.
Publish AWS CDK constructs to AWS CodeArtifact that turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to a CloudWatch Logs log group with a retention period of one day.
Turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging in each project account, send the logs to an Amazon S3 bucket, and encrypt the bucket with a customer managed AWS KMS key.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Publish AWS CDK constructs to AWS CodeArtifact that turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to a CloudWatch Logs log group with a data protection policy that masks PII.
AWS CDK constructs are reusable components that represent AWS CloudFormation resources and their settings. Every team here already uses the AWS CDK, so each team can add the shared constructs like any other library package from AWS CodeArtifact, a managed package repository. Model invocation logging is off by default. It records the request and response data of Amazon Bedrock calls in one account and Region. The constructs deploy with each project, so each project turns on logging in its own account and Region. A log event in CloudWatch Logs contains request and response bodies of up to 100 KB, and larger bodies need an Amazon S3 destination. The prompts and responses here are short text, so each log event contains the full prompt and response. The log group has a data protection policy, which masks PII when each log event arrives. Only users with the logs:Unmask permission can see the original values.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.1.3: "Create standardized technical components to ensure consistent implementation across multiple deployment scenarios"

Sources:

  • AWS CDK Constructs

  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3

  • Help protect sensitive log data with masking

INCORRECT: Create a custom lens in the AWS Well-Architected Tool with questions on PII masking and logging, and make each deployment pipeline wait until an architect approves the lens review of the workload.
A custom lens adds a company's own questions and best practices to Well-Architected reviews. It fits a company that wants to check workloads against its internal standards and track progress over time. A lens review asks questions about a workload, but it gives teams no ready-made setup. Each team must still build its own logging and PII masking. The approval step also stops every pipeline until an architect has time for the review, which adds work and waiting for every team.

INCORRECT: Publish AWS CDK constructs to AWS CodeArtifact that turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to a CloudWatch Logs log group with a retention period of one day.
These constructs give every team a ready-made setup, and every project now logs its prompts and responses. A short retention period fits a team that needs recent request data for troubleshooting and wants to keep little of it. But this log group has no data protection policy. Each log event shows the raw prompt with its PII for a full day, and the standard says that the logs mask PII.

INCORRECT: Turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging in each project account, send the logs to an Amazon S3 bucket, and encrypt the bucket with a customer managed AWS KMS key.
Invocation logs in an S3 bucket with a customer managed KMS key fit a company that must keep long records of model calls and control who can decrypt them. Encryption protects the files from people who have no access to the key. Anyone who can read the logs still sees each raw prompt with its PII, so the logs do not mask PII. Someone must also turn on the logging in each project account, and again for every new project, so this is not a ready-made setup that teams reuse.
