A company's claims app runs on AWS Lambda. Customers upload a PDF claim letter and ask a question about it. Today the function extracts the text with an open-source library and sends only that text to a model in Amazon Bedrock through the Converse API. The library fails on some letters, and the team must keep updating its code.
The team wants the model to read each PDF file itself, with no extraction or conversion step. The chosen model supports document input in Converse. Security rules do not allow the app to store customer files anywhere. Customer file names often hold underscores and periods.
Which combination of steps should the team take to build each request?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company's claims app runs on AWS Lambda. Customers upload a PDF claim letter and ask a question about it. Today the function extracts the text with an open-source library and sends only that text to a model in Amazon Bedrock through the Converse API. The library fails on some letters, and the team must keep updating its code.
The team wants the model to read each PDF file itself, with no extraction or conversion step. The chosen model supports document input in Converse. Security rules do not allow the app to store customer files anywhere. Customer file names often hold underscores and periods.
Which combination of steps should the team take to build each request?
Select TWO.

options.text: Add a document block to the user message with the format pdf, the file bytes as the source, and a plain name that the app sets, such as Claim letter.
Add a text block that holds the customer's question to the same user message as the document block, so the request carries the file and the question together.
Add a document block to the user message with the format pdf, the file bytes as the source, and the customer's original file name as the name.
Convert each page of the PDF to a PNG image in the function, and add one image block per page to the user message with the customer's question.
Upload the PDF to an Amazon S3 bucket, and add a document block to the user message with the format pdf and the S3 location of the file as the source.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a document block to the user message with the format pdf, the file bytes as the source, and a plain name that the app sets, such as Claim letter.
In the Converse API, a document block adds a file to a user message. The block holds the format, such as pdf, a name, and the source, and the source can be the raw bytes of the file. The model then reads the PDF itself, so the function needs no extraction or conversion step, and the file stays in memory for the request. The name may use only letters, numbers, single spaces, hyphens, parentheses and square brackets, so a plain name that the app sets always passes. A neutral name is also safer, because the model might read text in the name as an instruction.

CORRECT: Add a text block that holds the customer's question to the same user message as the document block, so the request carries the file and the question together.
When a user message holds a document block, it must also hold a text block. Here the text block carries the customer's question, so the model knows what to look for in the letter. A request with a document block and no text block in the message fails. Documents and images can appear only in messages with the user role, so both blocks go in the same user message.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.3: "Format input data for FM inference according to model-specific requirements"
Example: "JSON formatting for Amazon Bedrock API requests"

Sources:

  • Inference using Converse API

  • DocumentBlock

  • Message

INCORRECT: Add a document block to the user message with the format pdf, the file bytes as the source, and the customer's original file name as the name.
This block has the right format and source, and it fits files whose names the company controls and that use only the allowed characters. Here customer file names often hold underscores and periods, and the name field does not allow them, so many requests would fail. A name that a customer wrote could also hold text that the model reads as an instruction.

INCORRECT: Convert each page of the PDF to a PNG image in the function, and add one image block per page to the user message with the customer's question.
Image blocks carry pictures, such as PNG files, in a user message, and a model that accepts images reads the content of each picture. Turning pages into images fits a model that takes images but not documents. Here the chosen model supports document input, and the team wants no conversion step. This design adds one, because the function must turn every page into a PNG image before each call.

INCORRECT: Upload the PDF to an Amazon S3 bucket, and add a document block to the user message with the format pdf and the S3 location of the file as the source.
A document block can point to a file in Amazon S3 instead of carrying its bytes, for the models that support S3 locations. It fits files that are already stored in a bucket. Here the security rules do not allow the app to store customer files, and this design writes every letter to a bucket before the call.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A media company uses a generative AI application to summarize news articles. The application runs on AWS Lambda, and an Amazon SQS queue invokes the function for each new article. The application currently uses Amazon Nova Lite. The product team wants to perform an A/B test by routing 10% of the production traffic to Claude Haiku to evaluate if the summary quality justifies the cost difference. They require the ability to change this percentage within minutes, for example to 20% or back to 0%, without triggering a new CI/CD deployment or modifying the Lambda function code.
Which solution meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A media company uses a generative AI application to summarize news articles. The application runs on AWS Lambda, and an Amazon SQS queue invokes the function for each new article. The application currently uses Amazon Nova Lite. The product team wants to perform an A/B test by routing 10% of the production traffic to Claude Haiku to evaluate if the summary quality justifies the cost difference. They require the ability to change this percentage within minutes, for example to 20% or back to 0%, without triggering a new CI/CD deployment or modifying the Lambda function code.
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS AppConfig multi-variant feature flag whose split rule sends 10% to a Claude Haiku variant, and read it through the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension, passing the article ID.
Create a basic AWS AppConfig feature flag that sends all requests to Claude Haiku when the flag is on, and read it through the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension in the function.
Put an Amazon API Gateway REST API in front of the function, and create a canary release on its stage with a stage variable override that sends 10% to Claude Haiku.
Run an Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job for each model on a sample of past articles, and compare the summary scores before choosing a model for production.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an AWS AppConfig multi-variant feature flag whose split rule sends 10% to a Claude Haiku variant, and read it through the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension, passing the article ID.
A multi-variant feature flag in AWS AppConfig holds several variants, here one for Amazon Nova Lite and one for Claude Haiku. A rule with the split operator sends a set percentage of traffic to a variant, based on a consistent hash of a context value that the caller passes, such as the article ID. To read variants, the function must use AWS AppConfig Agent, which runs in Lambda as the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension. The extension keeps the flag in a local cache and polls AppConfig for new versions. To move from 10 percent to 20 percent, or back to 0, the team edits the rule and deploys the new flag version through AppConfig. The extension picks up that version on its next poll, with no code change and no pipeline run.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.2: "Create flexible architecture patterns to enable dynamic model selection and provider switching without requiring code modifications"
Example: "AWS AppConfig"

Sources:

  • Retrieving basic and multi-variant feature flags
  • Understanding multi-variant feature flag rules
  • Configuring the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension

INCORRECT: Create a basic AWS AppConfig feature flag that sends all requests to Claude Haiku when the flag is on, and read it through the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension in the function.
A basic feature flag is either on or off. It fits a full switch, for example moving all traffic to a new model in one step, or a quick rollback to the old one. It cannot send a share of the traffic to each model, and the product team wants 10 percent on Claude Haiku with the rest on Amazon Nova Lite.

INCORRECT: Put an Amazon API Gateway REST API in front of the function, and create a canary release on its stage with a stage variable override that sends 10% to Claude Haiku.
An API Gateway canary release sends a set percentage of the traffic on a stage to a canary, and a stage variable override can give the canary another model ID. This fits an application whose requests arrive through that API. Here an Amazon SQS queue invokes the function for each article. No request passes through an API that could split the traffic.

INCORRECT: Run an Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job for each model on a sample of past articles, and compare the summary scores before choosing a model for production.
An Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job scores a model's answers on a set of prompts. It fits an offline comparison before a model reaches production. The product team wants to send 10 percent of the live production traffic to Claude Haiku and change that share later. An evaluation job uses a fixed dataset and routes no production traffic.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A financial analytics firm uses a 70-billion parameter open-source Foundation Model (FM) to categorize complex investment documents. The data science team retrains the model weekly to adapt to new market terminologies. Currently, the team performs full fine-tuning and saves the entire model (approx. 140 GB) to Amazon S3 for every version. This approach has led to unsustainable storage costs and slow deployment times, making it difficult to roll back quickly if a new version degrades performance.
Which lifecycle management strategy should the GenAI Developer implement to resolve these issues while maintaining model performance?
questions.promptText:
A financial analytics firm uses a 70-billion parameter open-source Foundation Model (FM) to categorize complex investment documents. The data science team retrains the model weekly to adapt to new market terminologies. Currently, the team performs full fine-tuning and saves the entire model (approx. 140 GB) to Amazon S3 for every version. This approach has led to unsustainable storage costs and slow deployment times, making it difficult to roll back quickly if a new version degrades performance.
Which lifecycle management strategy should the GenAI Developer implement to resolve these issues while maintaining model performance?

options.text: Train LoRA adapters, register each adapter version in SageMaker Model Registry, and deploy it as an adapter inference component on the endpoint's base model inference component.
Train LoRA adapters, merge each adapter into a full copy of the base model weights, register the merged model in SageMaker Model Registry, and update the endpoint.
Keep full fine-tuning, move each older full version to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class, and restore that version when a rollback is needed.
Keep full fine-tuning, quantize each new version to lower precision, and deploy it to a new fleet of Amazon EC2 instances with an AWS CodeDeploy blue/green deployment.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Train LoRA adapters, register each adapter version in SageMaker Model Registry, and deploy it as an adapter inference component on the endpoint's base model inference component.
LoRA trains a small set of adapter weights and leaves the base model frozen. Each weekly version is then an adapter, not a new copy of the 140 GB model, so storage needs drop sharply. SageMaker Model Registry keeps each adapter as a versioned model package with an approval status, such as Approved or Rejected. On a SageMaker AI endpoint, the base model runs as an inference component, and each adapter runs as an adapter inference component on it. SageMaker adds, updates or deletes a single adapter without a new deployment of the endpoint, and the base model stays loaded. A rollback deploys the last approved adapter version, so it takes little time.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.4: "Implement FM customization deployment and lifecycle management"
Example: "SageMaker Model Registry for versioning and to deploy customized models"

Sources:

  • Fine-tune models with adapter inference components
  • Model management for LoRA fine-tuned models using Llama2 and Amazon SageMaker
  • Update the Approval Status of a Model

INCORRECT: Train LoRA adapters, merge each adapter into a full copy of the base model weights, register the merged model in SageMaker Model Registry, and update the endpoint.
Merging an adapter into the base weights produces one full model. Teams merge when they want to serve a single model with no adapter step at inference time. Here each merged version is again a full copy of the base model, so every week adds another large model to storage. Each release also loads a full model onto the endpoint, so the storage and deployment problems stay.

INCORRECT: Keep full fine-tuning, move each older full version to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class, and restore that version when a rollback is needed.
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is a low-cost storage class for data that people rarely read. It fits old model versions that a team keeps only for its records. An archived object must be restored before anyone can read it, so a rollback would first wait for the restore. Each release would also still load a full 140 GB model, so deployments stay slow.

INCORRECT: Keep full fine-tuning, quantize each new version to lower precision, and deploy it to a new fleet of Amazon EC2 instances with an AWS CodeDeploy blue/green deployment.
Quantization stores the weights at lower precision, so the model needs less memory. A CodeDeploy blue/green deployment moves traffic to a new set of EC2 instances and keeps the old set for a rollback. Both are real practices when memory or a safe cutover is the main problem. Here the team still saves a full fine-tuned model every week, so storage costs stay high, and lower precision can reduce output quality, while the firm must keep model performance.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
An insurance company is building a RAG application using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The source data consists of thousands of PDF claim forms containing dense tables with rows for medical codes and costs.
During testing, the developer notices that the application frequently answers questions about specific line items incorrectly. An analysis reveals that the default ingestion process is flattening the tables into unstructured text, causing the embedding model to lose the relationship between the columns.
Which configuration change should the developer implement to allow the Knowledge Base to interpret these tables correctly with the LEAST development effort?
questions.promptText:
An insurance company is building a RAG application using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The source data consists of thousands of PDF claim forms containing dense tables with rows for medical codes and costs.
During testing, the developer notices that the application frequently answers questions about specific line items incorrectly. An analysis reveals that the default ingestion process is flattening the tables into unstructured text, causing the embedding model to lose the relationship between the columns.
Which configuration change should the developer implement to allow the Knowledge Base to interpret these tables correctly with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Set up the data source with a foundation model, such as a Claude vision model, as its parser, so the parser reads each table, and ingest the claim forms again.
Set up the data source with the default parser and semantic chunking, so each chunk holds text with one meaning, and ingest the claim forms again.
Set up the data source with the default parser and hierarchical chunking, so each small chunk comes with its larger parent chunk, and ingest the claim forms again.
Add an AWS Lambda function that runs Amazon Textract table analysis on each PDF, save each table as a Markdown file in the bucket, and ingest the claim forms again.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set up the data source with a foundation model, such as a Claude vision model, as its parser, so the parser reads each table, and ingest the claim forms again.
A knowledge base data source can use one of three parsers. The default parser reads only text, and it does not extract figures, charts or tables, which is why the rows lose their columns.

A foundation model parser reads the tables and other visual content in each PDF during ingestion, so the chunks keep the link between each medical code and its cost.

The parser models are vision models, such as Claude vision models. The parser is a setting that the developer chooses when a data source is created, and it cannot be changed later. So the developer sets up a new data source with the foundation model parser and ingests the claim forms again, with no code to write.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.2: "Create data processing workflows to handle complex data types including text, image, audio, and tabular data with specialized processing requirements for FM consumption"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock multimodal models"

Sources:

  • Parsing options for your data source

  • Supported models and Regions for Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases

INCORRECT: Set up the data source with the default parser and semantic chunking, so each chunk holds text with one meaning, and ingest the claim forms again.
Semantic chunking splits text by its meaning, so each chunk holds sentences that belong together. It helps with long prose, where a fixed size would cut an idea in half. Here the default parser has already turned each table into plain text before chunking starts, and chunks built by meaning from that text still have no columns.

INCORRECT: Set up the data source with the default parser and hierarchical chunking, so each small chunk comes with its larger parent chunk, and ingest the claim forms again.
Hierarchical chunking searches small child chunks and then gives the model their larger parent chunks as context. It fits long documents where a matching sentence needs the text around it. The problem here starts earlier, during parsing. The default parser has already flattened the tables, so both the child chunks and the parent chunks hold rows with no columns.

INCORRECT: Add an AWS Lambda function that runs Amazon Textract table analysis on each PDF, save each table as a Markdown file in the bucket, and ingest the claim forms again.
Amazon Textract table analysis finds tables in a document and returns their cells, rows, columns and headers. A custom step like this fits a team that needs full control of how each table is written out. It would work, but the developer must write, test and run code for every file. The question asks for the least development effort, and a parser setting on the data source needs no code.

questions.promptHtml:
A digital marketing agency wants to use a Foundation Model on Amazon Bedrock to generate social media captions for a youth-focused fashion brand. The brand uses a highly specific, quirky "Gen Z" tone of voice that standard models fail to replicate, often sounding too formal. The agency has curated a high-quality dataset of 1,000 previous successful captions that perfectly capture this style. Each caption comes with its product brief.
The team needs to adapt a model to consistently generate text in this specific style. They want to avoid injecting multiple examples into every prompt to minimize inference token costs and latency.
Which customization strategy should the GenAI Developer choose?
questions.promptText:
A digital marketing agency wants to use a Foundation Model on Amazon Bedrock to generate social media captions for a youth-focused fashion brand. The brand uses a highly specific, quirky "Gen Z" tone of voice that standard models fail to replicate, often sounding too formal. The agency has curated a high-quality dataset of 1,000 previous successful captions that perfectly capture this style. Each caption comes with its product brief.
The team needs to adapt a model to consistently generate text in this specific style. They want to avoid injecting multiple examples into every prompt to minimize inference token costs and latency.
Which customization strategy should the GenAI Developer choose?

options.text: Fine-tune an Amazon Nova Lite model in Amazon Bedrock on a JSONL file whose records each hold a product brief as the input and its caption as the output.
Write a system prompt that describes the brand's tone of voice, and add five captions as examples to each request that the application sends to the model.
Use Amazon Bedrock model distillation, in which a larger teacher model writes captions for the product briefs and a smaller student model learns from those captions.
Store the 1,000 captions in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and add the five captions most similar to each brief as examples to each request that the application sends to the model.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Fine-tune an Amazon Nova Lite model in Amazon Bedrock on a JSONL file whose records each hold a product brief as the input and its caption as the output.
Supervised fine-tuning trains a model on labeled records, each with an input and the output the model should give. Amazon Bedrock takes the training data as a JSONL file, with one record on each line, and Amazon Nova Lite is one of the models that support fine-tuning. Here each record pairs a product brief with the caption that worked for the brand, so the model learns the tone and keeps it in its weights. At inference time, the prompt holds only the new brief, with no examples, so token costs and latency stay low.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.4: "Implement FM customization deployment and lifecycle management"

Sources:

  • Customize a model with fine-tuning in Amazon Bedrock
  • Prepare data for fine-tuning your models

INCORRECT: Write a system prompt that describes the brand's tone of voice, and add five captions as examples to each request that the application sends to the model.
A system prompt with a few examples shows a model a style with no training at all. It fits early tests, or a style that a model can already copy from a few examples. The team wants to avoid adding examples to every prompt, because each example adds input tokens and latency to every call.

INCORRECT: Use Amazon Bedrock model distillation, in which a larger teacher model writes captions for the product briefs and a smaller student model learns from those captions.
Model distillation trains a smaller student model on answers that a larger teacher model writes. It fits a team that wants a faster, lower-cost model that answers almost as well as a larger one. Here the standard models, which would act as the teacher, fail to write in the brand's tone and sound too formal. The student would learn that formal tone from the teacher's captions.

INCORRECT: Store the 1,000 captions in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and add the five captions most similar to each brief as examples to each request that the application sends to the model.
A knowledge base can find the stored captions that are most similar to each new brief, and the application can add them to the prompt as examples. This fits a team that wants the examples to change with each request. It still adds several captions to every prompt, and the team wants to avoid that to keep token costs and latency low.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
An e-commerce platform maintains a catalog of 50 million product images, each paired with a text description. The product team wants a "Universal Search" feature letting users search by typing a query or uploading a photo. The solution must embed both images and text into the same vector space so text queries can retrieve image vectors and vice versa.
Which approach supports both kinds of search?
questions.promptText:
An e-commerce platform maintains a catalog of 50 million product images, each paired with a text description. The product team wants a "Universal Search" feature letting users search by typing a query or uploading a photo. The solution must embed both images and text into the same vector space so text queries can retrieve image vectors and vice versa.
Which approach supports both kinds of search?

options.text: Caption every product image and each uploaded photo with Amazon Nova Pro, embed the captions and descriptions with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and store the vectors in OpenSearch Service.
Embed every product image and every description with Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings, store the vectors in one OpenSearch Service index, and embed each query or photo with that model.

Label every product image and each uploaded photo with Amazon Rekognition DetectLabels, embed the labels and descriptions with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and store the vectors in OpenSearch Service.
Embed every product description with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, store the vectors in one OpenSearch Service index, and embed each typed query with the same model before the search.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Embed every product image and every description with Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings, store the vectors in one OpenSearch Service index, and embed each query or photo with that model.
Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings turns text, images, or both into embeddings in a shared semantic space, and it is made for search and recommendation use cases. So the vector of a typed query such as "red running shoes" can sit close to the vectors of matching product photos, and an uploaded photo can find similar products. One OpenSearch Service index holds the image and description vectors, and every query goes through the same model. All the vectors can then be compared with each other, which is what the requirement asks for.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.2: "Select and configure optimal embedding solutions to create efficient vector representations for semantic search"
Example: "Amazon Titan embeddings based on dimensionality and domain fit"

Sources:

  • Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1
  • Titan Text Embeddings V2

INCORRECT: Caption every product image and each uploaded photo with Amazon Nova Pro, embed the captions and descriptions with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and store the vectors in OpenSearch Service.
Captioning turns each image into words, and a text embedding model then searches those words. Amazon Nova Pro accepts images as input, so this pipeline works when a search over text is enough. But no image is ever embedded here. The search compares caption text with description text, so images and text never share one vector space, which the question requires. Any detail that a caption leaves out is also lost to the search.

INCORRECT: Label every product image and each uploaded photo with Amazon Rekognition DetectLabels, embed the labels and descriptions with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and store the vectors in OpenSearch Service.
Amazon Rekognition DetectLabels finds objects and concepts in an image and returns them as labels. Teams use these labels to tag and filter large photo libraries. In this option the labels become text, and a text embedding model embeds that text. The images themselves are never embedded, so the search cannot compare image vectors with text vectors, as the question requires.

INCORRECT: Embed every product description with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, store the vectors in one OpenSearch Service index, and embed each typed query with the same model before the search.
Amazon Titan Text Embeddings is a good choice when users search a catalog only by typing. It takes text as input and returns an embedding. Here users can also upload a photo, and this model cannot take an image. The product images are never embedded either, so a typed query has no image vectors to find.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A global news agency based in the United States uses Amazon Bedrock to summarize breaking news in real time. The application experiences unpredictable traffic spikes during major world events and recently suffered downtime when throughput in us-east-1 was exhausted, causing ThrottlingException errors. Regulatory requirements mandate that all inference data must remain within the United States. The team requires a solution that automatically routes traffic across regions to maximize throughput with no client-side failover logic. The chosen model has US, EU and global cross-Region inference profiles.
Which way of calling the model meets all of these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A global news agency based in the United States uses Amazon Bedrock to summarize breaking news in real time. The application experiences unpredictable traffic spikes during major world events and recently suffered downtime when throughput in us-east-1 was exhausted, causing ThrottlingException errors. Regulatory requirements mandate that all inference data must remain within the United States. The team requires a solution that automatically routes traffic across regions to maximize throughput with no client-side failover logic. The chosen model has US, EU and global cross-Region inference profiles.
Which way of calling the model meets all of these requirements?

options.text: Call the model through the US geographic cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock can send each request to any of the US Regions in that profile.
Call the model through the global cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock can send each request to any supported commercial Region worldwide.
Call the model through an application inference profile created from the foundation model in us-east-1, so that Amazon Bedrock tracks the usage and cost of each request.
Call the model through the EU geographic cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock can send each request to any of the EU Regions in that profile.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Call the model through the US geographic cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock can send each request to any of the US Regions in that profile.
A geographic cross-Region inference profile keeps data processing inside one geography. A request made within the US stays in AWS Regions in the US, so the residency rule holds. On-demand capacity is Regional, and a workload that targets only us-east-1 can hit capacity errors at times of high demand. With the US profile, Amazon Bedrock can process each request in one of several US Regions. The application only calls the profile ID instead of the model ID, and it needs no failover logic of its own.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.3: "Design resilient AI systems to ensure continuous operation during service disruptions"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region Inference for models that have limited regional availability"

Sources:

  • Geographic cross-Region inference
  • Scaling and throughput best practices
  • Create an application inference profile

INCORRECT: Call the model through the global cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock can send each request to any supported commercial Region worldwide.
A global cross-Region inference profile is not limited to one geography. It sends requests to supported commercial AWS Regions around the world, which suits a company with no data residency rule. Here all inference data must stay in the United States. With the global profile, a request may be processed in a Region outside the US, so this option breaks the rule.

INCORRECT: Call the model through an application inference profile created from the foundation model in us-east-1, so that Amazon Bedrock tracks the usage and cost of each request.
An application inference profile tracks usage and cost for the requests that use it. When the team creates it from a foundation model, the profile covers that one Region only. Every request still goes to us-east-1, so the throttling during traffic spikes stays. To route across Regions, an application profile must be created from a cross-Region (system-defined) profile, and this option does not do that.

INCORRECT: Call the model through the EU geographic cross-Region inference profile, so that Amazon Bedrock can send each request to any of the EU Regions in that profile.
An EU geographic profile keeps every request inside Regions in the EU. That is the right choice for an application whose data must stay in the EU. This agency must keep its inference data in the United States, so sending requests to EU Regions breaks its rule.

questions.promptText:
A healthcare software company builds a clinical note summarizer on Amazon Bedrock. Regulations require every change to the system prompt to be versioned, tested, and approved by a compliance officer before the change reaches production. The compliance officer must run each prompt in the AWS Management Console before approving it. Developers keep editing the prompt while each review runs. The application calls the model with the Converse API, and the application must keep using the Converse API.
Which workflow meets these governance requirements?

options.text: Edit the prompt draft in Prompt Management, create a version with CreatePromptVersion, have the compliance officer test and approve that version, and send the version ARN as the model ID in Converse calls.

Store each prompt as an object in an Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning, have the compliance officer approve each object version, and have the application read that version before each Converse call.
Edit the prompt draft in Prompt Management, have the compliance officer test and approve the draft, then create a version at release time and send the version ARN as the model ID in Converse calls.
Place the prompt in a Prompt Flows prompt node, create a flow version, have the compliance officer test and approve that version, and invoke the flow from the application through a flow alias.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Edit the prompt draft in Prompt Management, create a version with CreatePromptVersion, have the compliance officer test and approve that version, and send the version ARN as the model ID in Converse calls.
A prompt version is a snapshot of the prompt that a team creates for use in production. The compliance officer can choose that version in the console and run it in the test window, so the officer tests and approves the exact text that will run. The Converse API accepts the ARN of a prompt version as its model ID. So the application keeps using the Converse API and runs only the approved snapshot. Later edits to the draft do not change this snapshot, and each new change needs a new version and a new review.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.3: "Implement comprehensive prompt management and governance systems to ensure consistency and oversight of FM operations"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to create parameterized templates and approval workflows"

Sources:

  • CreatePromptVersion

  • Test a prompt using Prompt management

  • Deploy a prompt to your application using versions in Prompt management

INCORRECT: Store each prompt as an object in an Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning, have the compliance officer approve each object version, and have the application read that version before each Converse call.
S3 Versioning keeps every version of every object in a bucket, so a versioned bucket works well as a store for prompt template files. The application can read a prompt file and send its text with the Converse API. But a text file in S3 cannot run. The compliance officer has no place in S3 to send the prompt to a model and test it, and the rules require a test before each approval.

INCORRECT: Edit the prompt draft in Prompt Management, have the compliance officer test and approve the draft, then create a version at release time and send the version ARN as the model ID in Converse calls.
Creating a version at release time is a normal step for a team with no review gate between the draft and production. Here developers keep editing the draft while each review runs. The officer approves the draft as it looked on the day of the review, but the version captures the draft as it looks at release. Any edit made in between reaches production with no approval, which the rules do not allow.

INCORRECT: Place the prompt in a Prompt Flows prompt node, create a flow version, have the compliance officer test and approve that version, and invoke the flow from the application through a flow alias.
A flow version is an immutable snapshot of the whole flow. An application runs a deployed flow by sending InvokeFlow requests to an alias that points to a version. This suits a team that deploys a chain of steps. The Converse API accepts a model, an inference profile or a prompt version as its model ID, but not a flow alias. So this application would have to stop using the Converse API, and the requirements say that the application keeps the Converse API.

The data engineering team already prepares the chat logs with an AWS Glue ETL job. The team wants to add the redaction as a step inside this existing job, with minimal custom code. Each detected value must be replaced with the same fixed redaction string.

Which solution meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A financial technology company collects customer chat logs in an Amazon S3 bucket to fine-tune a model. Before the training starts, all personally identifiable information (PII) in the logs must be redacted: names, credit card numbers, and US Social Security numbers (SSNs).
The data engineering team already prepares the chat logs with an AWS Glue ETL job. The team wants to add the redaction as a step inside this existing job, with minimal custom code. Each detected value must be replaced with the same fixed redaction string.
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add the Sensitive Data Detection transform to the existing AWS Glue ETL job, and set the action to replace each detected value with a chosen redaction string.
Add the Sensitive Data Detection transform to the existing AWS Glue ETL job, and set the transform to find the fields that contain PII, without changing any value.
Add the Sensitive Data Detection transform to the existing AWS Glue ETL job, and set the action to replace each detected value with its SHA-256 hash.
Create an AWS Glue DataBrew job that runs a recipe with a substitution step, which replaces each detected PII value with a realistic fake value.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add the Sensitive Data Detection transform to the existing AWS Glue ETL job, and set the action to replace each detected value with a chosen redaction string.
The Sensitive Data Detection transform runs as a step inside an AWS Glue ETL job. So the team adds the transform to the existing job and writes no custom code. The transform can find managed data types such as person names, US Social Security numbers, and credit card numbers. With the Redact detected text action, the transform replaces each value that it finds with a string that the team specifies. Every name, card number, and SSN is then replaced by the same redaction string before the job writes the data to S3 for training.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.3: "Create privacy-focused AI systems to protect user privacy while maintaining FM utility and effectiveness"
Example: "data masking techniques"

Sources:

  • Detect and process sensitive data

  • PIIDetection

  • Identifying and handling personally identifiable information (PII)

INCORRECT: Add the Sensitive Data Detection transform to the existing AWS Glue ETL job, and set the transform to find the fields that contain PII, without changing any value.
Detection at field level scans a sample of rows and finds the fields that contain PII. This is useful when a team first needs to learn where sensitive data is in a new dataset. In this option, no action changes the detected values. The job writes the real names, card numbers, and SSNs to the training data, and the requirement is to redact them.

INCORRECT: Add the Sensitive Data Detection transform to the existing AWS Glue ETL job, and set the action to replace each detected value with its SHA-256 hash.
The Apply cryptographic hash action passes each detected value to a SHA-256 hash function and puts the output in place of the value. A hash gives the same output for the same input, so teams use it when they must still match records on a value without reading the value. Each hash comes from the real value, so different values give different hashes. The requirement asks for the same fixed redaction string in place of every detected value.

INCORRECT: Create an AWS Glue DataBrew job that runs a recipe with a substitution step, which replaces each detected PII value with a realistic fake value.
AWS Glue DataBrew finds PII with a profile job and changes the PII with recipe steps. Substitution replaces PII with realistic fake values, which helps when a team needs test data that looks like real customer data. This option creates a separate DataBrew job beside the existing ETL job, not a step inside that job. The job also puts fake values in place of the PII instead of the fixed redaction string that the requirement asks for.

Which control should the developer add?
questions.promptText:
A wealth management firm is launching a "Portfolio Summarizer" RAG application using Amazon Bedrock. The application retrieves private investment documents from a Knowledge Base to generate client updates.
During testing, the compliance team discovered that when an update request named a stock not present in the client's portfolio, the model "hallucinated" a generic market summary based on its pre-training data, rather than stating the information was missing.
The firm requires a strict safety control that blocks any response not factually supported by the retrieved source documents.
Which control should the developer add?

options.text: Add a custom word filter to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that lists the tickers of stocks that the client does not hold, so that responses that name them are blocked.
Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model and the Faithfulness metric, so that summaries that hold information not found in the retrieved documents are flagged.
Add a prompt attack filter to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail, so that requests that try to make the model ignore the developer's instructions are blocked before the model runs.
Add a contextual grounding check to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with high grounding and relevance thresholds, and pass the retrieved documents as the grounding source of each response.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a contextual grounding check to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with high grounding and relevance thresholds, and pass the retrieved documents as the grounding source of each response.
A contextual grounding check compares each response with a reference source and the user query. The grounding score shows if the response is based on the source, and any new information counts as ungrounded. The relevance score shows if the response answers the query. A higher threshold blocks more ungrounded and irrelevant content. A market summary that is not in the retrieved documents fails the grounding check, and the guardrail blocks it before the client sees it. The check supports summarization and question answering, which fits these client updates.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.3: "Develop accuracy verification systems to reduce hallucinations in FM responses"

Sources:

  • Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses

  • Remove a specific list of words and phrases from conversations with word filters

  • Use metrics to understand model performance

INCORRECT: Add a custom word filter to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that lists the tickers of stocks that the client does not hold, so that responses that name them are blocked.
A custom word filter blocks exact words and phrases in prompts and responses. It is the right tool for a fixed list, such as product names that must never appear. Here each client holds different stocks, so the list would change for every client. A word filter also checks words, not facts: a response about a stock the client holds could still add figures that are not in the documents, and the filter would let it through.

INCORRECT: Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model and the Faithfulness metric, so that summaries that hold information not found in the retrieved documents are flagged.
An evaluation job with a judge model can score Faithfulness, which finds information in a response that is not in the context the model was given. This is a good way to measure a RAG application before a release. But an evaluation job scores responses after they are written. It does not stop a response while a client waits, and the firm needs a control that blocks unsupported responses at run time.

INCORRECT: Add a prompt attack filter to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail, so that requests that try to make the model ignore the developer's instructions are blocked before the model runs.
A prompt attack filter detects jailbreaks and prompt injection, such as a user who writes "Ignore everything earlier". It protects an application from users who try to override the developer's instructions. In this case the request was an ordinary update request, and no attack took place. The model added a market summary from its training data because the documents had no facts about that stock. This filter does not check the response against the documents, so it would let the summary through.

questions.promptText:
A government agency runs a classified document analysis tool on Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. The application calls Amazon Bedrock through a VPC interface endpoint. The agency fine-tuned its own custom models, and those models live in a single production account.
The agency belongs to an AWS Organizations organization that also holds sandbox accounts used by contractors. The security policy states that the EC2 instances must invoke only models that the production account owns. The instances must never send prompt data to models in any other account, inside or outside the organization.
Which VPC endpoint policy condition enforces this control?

options.text: Attach a VPC endpoint policy that denies Bedrock actions unless aws:ResourceAccount matches the production account ID, so calls reach only agency-owned models.
Attach a VPC endpoint policy that denies Bedrock actions unless aws:PrincipalAccount matches the production account ID, so only agency credentials can use the endpoint.
Attach a VPC endpoint policy that denies Bedrock actions unless aws:ResourceOrgID matches the agency organization ID, so every request stays inside the trusted organization.
Attach a VPC endpoint policy that denies Bedrock actions unless aws:SourceVpc matches the production VPC ID, so only traffic from that network reaches Bedrock.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Attach a VPC endpoint policy that denies Bedrock actions unless aws:ResourceAccount matches the production account ID, so calls reach only agency-owned models.
This is a resource perimeter control. The aws:ResourceAccount key checks that the resource a request reaches belongs to the AWS account named in the policy. In a VPC endpoint policy, it limits which resources the network can reach. Here the endpoint policy denies Amazon Bedrock calls unless the target resource belongs to the production account. A call to a model in any other account, inside or outside the organization, is denied at the endpoint.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.1: "Develop protected AI environments to ensure comprehensive security for FM deployments"
Example: "VPC endpoints to isolate networks"

Sources:

  • Establish permissions guardrails using data perimeters
  • Use interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) to create a private connection between your VPC and Amazon Bedrock
  • Share a model for another account to use

INCORRECT: Attach a VPC endpoint policy that denies Bedrock actions unless aws:PrincipalAccount matches the production account ID, so only agency credentials can use the endpoint.
This builds an identity perimeter. The aws:PrincipalAccount key checks the account of the caller, and it is the right key when only trusted identities may use a network. But it never checks which model a request targets. The production instances are trusted callers, so this policy would still let them call a model that the production account does not own. The requirement is about the owner of the model, not the owner of the credentials.

INCORRECT: Attach a VPC endpoint policy that denies Bedrock actions unless aws:ResourceOrgID matches the agency organization ID, so every request stays inside the trusted organization.
The aws:ResourceOrgID key checks that the resource a request reaches belongs to the organization named in the policy. In a VPC endpoint policy, it fits a company that trusts every account in its organization. This agency does not trust every account. The contractor sandbox accounts sit inside the same organization, so a model in one of those accounts passes the check. The security policy allows only models that the production account owns, so the condition must name that one account.

INCORRECT: Attach a VPC endpoint policy that denies Bedrock actions unless aws:SourceVpc matches the production VPC ID, so only traffic from that network reaches Bedrock.
This is a network perimeter control. The aws:SourceVpc key checks that the VPC endpoint a request travels through belongs to the VPC named in the policy. It limits where requests come from, which the private subnet design already handles. It does not check which account owns the target model, so it cannot keep the instances to models that the production account owns.

Which change should the developer make to the app?

options.text: Read the citations in each RetrieveAndGenerate response, and show each retrieved reference, with its text and S3 location, beside the generated text that the citation covers.
Write each question, answer and set of retrieved chunks with their text and S3 locations to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, so that lawyers can query the chunks behind any answer later.
Call the Retrieve API first, show every returned chunk with its text and S3 location below the answer, and then send the chunks to the model with the question.
Edit the knowledge base prompt template so that the model writes the S3 location of its source after each sentence, and show the answer text to the lawyers as the model writes it.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Read the citations in each RetrieveAndGenerate response, and show each retrieved reference, with its text and S3 location, beside the generated text that the citation covers.
RetrieveAndGenerate returns a list of citations with each answer. Each citation holds one part of the generated text, with the place where it begins and ends, and the retrieved references behind that part. Each reference holds the cited text from the source and the location of its file, such as the S3 URI. So the app can show each passage and a link to its file next to the sentence it supports, as soon as the answer appears. The evidence comes from the retrieval results, not from words the model writes, so the file names do not depend on the model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.4.1: "Develop transparent AI systems in FM outputs"
Example: "evidence presentation for source attribution"

Sources:

  • Query a knowledge base and generate responses based off the retrieved data
  • Citation
  • RetrieveAndGenerate

INCORRECT: Write each question, answer and set of retrieved chunks with their text and S3 locations to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, so that lawyers can query the chunks behind any answer later.
Writing each request and its passages to CloudWatch Logs builds a decision log, which helps auditors review answers after the fact. It shows the lawyers no evidence when an answer appears. They would have to search the logs later, and the log would still not show which passage supports which sentence.

INCORRECT: Call the Retrieve API first, show every returned chunk with its text and S3 location below the answer, and then send the chunks to the model with the question.
The Retrieve API returns the chunks that match a query, each with its content, its location and a relevance score. Showing them is useful on a search page, where users want to see every match. Here the lawyers must know which passage supports each sentence. A list under the answer ties no passage to any sentence, and it can also show chunks that the answer never used.

INCORRECT: Edit the knowledge base prompt template so that the model writes the S3 location of its source after each sentence, and show the answer text to the lawyers as the model writes it.
Teams edit the knowledge base prompt template to set the tone or the format of answers, and asking a model to name its sources in the text is common in RAG apps. But here the file names would come from the model's own words. The test showed that the model sometimes writes the wrong file name when it is asked to name its sources, so the lawyers could follow a link to the wrong file.

To comply with the EU AI Act and internal governance policies, the organization must keep one central record for the model. The record lists the intended use, the risk rating, the location of each training dataset, and the evaluation results. A change to this content must create a new version of the record, and every earlier version must stay unchanged. The internal audit system must read the record through an API.

Which approach meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A healthcare organization deploys a fine-tuned foundation model that helps doctors write diagnosis notes. To comply with the EU AI Act and internal governance policies, the organization must keep one central record for the model. The record lists the intended use, the risk rating, the location of each training dataset, and the evaluation results. A change to this content must create a new version of the record, and every earlier version must stay unchanged. The internal audit system must read the record through an API.
Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Turn on an AWS CloudTrail trail for SageMaker AI API calls with delivery to Amazon S3, and let the audit system read each model change from the log files.

Register the model in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry, store the intended use, risk rating, training datasets, and evaluation results as customer metadata properties, and let the audit system read them.
Create a model card in Amazon SageMaker AI with the intended use, risk rating, training datasets, and evaluation results, and let the audit system read each card version with DescribeModelCard.
Add tags to the model in Amazon SageMaker AI for the intended use, risk rating, training datasets, and evaluation results, and let the audit system read them with the ListTags API.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a model card in Amazon SageMaker AI with the intended use, risk rating, training datasets, and evaluation results, and let the audit system read each card version with DescribeModelCard.
A SageMaker model card documents a model in one place: its intended use and risk rating, its training details, and its evaluation results. The training details include the location of each training dataset. Every edit other than an approval status update creates a new card version, and the earlier versions stay as they were. The DescribeModelCard API returns the content of a card, and it can return any earlier version, so the audit system reads the whole record through the API.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.1: "Develop compliance frameworks to ensure regulatory compliance for FM deployments"
Example: "SageMaker AI to develop programmatic model cards"

Sources:

  • Amazon SageMaker Model Cards

  • DescribeModelCard

  • UpdateModelPackage

INCORRECT: Turn on an AWS CloudTrail trail for SageMaker AI API calls with delivery to Amazon S3, and let the audit system read each model change from the log files.
CloudTrail records the actions of users, roles and AWS services as events, so auditors can see who did what and when. That suits an audit of account activity. But a trail records API calls, not facts about the model. The intended use, the risk rating, the training datasets and the evaluation results never form one record for the model that the audit system can read.

INCORRECT: Register the model in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry, store the intended use, risk rating, training datasets, and evaluation results as customer metadata properties, and let the audit system read them.
Model Registry tracks model versions, and customer metadata properties add key and value pairs to a model version. They are useful for short labels, such as the name of the team that owns a model. But the UpdateModelPackage API can change or remove these properties on the same model version. A new risk rating would replace the old value without a new version, so the earlier content is lost.

INCORRECT: Add tags to the model in Amazon SageMaker AI for the intended use, risk rating, training datasets, and evaluation results, and let the audit system read them with the ListTags API.
Tags are key and value pairs that teams use to sort resources by purpose, owner or environment, for example in cost reports. The AddTags API adds a tag or overwrites the value of a tag that already exists. A new risk rating would replace the old one, so the tags keep no earlier versions of the record.

An energy company is building a RAG application using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to search internal engineering documents. The document repository contains both "General" manuals (accessible to all staff) and "Confidential" reactor specifications (accessible only to senior engineers).
The documents are stored in Amazon S3 and indexed in an Amazon OpenSearch Service vector store.
The developer needs to ensure that when a junior engineer searches the knowledge base, they are technically prevented from retrieving snippets from "Confidential" documents, even if those documents are semantically relevant to the query.
Some junior engineers know how to change the requests that their browser sends.
Which implementation satisfies this security requirement?

options.text: During ingestion, give each document a metadata file with a classification attribute, and add an equals filter on classification to each Retrieve call that the application sets from the user's group.
During ingestion, give each document a metadata file with a classification attribute, and add an equals filter on classification to each Retrieve call that the user's browser sends with each search.
During ingestion, give each document a metadata file with a classification attribute, and have a Lambda function remove every confidential chunk from the results of each Retrieve call.
Store the confidential documents under their own S3 prefix, and add a bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject on that prefix only to the IAM role of the senior engineers.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: During ingestion, give each document a metadata file with a classification attribute, and add an equals filter on classification to each Retrieve call that the application sets from the user's group.
This is metadata filtering at query time, with the filter value set on the server. Each document in Amazon S3 has a metadata file with the same name plus .metadata.json, and that file sets its classification attribute. When an engineer searches, the application reads the engineer's group from the sign-in and builds the equals filter on classification from that group. The filter goes into vectorSearchConfiguration in the Retrieve call, so the knowledge base returns only chunks whose classification matches it. The application sets the value, not the browser, so a junior engineer who changes a browser request still cannot remove the filter or change it.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.2: "Develop comprehensive metadata frameworks to improve search precision and context awareness for FM interactions"

Sources:

  • Configure and customize queries and response generation

  • Authorizing access to data with RAG implementations

INCORRECT: During ingestion, give each document a metadata file with a classification attribute, and add an equals filter on classification to each Retrieve call that the user's browser sends with each search.
The filter here works the same way as in the correct design, but the browser chooses its value. A filter that the user chooses is a common way to narrow a search, for example to the manuals of one plant. It is not a security control. The question states that some junior engineers know how to change the requests that their browser sends. Such an engineer can remove the filter or set it to confidential, and the knowledge base then returns chunks of the reactor specifications. A filter that must stop a user has to get its value on the server, from the user's group.

INCORRECT: During ingestion, give each document a metadata file with a classification attribute, and have a Lambda function remove every confidential chunk from the results of each Retrieve call.
Code that checks the returned chunks after a Retrieve call can add a second layer of protection, when it checks each chunk against the rights of the person who searched. This option checks no rights. It removes every confidential chunk for every user, so senior engineers lose the reactor specifications too, and they must be able to read them. The function also receives the confidential chunks on every search, while the requirement says that junior engineers must not retrieve them at all.

INCORRECT: Store the confidential documents under their own S3 prefix, and add a bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject on that prefix only to the IAM role of the senior engineers.
A bucket policy on a separate prefix controls who can read those files in Amazon S3. It fits a team that must stop people from opening the files directly in the bucket. The knowledge base reads the files with its own service role during each sync, when it creates the embeddings. A search reads the chunks from the OpenSearch index and does not read the files in Amazon S3 again. So the bucket policy is never checked during a search, and a junior engineer's search can still return confidential chunks.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A legal services company sends contracts to a model on Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API to extract key clauses. Contracts range from a few pages to several hundred pages. The chosen model supports document input, tool use, and token counting in Amazon Bedrock.

Before launch, the finance team sets a new rule. Each request has a budget of input tokens, and the budget is checked against the input tokens that Amazon Bedrock charges for that request. A request over the budget must never reach the model. If a contract would put a request over the budget, the application must split the contract into parts and send each part in its own request.

Which design enforces this rule?
questions.promptText:
A legal services company sends contracts to a model on Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API to extract key clauses. Contracts range from a few pages to several hundred pages. The chosen model supports document input, tool use, and token counting in Amazon Bedrock.
Before launch, the finance team sets a new rule. Each request has a budget of input tokens, and the budget is checked against the input tokens that Amazon Bedrock charges for that request. A request over the budget must never reach the model. If a contract would put a request over the budget, the application must split the contract into parts and send each part in its own request.
Which design enforces this rule?

options.text: Before each call, send the messages of the planned Converse request to the Amazon Bedrock CountTokens API, and split the contract when the count is over the budget.
Before each call, set maxTokens in the inference configuration of the Converse request to the budget, and split the contract when the response stops at that token limit.
After each call, read inputTokens in the usage field of the Converse response, and flag the contract when that input token count is over the budget.
After each call, have a CloudWatch alarm on the Amazon Bedrock InputTokenCount metric send a notification to the team when the value is over the budget.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Before each call, send the messages of the planned Converse request to the Amazon Bedrock CountTokens API, and split the contract when the count is over the budget.
CountTokens is an Amazon Bedrock runtime operation that returns the number of input tokens in a request before the request goes to the model. Token counting works only for models that support it, and the chosen model supports it. The application gives CountTokens the same messages that it plans to send with Converse. The count matches the number of input tokens that Amazon Bedrock would charge for that input, so the application checks the value that the finance rule uses. CountTokens calls cost nothing. When the count is over the budget, the application splits the contract into parts and counts each new request, so only requests within the budget reach the model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.1: "Develop token efficiency systems to reduce FM costs while maintaining effectiveness"
Example: "token estimation and tracking"

Sources:

  • Monitor your token usage by counting tokens before running inference

  • Converse

  • Monitor bedrock-runtime inference using CloudWatch metrics

INCORRECT: Before each call, set maxTokens in the inference configuration of the Converse request to the budget, and split the contract when the response stops at that token limit.
maxTokens sets the largest number of tokens that the model may generate in its response. It fits a team that wants to cap the length and the output cost of each answer. It does not limit the input in any way. A contract of several hundred pages still reaches the model in full, and Amazon Bedrock charges all of its input tokens. The finance rule is about input tokens, so this setting cannot enforce it.

INCORRECT: After each call, read inputTokens in the usage field of the Converse response, and flag the contract when that input token count is over the budget.
The usage field of each Converse response reports the input and output tokens of that call. It is a good way to record the real token use and cost of each contract after the work is done. The finance rule is stricter: a request over the budget must never reach the model. The usage field arrives only with the response, after the model has read the whole contract, so the check comes too late.

INCORRECT: After each call, have a CloudWatch alarm on the Amazon Bedrock InputTokenCount metric send a notification to the team when the value is over the budget.
Amazon Bedrock publishes the InputTokenCount metric to CloudWatch, and an alarm on the metric can notify a team when token use rises above a threshold. This fits the monitoring of token use over time. In this option, the alarm acts only after each call. By then, the request has already reached the model, and Amazon Bedrock charges the input tokens of that request. The rule says that a request over the budget must never reach the model, and a notification after the call cannot stop that request.

questions.promptHtml:
A gaming studio uses generative AI to create dynamic NPC dialogue. They have fine-tuned a Meta Llama model with LoRA on 50 different character personas, such as "Pirate," "Merchant" and "Guard".
Currently, the team deploys a separate Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for each persona to ensure isolation. This architecture is incurring massive costs because most endpoints sit idle 90% of the time, yet the GPU instances are billed 24/7.
The studio needs to consolidate these models to reduce infrastructure costs while keeping the ability to serve any persona instantly with low latency.
Which deployment strategy provides the most significant cost reduction?
questions.promptText:
A gaming studio uses generative AI to create dynamic NPC dialogue. They have fine-tuned a Meta Llama model with LoRA on 50 different character personas, such as "Pirate," "Merchant" and "Guard".
Currently, the team deploys a separate Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for each persona to ensure isolation. This architecture is incurring massive costs because most endpoints sit idle 90% of the time, yet the GPU instances are billed 24/7.
The studio needs to consolidate these models to reduce infrastructure costs while keeping the ability to serve any persona instantly with low latency.
Which deployment strategy provides the most significant cost reduction?

options.text: Host the base model once as an inference component on one endpoint, and add each persona's LoRA adapter as an adapter inference component.
Merge each persona's LoRA adapter into a full copy of the model, and host all 50 copies together on one multi-model endpoint.
Merge each persona's LoRA adapter into a full copy of the model, and host each of the 50 copies on its own serverless inference endpoint.
Keep one endpoint for each persona, host each persona's model as an inference component, and set the minimum instance count to zero for idle periods.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Host the base model once as an inference component on one endpoint, and add each persona's LoRA adapter as an adapter inference component.
This is multi-adapter inference on SageMaker AI. The endpoint holds one inference component with the base model. Each persona's LoRA adapter becomes an adapter inference component, which uses the compute of the base component. A request names the adapter of the persona it needs, and SageMaker AI loads that adapter from GPU memory, CPU memory or local disk in milliseconds. All 50 personas now share one GPU endpoint in place of 50, so the studio stops paying for 49 idle endpoints, and every persona can still answer at once.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.2.4: "Implement FM customization deployment and lifecycle management"
Example: "parameter-efficient adaptation techniques such as low-rank adaptation [LoRA] and adapters for model deployment"

Sources:

  • Easily deploy and manage hundreds of LoRA adapters with SageMaker efficient multi-adapter inference

  • Fine-tune models with adapter inference components

  • Deploy models with Amazon SageMaker Serverless Inference

INCORRECT: Merge each persona's LoRA adapter into a full copy of the model, and host all 50 copies together on one multi-model endpoint.
A multi-model endpoint hosts many models on shared instances, and it supports GPU instances. It loads a model into memory when a request for that model arrives, and it unloads models that are not in use when memory runs short. It fits a large set of models when the application accepts some delay for models that are rarely called. Here each merged copy is a full model. A persona that no one has called for a while waits while its whole model loads, and the studio needs every persona to answer at once.

INCORRECT: Merge each persona's LoRA adapter into a full copy of the model, and host each of the 50 copies on its own serverless inference endpoint.
Serverless Inference scales an endpoint down to zero when no requests arrive, so the studio would pay only while requests run. It fits models that have idle periods and can accept cold starts. Serverless Inference does not support GPUs, and its largest memory size is 6 GB, while these personas run on GPU instances today. An idle serverless endpoint also needs time to start again, so a persona could not answer at once.

INCORRECT: Keep one endpoint for each persona, host each persona's model as an inference component, and set the minimum instance count to zero for idle periods.
With inference components, a real-time endpoint can scale down to zero instances when no requests arrive. This cuts the cost of endpoints that stay idle for long periods, and it fits work that can wait while an instance starts. When a request reaches an endpoint with zero instances, that request fails, and the new instance takes minutes to start and load the model. The studio needs every persona to answer at once, so it cannot wait for this start.

An internal research agent reviews supplier contracts in many steps during the day. Each step waits for the answer to the step before it, and the results are due the next morning.
The bill is too high, and most of the tokens come from the research agent. The quality team approved only this model for both workloads, and chat response times must not get slower. The model supports the Standard, Priority and Flex service tiers.
Which change lowers the cost within these rules?
questions.promptText:
A company uses one model on Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API for two workloads. A customer chat assistant answers while the customer waits, and its response times meet the target today. An internal research agent reviews supplier contracts in many steps during the day. Each step waits for the answer to the step before it, and the results are due the next morning.
The bill is too high, and most of the tokens come from the research agent. The quality team approved only this model for both workloads, and chat response times must not get slower. The model supports the Standard, Priority and Flex service tiers.
Which change lowers the cost within these rules?

options.text: Set the service tier of the research agent's Converse requests to flex, and leave the chat assistant's requests on the default standard tier.
Set the service tier of the chat assistant's Converse requests to priority, and leave the research agent's requests on the default standard tier.
Write the research agent's prompts to JSONL files in Amazon S3, and run them each night as Amazon Bedrock batch inference jobs.
Send each research agent request to a smaller, lower-cost model first, and pass it to the current model only when that answer scores low.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set the service tier of the research agent's Converse requests to flex, and leave the chat assistant's requests on the default standard tier.
Amazon Bedrock offers service tiers, and each request chooses its tier with one parameter in the same Converse call. The Flex tier is priced at a discount to the Standard tier. It fits work that can accept longer processing times, such as multistep agentic workflows, and when demand is high, Flex requests get lower priority than Standard requests. The research agent produces most of the tokens, and its results are due the next morning, so slower answers do no harm. A request that names no tier goes to the Standard tier, so the chat assistant keeps its response times. Both workloads keep the approved model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.2: "Create cost-effective model selection frameworks"
Example: "efficient inference patterns"

Sources:

  • Service tiers for optimizing performance and cost
  • Amazon Bedrock introduces Priority and Flex inference service tiers
  • Process multiple prompts with batch inference

INCORRECT: Set the service tier of the chat assistant's Converse requests to priority, and leave the research agent's requests on the default standard tier.
The Priority tier gives the fastest response times, and its requests are served before Standard and Flex requests. It fits customer-facing work where every second counts, and it costs more than the Standard tier. Here the chat response times already meet the target, and the company wants a lower bill. This change raises the cost of the chat assistant and leaves the cost of the research agent as it is.

INCORRECT: Write the research agent's prompts to JSONL files in Amazon S3, and run them each night as Amazon Bedrock batch inference jobs.
Batch inference runs many prompts from JSONL files in Amazon S3 as one asynchronous job, and for supported models it costs less than on-demand calls. It fits a set of independent prompts that are all known before the job starts. The research agent works in steps, and each step needs the answer to the step before it. The agent cannot write all of its prompts in advance, so a nightly batch job does not fit how it works.

INCORRECT: Send each research agent request to a smaller, lower-cost model first, and pass it to the current model only when that answer scores low.
Model cascading sends each request to a small model first and moves it to a stronger model only when the first answer is weak. It lowers the cost when a smaller model can answer many requests well. Here the quality team approved only the current model for both workloads. Answers from the smaller model would break that rule.
