questions.promptText:
An e-commerce company runs a product description generator using Amazon Bedrock. Two other applications call the same model. The finance team has noticed that the bill for Amazon Bedrock has doubled in the last month, even though the number of generated descriptions has remained steady.
The engineering team suspects that a recent update to the prompt template is causing the model to generate excessively verbose output, but they lack visibility into the token counts per request.
Which monitoring solution enables the team to identify the root cause with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Turn on model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs, and run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query that lists the input and output token counts of each request.
Turn on model invocation logging to Amazon S3, create an Amazon Athena table over the log files, and query the token counts of each request.
Build a CloudWatch dashboard on the InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount metrics that Amazon Bedrock publishes, and compare the daily totals for the last month.
Turn on model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs, create a metric filter on the output token count, and add an alarm when the average passes a threshold.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs, and run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query that lists the input and output token counts of each request.
Model invocation logging records the request, the response and the metadata of each model call, from the moment the team turns it on. For CloudWatch Logs, the team needs a log group and an IAM role that Amazon Bedrock can assume, and the application code does not change. Each log record holds the prompt, the role that made the call, inputTokenCount and outputTokenCount. CloudWatch Logs Insights reads these JSON fields directly, so one query lists the token counts of each request next to its prompt. The team can filter on the caller's role or on the prompt text to leave out the other two applications. Every new description request uses the updated template, so the query shows at once whether this template makes the model write long answers.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.2: "Implement comprehensive GenAI monitoring systems to proactively identify issues and evaluate key performance indicators specific to FM implementations"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logs to perform detailed request and response analysis"

Sources:

  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3
  • Monitor bedrock-runtime inference using CloudWatch metrics
  • Supported logs and discovered fields

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging to Amazon S3, create an Amazon Athena table over the log files, and query the token counts of each request.
Logs in Amazon S3 with Amazon Athena queries fit long-term storage and large SQL reports. This option needs an S3 bucket with a bucket policy that lets Amazon Bedrock write the logs, and an Athena table over the log files before the first query can run. The question asks for the least operational overhead, and CloudWatch Logs Insights reaches the same token counts without these steps.

INCORRECT: Build a CloudWatch dashboard on the InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount metrics that Amazon Bedrock publishes, and compare the daily totals for the last month.
Amazon Bedrock publishes these token metrics in CloudWatch with no setup, so a dashboard on them is a quick way to watch token use over time. The metrics are published per model, and two other applications call the same model, so the daily totals mix the traffic of all three applications. Totals also do not show the token count of each request, which is the detail the team lacks.

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs, create a metric filter on the output token count, and add an alarm when the average passes a threshold.
A metric filter turns a value in log events into a CloudWatch metric, and an alarm can warn the team when that value passes a threshold. This fits ongoing monitoring once the team knows its normal token use. Here the team needs to find a cause, not to get an alert. The metric and the alarm show numbers over time, not the token counts and the prompt of each request.

A news aggregator uses a RAG architecture with Amazon OpenSearch Service (Provisioned) as the vector store. The system ingests breaking news in real-time, performing thousands of vector insertions per minute.
Users are reporting that the "Related Articles" search is becoming increasingly slow (high latency) during these ingestion spikes. The OpenSearch cluster metrics show high CPU utilization and high JVM memory pressure.
The index is configured with the standard settings for k-NN search. Spikes can last an hour, each new article must appear in search within one minute, and the index must always keep a replica.
Which index configuration change should the developer apply to improve search performance under heavy ingestion load?
questions.promptText:
A news aggregator uses a RAG architecture with Amazon OpenSearch Service (Provisioned) as the vector store. The system ingests breaking news in real-time, performing thousands of vector insertions per minute.
Users are reporting that the "Related Articles" search is becoming increasingly slow (high latency) during these ingestion spikes. The OpenSearch cluster metrics show high CPU utilization and high JVM memory pressure.
The index is configured with the standard settings for k-NN search. Spikes can last an hour, each new article must appear in search within one minute, and the index must always keep a replica.
Which index configuration change should the developer apply to improve search performance under heavy ingestion load?

options.text: Set refresh_interval on the k-NN index to 30 seconds, so OpenSearch refreshes the index less often while the system writes the new articles.
Set refresh_interval on the k-NN index to -1 when each ingestion spike starts, and set it back to one second when the spike ends.
Set number_of_replicas on the k-NN index to 0 when each ingestion spike starts, and set it back to one when the spike ends.
Add an ISM policy to the k-NN index that runs a force merge every hour, so the index keeps fewer and larger segments.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set refresh_interval on the k-NN index to 30 seconds, so OpenSearch refreshes the index less often while the system writes the new articles.
A refresh makes recent writes visible to search. The default refresh interval is one second, so during heavy writing OpenSearch refreshes the index every second. Each refresh writes a new small segment, and in a k-NN index each new segment needs its own vector index build. The less often an index refreshes, the better its indexing performance, and the best practice is a refresh interval of 30 seconds or more. With 30 seconds, the index refreshes far less often and builds far fewer small segments. This lowers the indexing load on the cluster during the spikes, when the "Related Articles" search slows down. Each new article appears in search within about 30 seconds, which meets the one minute rule, and the replica stays in place.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.2: "Enhance retrieval performance to improve the relevance and speed of retrieved information for FM context augmentation"
Example: "index optimization"

Sources:

  • Operational best practices for Amazon OpenSearch Service
  • AOSPERF06-BP01 Identify index refresh controls for optimal ingestion performance

INCORRECT: Set refresh_interval on the k-NN index to -1 when each ingestion spike starts, and set it back to one second when the spike ends.
A value of -1 turns automatic refresh off. It is a good choice for a batch load: the team turns refresh off just before the load and back on when the load ends, which speeds up indexing. While refresh is off, new writes do not appear in search. Here a spike can last an hour, and each new article must appear in search within one minute. With refresh off for the whole spike, new articles would stay hidden far longer than that.

INCORRECT: Set number_of_replicas on the k-NN index to 0 when each ingestion spike starts, and set it back to one when the spike ends.
Each replica shard is a full copy of the primary shards, and OpenSearch sends each indexing request to the primary shards first and then to the replica shards. So before a large load, such as a reindex, teams sometimes set the replica count to 0 and set it back when the load ends. At least one replica for each index protects the data when a node stops or restarts without warning. Here the index must always keep a replica, so this change breaks that rule.

INCORRECT: Add an ISM policy to the k-NN index that runs a force merge every hour, so the index keeps fewer and larger segments.
A force merge joins the segments of an index into fewer, larger ones. It suits indexes that no longer receive writes, such as an index of older articles. This index receives thousands of writes every minute, and it still refreshes every second. New small segments appear again right after each merge, so the hourly merge adds work to the nodes and leaves the cause of the slow searches in place.

An EdTech company has released a "History Tutor" chatbot using RAG. It retrieves content from a verified textbook indexed in an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base. Teachers have reported that the chatbot sometimes ignores the retrieved textbook content and invents historical facts based on its pre-training data. The developer needs to run an automated evaluation job to quantify how often the model's generated answer contradicts or deviates from the retrieved source context.
Which built-in metric should the developer select in the Amazon Bedrock RAG Evaluation job?
questions.promptText:
An EdTech company has released a "History Tutor" chatbot using RAG. It retrieves content from a verified textbook indexed in an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base. Teachers have reported that the chatbot sometimes ignores the retrieved textbook content and invents historical facts based on its pre-training data. The developer needs to run an automated evaluation job to quantify how often the model's generated answer contradicts or deviates from the retrieved source context.
Which built-in metric should the developer select in the Amazon Bedrock RAG Evaluation job?

options.text: Select the Faithfulness (Builtin.Faithfulness) metric in a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job. This metric measures how well the generated response avoids hallucination with respect to the retrieved textbook passages.

Select the Correctness (Builtin.Correctness) metric in a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job. This metric measures factual accuracy of the generated response against a supplied ground truth reference answer.
Select the Context Relevance (Builtin.ContextRelevance) metric in a retrieve-only evaluation job. This metric measures how contextually relevant the retrieved passages are to the user's question.

Select the Completeness (Builtin.Completeness) metric in a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job. This metric measures how thoroughly the generated response resolves all aspects of the user's question.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Select the Faithfulness (Builtin.Faithfulness) metric in a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job. This metric measures how well the generated response avoids hallucination with respect to the retrieved textbook passages.
Faithfulness is a built-in metric for retrieve-and-generate jobs. It checks whether each generated answer holds only information that the retrieved passages contain or support. A response that adds facts from the model's training, which the textbook passages do not hold, gets a low score. Each score is a value between 0 and 1, so the job shows how often and how far the answers move away from the retrieved textbook content. That is the problem the teachers reported.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.5: "Develop comprehensive assessment systems to ensure thorough evaluation from multiple perspectives for FM outputs"
Example: "RAG evaluation"

Sources:

  • Use metrics to understand RAG system performance
  • Review metrics for RAG evaluations that use LLMs (console)

INCORRECT: Select the Correctness (Builtin.Correctness) metric in a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job. This metric measures factual accuracy of the generated response against a supplied ground truth reference answer.
Correctness measures how accurate the response is as an answer to the question. This option uses it with a reference answer in the dataset. In that form, the judge model compares the response only with the reference answer, and it does not look at the passages that the knowledge base retrieved. A response that repeats a well-known fact from the model's training can match the reference answer and get a good score, even when the textbook passages do not support that fact. The teachers report answers that move away from the retrieved textbook content, and Correctness with a reference answer does not measure that.

INCORRECT: Select the Context Relevance (Builtin.ContextRelevance) metric in a retrieve-only evaluation job. This metric measures how contextually relevant the retrieved passages are to the user's question.
Context relevance is a retrieve-only metric. It measures how relevant the retrieved passages are to each question, so it tests the retrieval step of the RAG system. It fits a team that suspects the knowledge base returns the wrong passages. A retrieve-only job does not generate answers, so it cannot show what the model does with the passages. The teachers report that the model ignores the textbook content when it writes answers, which is a problem in the generation step.

INCORRECT: Select the Completeness (Builtin.Completeness) metric in a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job. This metric measures how thoroughly the generated response resolves all aspects of the user's question.
Completeness measures whether the response answers every part of the question. It fits a team whose users say that the answers leave out parts of what they asked. It does not check whether the answer stays with the retrieved passages. A response that covers every part of a question with invented historical facts can still get a high Completeness score, so this metric cannot show the problem the teachers reported.

A customer service chatbot for an online pharmacy uses Amazon Bedrock. Users report the bot abruptly responds with "I cannot answer that question" when asking for "Prescription refill instructions." Every refusal is the same sentence, word for word. The developer finds HTTP 200 responses from Amazon Bedrock in CloudWatch Logs, and the response body holds the refusal message. The application has no custom refusal logic in the Lambda function.
What is the most likely cause?
questions.promptText:
A customer service chatbot for an online pharmacy uses Amazon Bedrock. Users report the bot abruptly responds with "I cannot answer that question" when asking for "Prescription refill instructions." Every refusal is the same sentence, word for word. The developer finds HTTP 200 responses from Amazon Bedrock in CloudWatch Logs, and the response body holds the refusal message. The application has no custom refusal logic in the Lambda function.
What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The guardrail on each call has a denied topic for prescription requests with the input action set to BLOCK, so it returns the blocked input message.
The guardrail on each call has a denied topic for prescription requests with the input action set to NONE, so it adds the topic to the trace.
The guardrail on each call has a sensitive information filter that masks customer names in prompts, so the model receives a tag in place of each name.
The guardrail on each call cannot be applied, because the function's IAM role lacks the bedrock:ApplyGuardrail permission on that guardrail resource.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: The guardrail on each call has a denied topic for prescription requests with the input action set to BLOCK, so it returns the blocked input message.
A denied topic describes a subject that the application must not discuss. With the input action set to BLOCK, the guardrail checks each prompt before the model answers. When a prompt matches the topic, Amazon Bedrock discards the model inference and returns the message that the guardrail holds for blocked prompts (blockedInputMessaging). The call still succeeds with HTTP 200, and the response body holds this fixed sentence. That explains every symptom: the status is 200, every refusal is the same sentence, and no application code writes it.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.2: "Diagnose and resolve FM integration issues to identify and fix API integration problems specific to GenAI services"
Example: "response analysis"

Sources:

  • How Amazon Bedrock Guardrails works
  • CreateGuardrail
  • Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters

INCORRECT: The guardrail on each call has a denied topic for prescription requests with the input action set to NONE, so it adds the topic to the trace.
With the action set to NONE, a denied topic takes no action and only returns what it detected in the trace response. Teams use this to watch how a new topic behaves on real traffic before they block anything. The prompt goes on to the model, and the model's own answer reaches the user. These users get one fixed refusal sentence, so something blocks their prompts.

INCORRECT: The guardrail on each call has a sensitive information filter that masks customer names in prompts, so the model receives a tag in place of each name.
A sensitive information filter with the mask action replaces each detected item, such as a name, with a tag like {NAME}. It fits an application that must keep personal data away from the model. The masked prompt still goes to the model, and the model writes its own answer. A model writes its answers in varied words, while these users get the same sentence every time.

INCORRECT: The guardrail on each call cannot be applied, because the function's IAM role lacks the bedrock:ApplyGuardrail permission on that guardrail resource.
To use a guardrail during model inference, the caller's role needs the bedrock:ApplyGuardrail permission on that guardrail, next to the permission to invoke the model. A missing permission is a common cause of failed calls after a team adds a guardrail. A call that the caller has no permission for fails with an AccessDeniedException, which has HTTP status code 403. Here every call returns HTTP 200, so Amazon Bedrock accepted and processed each one.

Which caching setup meets these requirements?

A travel website shows city guides that a model in Amazon Bedrock writes. Browsers load each guide with a GET request, such as /guide?city=lisbon&lang=pt, to an Amazon API Gateway REST API in a US Region. An AWS Lambda function calls the model for every request, even when it wrote the same guide minutes before.
A guide for one city and language stays the same for a full day. Most readers live in Asia and Europe. Links shared on social media add tracking parameters, such as utm_source, that never change the guide.
The team wants repeated requests answered from a cache close to the readers, with no call to the function or the model.
Which caching setup meets these requirements?

options.text: Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API, with a cache policy that keeps each response for one day and puts the whole URL path but no query strings in the cache key.
Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API, with a cache policy that keeps each response for one day and puts the city and lang query strings in the cache key.
Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API, with a cache policy that keeps each response for one day and puts the whole URL path and all query strings in the cache key.
Turn on caching for the API Gateway stage of the REST API, and use the city and lang query strings as the cache key parameters for each cached guide response.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API, with a cache policy that keeps each response for one day and puts the city and lang query strings in the cache key.
CloudFront answers GET requests from caches at edge locations, close to the readers. A cache policy decides what goes into the cache key and how long a response stays in the cache. With only city and lang in the key, each city and language gets its own cached guide, and the tracking parameters create no extra copies. A request for a guide that is not in the cache yet reaches the function and the model. Later requests for that guide come from the cache, with no call to either one.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.4: "Create intelligent caching systems to reduce costs and improve response times by avoiding unnecessary FM invocations"
Example: "edge caching"

Sources:

  • Understand the cache key

  • Cache content based on query string parameters

  • Cache settings for REST APIs in API Gateway

INCORRECT: Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API, with a cache policy that keeps each response for one day and puts the whole URL path but no query strings in the cache key.
A cache policy with no query strings in the cache key fits a path whose response never depends on the query string, such as a fixed image or script. Here the city and lang values decide which guide a reader gets. With no query strings in the key, every request for the guide path shares one cache key. So a reader who asks for Tokyo in English can get the cached Lisbon guide in Portuguese. Unless an origin request policy adds them, CloudFront also does not send the query strings to the origin, so the function cannot tell which guide to write.

INCORRECT: Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API, with a cache policy that keeps each response for one day and puts the whole URL path and all query strings in the cache key.
Putting all query strings in the cache key fits an API where every parameter changes the response. Here the tracking parameters never change the guide. CloudFront caches a separate copy for every value of each query string in the cache key, even when the origin returns the same guide. So each new utm_source value misses the cache and calls the function and the model again.

INCORRECT: Turn on caching for the API Gateway stage of the REST API, and use the city and lang query strings as the cache key parameters for each cached guide response.
API Gateway stage caching keeps responses in a cache for the stage and can use query strings as cache key parameters. It stops repeat calls to the function, so it suits readers who are close to the API. But the cache sits with the API in its US Region. A reader in Asia or Europe still waits for every request to travel to that Region and back, and the team wants repeated requests answered close to readers.

questions.promptHtml:
A support company keeps its troubleshooting records as JSON documents in an existing Amazon DocumentDB instance-based cluster on the latest engine version. Each record has a problem description, a product line, and a fix. The support application writes every new or changed record to the cluster, and the support team maintains the code of that application.

A new assistant on Amazon Bedrock must find the records whose problem description means the same as a user's question, even when the question uses different words.

The security team approved only this cluster to store the records and any data made from them, such as embeddings.

Which design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A support company keeps its troubleshooting records as JSON documents in an existing Amazon DocumentDB instance-based cluster on the latest engine version. Each record has a problem description, a product line, and a fix. The support application writes every new or changed record to the cluster, and the support team maintains the code of that application.
A new assistant on Amazon Bedrock must find the records whose problem description means the same as a user's question, even when the question uses different words.
The security team approved only this cluster to store the records and any data made from them, such as embeddings.
Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a text index on the problem description field in the cluster, and run text search queries that look for the words of each question in those descriptions.
Export the records to Amazon S3 each night, sync them into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store, and query the knowledge base.
Add an embedding of the problem description as a new field in each record, create an HNSW vector index on that field, and search the index with the embedding of each question.

Send each change from DocumentDB change streams to an AWS Lambda function that writes an embedding of the problem description to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector, and search the embeddings in Aurora.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add an embedding of the problem description as a new field in each record, create an HNSW vector index on that field, and search the index with the embedding of each question.
Amazon DocumentDB can run vector search in an instance-based cluster, on the JSON documents that the cluster already stores. The embedding becomes one more field in each record, beside the problem description, the product line, and the fix. The support application writes every new or changed record, so the application can call an Amazon Bedrock embedding model and add the embedding in the same write. The team adds the new field to the existing records once. AWS recommends the HNSW index type for most vector search uses. Each question is embedded with the same model, and the search returns the records whose meaning is closest. The records and their embeddings stay in the approved cluster.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.1: "Create advanced vector database architectures specifically for FM augmentation to enable efficient semantic retrieval beyond traditional search capabilities"

Sources:

  • Vector search for Amazon DocumentDB

  • Amazon DocumentDB now supports vector search with HNSW index

  • Performing text search with Amazon DocumentDB

INCORRECT: Create a text index on the problem description field in the cluster, and run text search queries that look for the words of each question in those descriptions.
A text index in DocumentDB uses an inverted index with a term frequency algorithm, so it finds records that contain the words of a query. It works well when users search for exact words, such as an error code. Here users describe a problem in their own words, and a record may use other words for the same problem. Word matching misses those records, so it cannot find records by meaning.

INCORRECT: Export the records to Amazon S3 each night, sync them into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store, and query the knowledge base.
A knowledge base with an S3 data source is a common way to build retrieval augmented generation (RAG). Each sync turns the files into embeddings and writes the embeddings to the vector store. This design stores the records in Amazon S3 and their embeddings in the OpenSearch Serverless vector store. The security team approved only the DocumentDB cluster to store the records and any data made from them.

INCORRECT: Send each change from DocumentDB change streams to an AWS Lambda function that writes an embedding of the problem description to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector, and search the embeddings in Aurora.
With Amazon DocumentDB change streams, an AWS Lambda function can receive each change in a cluster and copy the change to a second store. Lambda supports this integration only on some DocumentDB engine versions. Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector is a strong vector store for teams that already run PostgreSQL. Even on a supported engine version, this design breaks the security team's rule. The function writes an embedding of each problem description to an Aurora table. An embedding is data made from a record, and the security team approved only the DocumentDB cluster to store such data.

Users sign in through Amplify Auth with Amazon Cognito. Customers ask follow-up questions, so the bot must keep the earlier messages of each chat. Each reply must appear in the UI while the model writes it. The frontend team has limited backend experience and wants a declarative, low-code approach.
Which solution meets these requirements with the least custom code?
questions.promptText:
A startup is building a customer support portal in React with AWS Amplify. It wants a "Chat with Support Bot" feature that uses a Claude Haiku model in Amazon Bedrock. Users sign in through Amplify Auth with Amazon Cognito. Customers ask follow-up questions, so the bot must keep the earlier messages of each chat. Each reply must appear in the UI while the model writes it. The frontend team has limited backend experience and wants a declarative, low-code approach.
Which solution meets these requirements with the least custom code?

options.text: Define a conversation route in the Amplify data schema with a Claude Haiku model, and use the useAIConversation hook in the chat component to send messages and show replies.
Define a generation route in the Amplify data schema with a Claude Haiku model, and use the useAIGeneration hook in the chat component to send messages and show replies.
Define a conversation route in the Amplify data schema with a Claude Haiku model, and in the chat component use the data client to send messages and handle each stream event.
Define a custom query in the Amplify data schema with an AWS Lambda function that calls a Claude Haiku model, and call the query from the chat component to show replies.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Define a conversation route in the Amplify data schema with a Claude Haiku model, and use the useAIConversation hook in the chat component to send messages and show replies.
A conversation route in the Amplify AI kit is a streaming, multi-turn API. Amplify stores each conversation and its messages in Amazon DynamoDB, so the bot keeps the earlier messages of each chat, and the reply streams to the UI while the model writes it. Conversations belong to one user, so users must sign in with Amplify Auth, which the startup already uses. The useAIConversation hook is the React hook for this route. It manages the multi-turn chat and its messages for the component. The team declares the route in the schema and calls one hook, so it writes very little code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.2: "Develop accessible AI interfaces to accelerate adoption and integration of FMs"
Example: "AWS Amplify to develop declarative UI components"

Sources:

  • Set up AI
  • Architecture
  • Models

INCORRECT: Define a generation route in the Amplify data schema with a Claude Haiku model, and use the useAIGeneration hook in the chat component to send messages and show replies.
A generation route is a single synchronous request and response API, and useAIGeneration is its React hook. It fits one-shot tasks, for example turning a short product description into structured data. Each call is one request and one response, so the earlier messages of a chat are not part of the next question. The reply also comes back as one complete response, so the text cannot appear while the model writes it.

INCORRECT: Define a conversation route in the Amplify data schema with a Claude Haiku model, and in the chat component use the data client to send messages and handle each stream event.
The Amplify data client can also work with a conversation route directly. The code creates or gets the conversation, subscribes to its stream events and sends each message. This fits a frontend that does not use the React hook, such as a plain JavaScript app. Here the portal is built in React, and the team wants the least custom code. With the data client, the component must build each reply from the stream events itself, and the events can arrive out of order. The useAIConversation hook already does this work.

INCORRECT: Define a custom query in the Amplify data schema with an AWS Lambda function that calls a Claude Haiku model, and call the query from the chat component to show replies.
A custom query lets a team write its own business logic in an AWS Lambda function and call it from the generated data client. It fits a task that needs code of its own, which the AI kit routes do not cover. Here the frontend team has limited backend experience and wants the least custom code. The team would write and maintain the function, and it would also build its own storage for the earlier messages of each chat.

questions.promptHtml:
An insurance company builds a customer assistant with Strands Agents and models in Amazon Bedrock. Three specialist agents exist: one explains policy terms, one reads a customer's claims history, and one prices a change to a policy. Each agent has its own prompt, model and tools.
Some requests need one specialist, and others need two or all three. A call to a specialist that a request does not need wastes time. The team will not write routing rules, so a model must choose the specialists for each request. Each specialist must receive only the part of the request that it answers.
Which design should the team use for the assistant?
questions.promptText:
An insurance company builds a customer assistant with Strands Agents and models in Amazon Bedrock. Three specialist agents exist: one explains policy terms, one reads a customer's claims history, and one prices a change to a policy. Each agent has its own prompt, model and tools.
Some requests need one specialist, and others need two or all three. A call to a specialist that a request does not need wastes time. The team will not write routing rules, so a model must choose the specialists for each request. Each specialist must receive only the part of the request that it answers.
Which design should the team use for the assistant?

options.text: Build an orchestrator agent in Strands Agents that calls the specialist agents as its own tools, and that combines the answers they return into one customer reply.
Build a Strands Agents graph that runs the specialist agents as nodes, with edges and conditions that the team writes to choose which specialists each request reaches.
Build a Strands Agents workflow that runs the specialist agents as tasks, with a fixed order that the team writes, so all three specialists answer each request.
Build a Strands Agents swarm in which the specialist agents share one memory of the request, hand the work to each other, and build on each other's answers.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Build an orchestrator agent in Strands Agents that calls the specialist agents as its own tools, and that combines the answers they return into one customer reply.
This is the agents as tools pattern. The team wraps each specialist agent as a tool of a top-level orchestrator agent. A model in the orchestrator agent decides which tools to call for each part of the customer's request. A specialist receives only the information that the orchestrator passes to it, usually its own subtask, and returns its answer. The orchestrator then uses those answers to write one reply. A question about policy terms calls one specialist, and a question about the price of a change after a claim can call all three. Each specialist keeps its own prompt, model and tools, and the team writes no routing rules.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.1: "Develop intelligent autonomous systems with appropriate memory and state management capabilities"
Example: "Strands Agents and AWS Agent Squad for multi-agent systems"

Sources:

  • Multi-Agent collaboration patterns with Strands Agents and Amazon Nova

INCORRECT: Build a Strands Agents graph that runs the specialist agents as nodes, with edges and conditions that the team writes to choose which specialists each request reaches.
A graph in Strands Agents is a network of agents with directed connections. The developers define which agent passes work to which, and conditions on the edges choose the path. A graph fits a multi-stage decision process where the team wants to control every path itself. Here the team will not write routing rules, and a model must choose the specialists. In a graph, the path follows the edges and conditions that the team writes.

INCORRECT: Build a Strands Agents workflow that runs the specialist agents as tasks, with a fixed order that the team writes, so all three specialists answer each request.
A workflow runs agents as a series of tasks in a set order, with dependencies that the team defines. It fits a multi-step task with clear stages that every request goes through. Here many requests need only one specialist, and a call that a request does not need wastes time. A workflow that runs all three agents for every request makes those extra calls.

INCORRECT: Build a Strands Agents swarm in which the specialist agents share one memory of the request, hand the work to each other, and build on each other's answers.
In a swarm, peer agents work together through a shared memory. They exchange findings over several rounds, and each agent refines its results with what the others found. A swarm fits brainstorming and complex reasoning, where agents improve on each other's ideas. Here each specialist must receive only the part of the request that it answers, but a swarm shares its memory of the work with every agent.

A retail company's mobile app calls a REST API in Amazon API Gateway for product answers. The company now adds a review summary feature. A fine-tuned open-weight model writes the summaries. It runs on Amazon ECS tasks in private subnets, behind an internal Network Load Balancer.
The security team allows no public endpoint on the model service or on any load balancer in front of it. The mobile app must reach the new feature through the same REST API over the internet. The team will not add code between the API and the model service.
How should the team connect the REST API to the model service?
questions.promptText:
A retail company's mobile app calls a REST API in Amazon API Gateway for product answers. The company now adds a review summary feature. A fine-tuned open-weight model writes the summaries. It runs on Amazon ECS tasks in private subnets, behind an internal Network Load Balancer.
The security team allows no public endpoint on the model service or on any load balancer in front of it. The mobile app must reach the new feature through the same REST API over the internet. The team will not add code between the API and the model service.
How should the team connect the REST API to the model service?

options.text: Create a VPC link for the internal Network Load Balancer, and add a private integration from the new REST API method to the model service through that VPC link.
Put an internet-facing Network Load Balancer in front of the model service, and add an HTTP integration from the new REST API method to its public DNS name.
Change the REST API to a private API, and give the mobile app access to the new method through an interface VPC endpoint in the model service's VPC.
Attach an AWS Lambda function to the model service's VPC, and add a Lambda proxy integration from the new REST API method that forwards each request to the load balancer.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a VPC link for the internal Network Load Balancer, and add a private integration from the new REST API method to the model service through that VPC link.
A private integration lets API Gateway expose HTTP or HTTPS resources inside a VPC to clients outside the VPC. The team creates a VPC link, and the new method gets an HTTP proxy integration that sends each request through the VPC link to the internal Network Load Balancer. An internal load balancer has only private IP addresses, so the model service still has no public endpoint. The mobile app keeps calling the public REST API over the internet, and API Gateway passes each request to the model service with no code in between.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.2: "Develop integrated AI capabilities to enhance existing applications with GenAI functionality"
Example: "API Gateway to implement microservice integrations"

Sources:

  • Private integrations for REST APIs in API Gateway
  • Set up a private integration
  • Private REST APIs in API Gateway

INCORRECT: Put an internet-facing Network Load Balancer in front of the model service, and add an HTTP integration from the new REST API method to its public DNS name.
An internet-facing load balancer has public IP addresses, and its DNS name resolves to them, so it can take requests from clients over the internet. An HTTP integration to that name works well when the backend may have a public endpoint. Here the security team allows no public endpoint on any load balancer in front of the model service.

INCORRECT: Change the REST API to a private API, and give the mobile app access to the new method through an interface VPC endpoint in the model service's VPC.
A private API is a REST API that clients can call only from within a VPC, through an interface VPC endpoint. Its traffic stays isolated from the public internet. It fits internal tools that run inside the company's network. Here the mobile app calls the API over the internet, so it cannot reach a private API.

INCORRECT: Attach an AWS Lambda function to the model service's VPC, and add a Lambda proxy integration from the new REST API method that forwards each request to the load balancer.
A Lambda function attached to a VPC can reach resources in the private subnets of that VPC, such as the internal load balancer. A function between the API and the backend fits when each request needs logic of its own on the way, such as a change to its format. Here the team will not add code between the API and the model service, and this function is new code that the team must write and maintain.

A legal services company hosts a fine-tuned open-weight assistant model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Company data rules allow user prompts and answers to be sent only to the company's own SageMaker AI endpoints. The trust team has written its own list of unsafe content categories in plain text. Testers found prompts that make the assistant ignore the rules in its system prompt.
No unsafe prompt may reach the assistant, and no unsafe answer may reach a user.

questions.promptText:
A legal services company hosts a fine-tuned open-weight assistant model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Company data rules allow user prompts and answers to be sent only to the company's own SageMaker AI endpoints. The trust team has written its own list of unsafe content categories in plain text. Testers found prompts that make the assistant ignore the rules in its system prompt.
No unsafe prompt may reach the assistant, and no unsafe answer may reach a user.
Which design adds the safety check that the company needs?

options.text: Deploy a Llama Guard model from SageMaker JumpStart to an endpoint, check each prompt and each answer against the trust team's categories, and stop each one that it marks unsafe.
Deploy a Llama Guard model from SageMaker JumpStart to an endpoint, check the logged prompts and answers of each day against the trust team's categories at night, and report unsafe ones.
Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic for each category, call the ApplyGuardrail API on each prompt and each answer, and stop each one that it blocks.
Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic for each category, call the ApplyGuardrail API on the logged prompts and answers of each day at night, and report unsafe ones.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Deploy a Llama Guard model from SageMaker JumpStart to an endpoint, check each prompt and each answer against the trust team's categories, and stop each one that it marks unsafe.
Llama Guard is a safety classifier model that gives input and output safeguards for applications that use large language models. SageMaker JumpStart deploys it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in the company's own account, so prompts and answers go only to the company's own endpoints. The team writes the meaning of each unsafe content category in plain text in the Llama Guard prompt, so the trust team's own list works. Llama Guard answers "safe" or "unsafe", and for unsafe content it lists the categories that were violated. The application checks each prompt before the assistant reads it, and each answer before the user sees it. Llama Guard is a separate model with its own prompt, so the check does not depend on the assistant following its system prompt.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.5: "Implement advanced threat detection to protect against adversarial inputs and security vulnerabilities"
Example: "safety classifiers"

Sources:

  • Llama Guard is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
  • Use the ApplyGuardrail API in your application
  • Block denied topics to help remove harmful content

INCORRECT: Deploy a Llama Guard model from SageMaker JumpStart to an endpoint, check the logged prompts and answers of each day against the trust team's categories at night, and report unsafe ones.
The same Llama Guard endpoint can also check prompts and answers later, from the logs. A nightly check fits an audit, where the trust team reviews what happened in past chats. Here no unsafe answer may reach a user. A check that runs at night finds an unsafe answer only after the user has already read it.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic for each category, call the ApplyGuardrail API on each prompt and each answer, and stop each one that it blocks.
The ApplyGuardrail API checks text with an existing Amazon Bedrock guardrail without calling a foundation model, so it can also check the prompts and answers of a model that runs on SageMaker AI. A denied topic has a name and a plain language definition, so each category could become one topic. This design fits a company that may send its text to Amazon Bedrock. Here the data rules allow prompts and answers to be sent only to the company's own SageMaker AI endpoints, and the guardrail check runs in Amazon Bedrock.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic for each category, call the ApplyGuardrail API on the logged prompts and answers of each day at night, and report unsafe ones.
This design runs the same guardrail as an audit. Each night, the team sends the logged prompts and answers of the day to the ApplyGuardrail API and reports what the guardrail would block. It fits a company that may send its text to Amazon Bedrock and wants to review past chats. Here it fails two needs. The data rules keep prompts and answers inside the company's own SageMaker AI endpoints, and a check at night comes after the user has already read an unsafe answer.

questions.promptHtml:
A company runs a public generative AI chatbot on Amazon Bedrock behind Amazon API Gateway. Users connect from many countries. A botnet recently flooded the endpoint with millions of junk requests. The flood consumed the Bedrock provisioned throughput, and real users started receiving throttling errors.
The security team must stop this traffic before it reaches Bedrock. The company also requires that blocked requests produce no request charges and no data transfer charges from the service that receives the traffic first. The solution must rely on managed features and avoid custom code.
Which solution meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A company runs a public generative AI chatbot on Amazon Bedrock behind Amazon API Gateway. Users connect from many countries. A botnet recently flooded the endpoint with millions of junk requests. The flood consumed the Bedrock provisioned throughput, and real users started receiving throttling errors.
The security team must stop this traffic before it reaches Bedrock. The company also requires that blocked requests produce no request charges and no data transfer charges from the service that receives the traffic first. The solution must rely on managed features and avoid custom code.
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Put Amazon CloudFront in front of API Gateway. Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the distribution and add a rate-based rule that blocks offending addresses.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL directly with the API Gateway stage. Add a rate-based rule that blocks any IP address exceeding the request threshold.
Put Amazon CloudFront in front of API Gateway. Set the AWS WAF rate-based rule action to Count, then trigger a Lambda function to update an IP set.
Create an API Gateway usage plan with throttling and quota limits. Apply the plan to the chatbot stage so the service rejects clients that exceed the rate.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Put Amazon CloudFront in front of API Gateway. Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the distribution and add a rate-based rule that blocks offending addresses.
AWS WAF rules attached to a CloudFront distribution run in every edge location worldwide, and blocked requests stop before they reach the backend. This suits a global user base. It also satisfies the billing requirement, because CloudFront applies no request or data transfer charges to requests that AWS WAF blocks. Rate-based rules track request volume per address automatically, so the team writes no code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.3: "Create resilient FM systems to ensure reliable operations"

Sources:

  • Amazon CloudFront no longer charges for requests blocked by AWS WAF
  • Rate-based rule high-level settings in AWS WAF
  • API Gateway pricing

INCORRECT: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL directly with the API Gateway stage. Add a rate-based rule that blocks any IP address exceeding the request threshold.
A web ACL on the API Gateway stage is a regional AWS WAF setup. Its rate-based rule blocks the flood before it reaches Bedrock, with no custom code, and it fits an API that does not sit behind CloudFront. Here the company also requires that blocked requests produce no request charges and no data transfer charges from the service that receives the traffic first. In this design, API Gateway receives the traffic first, and AWS publishes this waiver for requests blocked on CloudFront only.

INCORRECT: Put Amazon CloudFront in front of API Gateway. Set the AWS WAF rate-based rule action to Count, then trigger a Lambda function to update an IP set.
The Count action only records matching requests and lets them continue to the origin. Nothing gets blocked while the workflow runs, so the flood still reaches Bedrock. The billing waiver applies only to requests that a Block action stops, so counted requests remain billable. The Lambda and IP set logic also adds custom code, which the requirement rules out.

INCORRECT: Create an API Gateway usage plan with throttling and quota limits. Apply the plan to the chatbot stage so the service rejects clients that exceed the rate.
A usage plan sets a request rate and a quota for each API key, and API Gateway uses the key to tell clients apart. It fits an API whose known clients each hold their own key. This chatbot is public, and its real users carry no API key. If the chatbot methods required a key, API Gateway would reject the real users together with the botnet. AWS also advises against relying on usage plan throttling and quotas to block access to an API, because API Gateway applies them on a best-effort basis.

After some releases, a few letters take far longer or fail. The team uses AWS X-Ray, but each trace shows only the function itself. When the team opens a slow trace, it must see each model call with the template name and version that this call used.
What should the team change in the function?
questions.promptText:
A bank's AWS Lambda function, written in Python, drafts each loan letter with three calls to a model through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. Each call uses its own prompt template, and the team stores a name and a version number with each template. New template versions ship every week.
After some releases, a few letters take far longer or fail. The team uses AWS X-Ray, but each trace shows only the function itself. When the team opens a slow trace, it must see each model call with the template name and version that this call used.
What should the team change in the function?

options.text: Add an ADOT Lambda layer to the function, wrap each Amazon Bedrock call in its own span, and set the template name and version as attributes on that span.
Add an ADOT Lambda layer to the function, keep the Amazon Bedrock calls as they are, and set all three template names and versions as attributes on the root span.
Send the template name and version in the requestMetadata of each Converse call, turn on model invocation logging, and find the slow calls with CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Publish a CloudWatch custom metric with the duration of each Converse call, add the template name and version as dimensions, and graph the slow calls on a dashboard.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add an ADOT Lambda layer to the function, wrap each Amazon Bedrock call in its own span, and set the template name and version as attributes on that span.
AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) Lambda layers package what the function needs to collect traces with OpenTelemetry, and AWS recommends OpenTelemetry instrumentation to trace Lambda functions in X-Ray. In the code, the team starts a span around each model call and adds the template name and version to it with set_attribute. Each span has its own start and end time, so the trace shows how long each of the three calls took. X-Ray shows span attributes as metadata on that part of the trace by default, and the keys that the team lists under aws.xray.annotations become annotations that it can search. When the team opens a slow trace, it sees which call took long and which template version that call used.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.5: "Troubleshoot prompt maintenance issues to continuously improve the performance of FM interactions"
Example: "X-Ray to implement prompt observability pipelines"

Sources:

  • Migrate to OpenTelemetry Python

  • Instrumenting Python code in AWS Lambda

  • Converse

INCORRECT: Add an ADOT Lambda layer to the function, keep the Amazon Bedrock calls as they are, and set all three template names and versions as attributes on the root span.
The root span stands for the whole invocation of the function. Attributes on it fit a function that uses one template in each invocation, because the one name and version then describe the whole trace. Here each letter uses three templates. The trace would show all three names and versions together on the root span, not on the call that used each one. When one call is slow, the trace does not say which template that call used.

INCORRECT: Send the template name and version in the requestMetadata of each Converse call, turn on model invocation logging, and find the slow calls with CloudWatch Logs Insights.
The requestMetadata field of a Converse call holds key and value pairs that the team can use to filter model invocation logs. With logging on, CloudWatch Logs Insights can find all the calls of one template version. This fits a search across many logged calls. Here the team must see the template and version inside the X-Ray trace that it opens, and the invocation logs are not part of that trace.

INCORRECT: Publish a CloudWatch custom metric with the duration of each Converse call, add the template name and version as dimensions, and graph the slow calls on a dashboard.
A custom metric with a dimension for each template name and version lets a dashboard show how the call time of each template version changes over time. This fits trends and alarms. A metric holds numbers over time, not single requests. It does not show which template each call used inside the slow trace that the team opens.

questions.promptText:
A media company wants to build a "Meeting Minutes Generator" using Amazon Bedrock. The input data consists of MP3 audio recordings of meetings stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The Claude Sonnet model that the team uses on Amazon Bedrock cannot read MP3 files.
An outside vendor also transcribes some meetings. It uploads its transcript files, in the same JSON format that Amazon Transcribe writes, to the S3 bucket where the pipeline keeps transcripts.
Which processing pipeline prepares this data for the model with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: An S3 event notification starts a Lambda function that calls StartTranscriptionJob with the transcripts bucket as OutputBucketName. S3 event notifications on that bucket start a function that sends the text to Amazon Bedrock.

An S3 event notification starts a Lambda function that calls StartTranscriptionJob with the transcripts bucket as OutputBucketName. An EventBridge rule on Transcribe job COMPLETED events starts a function that sends the text to Amazon Bedrock.

An S3 event notification starts a Lambda function that calls StartTranscriptionJob. The same function calls GetTranscriptionJob in a loop until the status is COMPLETED, then sends the transcript text to Amazon Bedrock.

An S3 event notification starts a Lambda function that sends the MP3 file to Amazon Transcribe streaming with StartStreamTranscription. The same function then sends the returned transcript text to Amazon Bedrock.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: An S3 event notification starts a Lambda function that calls StartTranscriptionJob with the transcripts bucket as OutputBucketName. S3 event notifications on that bucket start a function that sends the text to Amazon Bedrock.
This pipeline has two steps, and Amazon S3 starts both of them. The first function starts a batch transcription job. Amazon Transcribe reads the MP3 file from S3 and writes the transcript as a JSON file to the bucket that OutputBucketName names. When a JSON file lands in that bucket, an S3 event notification starts the second function. That function reads the transcript text out of the JSON file and sends it to the Claude Sonnet model. The vendor puts its transcripts in the same bucket, so the same notification starts the second step for those files too. The team writes nothing extra for the vendor files.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.2: "Create data processing workflows to handle complex data types including text, image, audio, and tabular data with specialized processing requirements for FM consumption"
Example: "AWS Transcribe"

Sources:

  • StartTranscriptionJob

  • Using Amazon EventBridge with Amazon Transcribe

  • Data input and output

INCORRECT: An S3 event notification starts a Lambda function that calls StartTranscriptionJob with the transcripts bucket as OutputBucketName. An EventBridge rule on Transcribe job COMPLETED events starts a function that sends the text to Amazon Bedrock.
Amazon Transcribe sends a Transcribe Job State Change event to Amazon EventBridge when a transcription job ends with the status COMPLETED or FAILED. A rule on that event is a good way to start the next step when every transcript comes from a Transcribe job. Here, the vendor uploads some transcripts itself. No Transcribe job runs for those files, so no event is sent, and those meetings never get minutes.

INCORRECT: An S3 event notification starts a Lambda function that calls StartTranscriptionJob. The same function calls GetTranscriptionJob in a loop until the status is COMPLETED, then sends the transcript text to Amazon Bedrock.
GetTranscriptionJob returns the status of a job, and COMPLETED means that the transcript is ready. A loop that checks the status can work in a simple script for a short audio clip. Here, the function waits and uses compute time for the whole transcription of each meeting. The loop also runs only for jobs that this function started. The vendor's transcripts never pass through it, so they never reach the model.

INCORRECT: An S3 event notification starts a Lambda function that sends the MP3 file to Amazon Transcribe streaming with StartStreamTranscription. The same function then sends the returned transcript text to Amazon Bedrock.
Amazon Transcribe streaming turns audio into text in real time, for example for live captions or call center monitoring. Streaming accepts FLAC, Ogg Opus and PCM audio. It does not accept MP3. The meeting recordings are MP3 files, so this function cannot send them as they are. Batch transcription with StartTranscriptionJob reads MP3 files from S3 directly.

A company keeps its closed support cases and their resolution notes in Salesforce. Its support assistant answers from a customer-managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with one Amazon S3 data source, which already holds every older case. A schedule already starts a sync of the knowledge base every morning.
Each night's new and changed cases must be in the knowledge base after the next sync. The team will keep the one S3 data source. The Salesforce administrators will not turn on Change Data Capture. No one will run a manual step, and the team will maintain no custom code.
Which solution meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A company keeps its closed support cases and their resolution notes in Salesforce. Its support assistant answers from a customer-managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with one Amazon S3 data source, which already holds every older case. A schedule already starts a sync of the knowledge base every morning.
Each night's new and changed cases must be in the knowledge base after the next sync. The team will keep the one S3 data source. The Salesforce administrators will not turn on Change Data Capture. No one will run a manual step, and the team will maintain no custom code.
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon AppFlow flow from Salesforce to the S3 bucket that runs every night on a schedule and writes the new and changed case records as CSV files.
Create an Amazon AppFlow flow from Salesforce to the S3 bucket that runs on each Salesforce change event and writes every new or changed case record as a CSV file.
Create an AWS Lambda function that an Amazon EventBridge rule on the Salesforce partner event bus starts on each case change, and that writes the record to the bucket as a CSV file.
Create an AWS Lambda function that a nightly EventBridge Scheduler schedule starts, and that calls the Salesforce REST API and writes new and changed cases to the bucket as CSV files.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an Amazon AppFlow flow from Salesforce to the S3 bucket that runs every night on a schedule and writes the new and changed case records as CSV files.
Amazon AppFlow copies data between SaaS applications, such as Salesforce, and AWS services without code. A flow with a schedule trigger runs by itself, so it copies the cases every night with no manual step. With incremental transfer, the flow copies only the records that were added or changed since the last successful run. The older cases are already in the bucket, so new and changed records are all that the flow needs to copy. The S3 destination can write CSV files, a format that a knowledge base reads. The next morning's sync then picks up the new files from the same S3 data source.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.4: "Use AWS services to create integration components to connect with resources"
Example: "knowledge bases"

Sources:

  • Flow triggers
  • Salesforce connector for Amazon AppFlow
  • Connect to Amazon S3 for your knowledge base

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon AppFlow flow from Salesforce to the S3 bucket that runs on each Salesforce change event and writes every new or changed case record as a CSV file.
A flow can also run on an event from Salesforce. This fits when each change must reach AWS a short time after it happens. To use event triggers, Salesforce must have Change Data Capture turned on. The administrators will not turn it on, so this flow never receives an event and never runs.

INCORRECT: Create an AWS Lambda function that an Amazon EventBridge rule on the Salesforce partner event bus starts on each case change, and that writes the record to the bucket as a CSV file.
Salesforce can send change events to a partner event bus in Amazon EventBridge, and a rule on that bus can start a Lambda function for each event. This fits a team that wants its own code to act on each change soon after it happens. Here the team will maintain no custom code. This design needs a function that the team writes and maintains, which turns each event into a case record and writes the CSV files, while Amazon AppFlow already has a managed connector for Salesforce.

INCORRECT: Create an AWS Lambda function that a nightly EventBridge Scheduler schedule starts, and that calls the Salesforce REST API and writes new and changed cases to the bucket as CSV files.
A Lambda function on a schedule can read records through the Salesforce API and write them to Amazon S3. This fits a source that has no managed connector. Here, the team would own that code: the sign-in, the queries for changed records, the paging and the file writing. The team will maintain no custom code, and Amazon AppFlow already has a managed connector for Salesforce.
