questions.promptHtml:
An e-commerce company is fine-tuning a model on product reviews. The training data is stored in Amazon S3 as CSV files. A data scientist discovers that 15% of the reviews are empty strings or NULL values, which will degrade model quality.
An AWS Glue ETL job loads each new dataset into the training bucket. The team needs an automated solution that blocks a dataset from the training pipeline when 2% or more of its reviews are empty or NULL. Datasets with fewer such reviews must still reach the training pipeline.
Which solution should the developer implement?
questions.promptText:
An e-commerce company is fine-tuning a model on product reviews. The training data is stored in Amazon S3 as CSV files. A data scientist discovers that 15% of the reviews are empty strings or NULL values, which will degrade model quality.
An AWS Glue ETL job loads each new dataset into the training bucket. The team needs an automated solution that blocks a dataset from the training pipeline when 2% or more of its reviews are empty or NULL. Datasets with fewer such reviews must still reach the training pipeline.
Which solution should the developer implement?

options.text: In the Glue ETL job, add an Evaluate Data Quality node with the rule ColumnValues "review_text" not in [NULL, EMPTY] with threshold > 0.98, and fail the job without loading data.
In the Glue ETL job, add an Evaluate Data Quality node with the rule Completeness "review_text" > 0.98, and send the results to Amazon EventBridge.
In the Glue ETL job, add an Evaluate Data Quality node with the rule Completeness "review_text" > 0.98, and fail the job without loading data.
In the Glue ETL job, add an Evaluate Data Quality node with the rule ColumnValues "review_text" not in [NULL, EMPTY] with threshold > 0.98, and send the results to Amazon EventBridge.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: In the Glue ETL job, add an Evaluate Data Quality node with the rule ColumnValues "review_text" not in [NULL, EMPTY] with threshold > 0.98, and fail the job without loading data.
ColumnValues checks the value in each row. The not in list names the values that count as bad: NULL, and EMPTY, the keyword for an empty string. A not in rule passes NULL rows unless NULL is in the list, so here both kinds of bad review fail the check. The with threshold clause sets the share of rows that must pass, here more than 98 percent. A dataset with 2 percent or more bad reviews fails the ruleset, and a dataset with fewer passes. The job action "Fail job without loading to target data" stops the job at once when the ruleset fails, so the dataset never reaches the training bucket.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.1: "Create comprehensive data validation workflows to ensure data meets quality standards for FM consumption"
Example: "AWS Glue Data Quality"

Sources:

  • Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL) reference
  • Evaluating data quality for ETL jobs in AWS Glue Studio
  • ColumnValues

INCORRECT: In the Glue ETL job, add an Evaluate Data Quality node with the rule Completeness "review_text" > 0.98, and send the results to Amazon EventBridge.
Completeness measures the share of values in a column that are not NULL. Here it checks that more than 98 percent of the reviews are not NULL, and Amazon EventBridge receives the result of each evaluation, so a rule can alert the team. This fits a team that only needs a notice, for a column where missing data shows up as NULL. Two stated facts rule it out here. First, the reviews sit in CSV files, and a blank value in a string column is read as an empty string, not as NULL, so empty reviews do not fail this rule. Second, the team must block bad datasets. Sending results to EventBridge does not stop the job, and the job keeps the default action on ruleset failure, None, so it still loads every dataset.

INCORRECT: In the Glue ETL job, add an Evaluate Data Quality node with the rule Completeness "review_text" > 0.98, and fail the job without loading data.
Completeness measures the share of values in a column that are not NULL, and a value such as 0.98 sets the minimum share. It fits columns where missing data shows up as NULL. In a CSV file, a blank value in a string column is read as an empty string, not as NULL, so it does not fail this rule. A dataset full of empty reviews can still pass and reach the training bucket.

INCORRECT: In the Glue ETL job, add an Evaluate Data Quality node with the rule ColumnValues "review_text" not in [NULL, EMPTY] with threshold > 0.98, and send the results to Amazon EventBridge.
This rule finds the bad datasets correctly. Glue Data Quality can publish its results to Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon EventBridge, and a rule can then send an alert. That fits a team that only needs a notice. Here, the job keeps the default action on ruleset failure, None, so it does not fail and still loads the dataset. The team must block bad datasets, not only hear about them.

questions.promptHtml:
A legal research company runs an AI agent for lawyers from many client firms. In each conversation, a lawyer uploads case files, and the agent keeps the files and its working notes in memory and on disk across many turns. Each conversation lasts less than one hour.

Security rules say that no conversation may reach the files or data of another conversation. This rule also applies to two lawyers at the same firm. A conversation ends when the lawyer sends no message for 15 minutes. The hosting service must then delete the data of that conversation on its own. The team will not build code that starts and stops compute for each conversation.

Which hosting design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A legal research company runs an AI agent for lawyers from many client firms. In each conversation, a lawyer uploads case files, and the agent keeps the files and its working notes in memory and on disk across many turns. Each conversation lasts less than one hour.
Security rules say that no conversation may reach the files or data of another conversation. This rule also applies to two lawyers at the same firm. A conversation ends when the lawyer sends no message for 15 minutes. The hosting service must then delete the data of that conversation on its own. The team will not build code that starts and stops compute for each conversation.
Which hosting design meets these requirements?

options.text: Host the agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, and have the backend send a new runtimeSessionId for each conversation and the same ID with every turn of that conversation.
Host the agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, and have the backend send one runtimeSessionId for each client firm and the same ID with every turn of that firm's conversations.
Host the agent in an AWS Lambda function, and keep each conversation's case files and working notes in the /tmp directory so that later turns can read them.
Host the agent on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate, and have the backend start one task for each conversation and stop that task when the conversation ends.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Host the agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, and have the backend send a new runtimeSessionId for each conversation and the same ID with every turn of that conversation.
AgentCore Runtime gives each session its own microVM, with its own compute, memory, and file system. The backend starts a session on the first call with a new runtimeSessionId. Later calls with the same ID reach the same microVM while the microVM runs. By default, AgentCore Runtime stops the microVM after 15 minutes with no requests. A conversation ends at the same point, so every pause inside a conversation is shorter than 15 minutes, and the microVM keeps running. A microVM can run for up to 8 hours, and each conversation lasts less than one hour. So the conversation keeps its files and notes for every turn. A conversation in one microVM cannot reach the data of a conversation in another. When the microVM stops, AgentCore Runtime terminates the microVM and sanitizes its memory, with no call from the backend.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.1: "Develop intelligent autonomous systems with appropriate memory and state management capabilities"

Sources:

  • Use isolated sessions for agents

  • Understanding the Lambda execution environment lifecycle

  • Fargate security considerations for Amazon ECS

INCORRECT: Host the agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, and have the backend send one runtimeSessionId for each client firm and the same ID with every turn of that firm's conversations.
This design uses AgentCore Runtime, but one session covers a whole firm instead of one conversation. Calls with the same session ID reach the same microVM, so they share its memory and its files. One session for a whole group fits only when everyone in that group may see the same files. Here, all conversations of one firm would run in one microVM, so one lawyer's files would be open to the other lawyers of that firm. The security rules forbid that, even inside one firm. Each conversation needs its own session ID.

INCORRECT: Host the agent in an AWS Lambda function, and keep each conversation's case files and working notes in the /tmp directory so that later turns can read them.
Lambda keeps an execution environment after a call and can reuse it for later calls of the same function. Files in /tmp stay there between those calls, which makes /tmp a good cache for shared reference data. But the environment does not belong to one conversation. A later call from another conversation can run in the same environment and find the files. Lambda also ends environments on its own schedule, for example every few hours for maintenance, not when a conversation ends.

INCORRECT: Host the agent on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate, and have the backend start one task for each conversation and stop that task when the conversation ends.
Each Fargate task runs in its own isolated environment and shares no CPU, memory, storage or network interface with other tasks. So one task for each conversation meets the security rules. This fits a team that wants full control of the containers. Here, the team must write the code that starts a task for each new conversation, sends each turn to the right task, and stops the task at the end. The team will not build that code.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
A company's help center app stores its articles in an Amazon Aurora database. A support chatbot answers from a customer-managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Editors publish, change and remove articles all day.
Each published, changed or removed article must show in the chatbot's answers within a minute. The legal team allows article text in only two places: the database and the knowledge base. The team will write no chunking or embedding code.
Which design keeps the knowledge base current?
questions.promptText:
A company's help center app stores its articles in an Amazon Aurora database. A support chatbot answers from a customer-managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Editors publish, change and remove articles all day.
Each published, changed or removed article must show in the chatbot's answers within a minute. The legal team allows article text in only two places: the database and the knowledge base. The team will write no chunking or embedding code.
Which design keeps the knowledge base current?

options.text: Add a custom data source to the knowledge base, and have the app call IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments for each new or changed article and DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments for each removed one.
Add an S3 data source to the knowledge base, have the app write and delete article files in its bucket, and start a sync of that data source every hour.
Add an S3 data source to the knowledge base, have the app write and delete article files in its bucket, and call StartIngestionJob after each change.
Have the app chunk each changed article, embed the chunks with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and update an OpenSearch Serverless index that the chatbot searches directly.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a custom data source to the knowledge base, and have the app call IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments for each new or changed article and DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments for each removed one.
A custom data source takes documents that the application sends through API calls. IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments adds or updates documents, and DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments removes them. Each call indexes the change into the vector store in a single step, so the app never waits for a sync job. The app can send the article text inline in the call, so no copy goes to another store. The knowledge base chunks each document with the chunking settings of the data source and embeds it with its own embedding model, so the team writes no chunking or embedding code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.4.5: "Design and deploy data maintenance systems to ensure that vector stores contain current and accurate information for FM augmentation"
Example: "incremental update mechanisms"

Sources:

  • Ingest changes directly into a knowledge base
  • Connect your knowledge base to a custom data source
  • Sync your data with your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base

INCORRECT: Add an S3 data source to the knowledge base, have the app write and delete article files in its bucket, and start a sync of that data source every hour.
An S3 data source with a scheduled sync is a simple pattern for content that changes a few times a day. Each sync processes only the files that were added, changed or deleted since the last sync. Here, a change can wait up to an hour for the next sync, and the rule is one minute. The bucket also holds a copy of every article, and the legal team allows article text only in the database and the knowledge base.

INCORRECT: Add an S3 data source to the knowledge base, have the app write and delete article files in its bucket, and call StartIngestionJob after each change.
StartIngestionJob starts a sync of the data source, and the sync processes only the changed files. This fits documents that already live in Amazon S3. Here, the app must first write every article as a file to the bucket. That bucket becomes a third place that holds article text, which the legal team does not allow.

INCORRECT: Have the app chunk each changed article, embed the chunks with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and update an OpenSearch Serverless index that the chatbot searches directly.
A team that builds its own retrieval pipeline splits each document into chunks, creates embeddings for the chunks and writes them to its own vector index. This fits a team that wants full control of each step. Here, the team will write no chunking or embedding code, and this design needs both. The chatbot would also stop using the knowledge base.

questions.promptHtml:
A manufacturer builds an order tracking agent with Strands Agents. Each morning, the agent must check the status of open orders in a supplier's web portal. The supplier offers no API. The portal shows an order's status only after a user signs in and clicks through pages that JavaScript builds after they load.
The team will not run or patch its own servers or containers for this task.
Which tool should the team give the agent?
questions.promptText:
A manufacturer builds an order tracking agent with Strands Agents. Each morning, the agent must check the status of open orders in a supplier's web portal. The supplier offers no API. The portal shows an order's status only after a user signs in and clicks through pages that JavaScript builds after they load.
The team will not run or patch its own servers or containers for this task.
Which tool should the team give the agent?

options.text: Give the agent the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser tool, so it drives a managed browser session with Playwright to sign in and read each order status.
Give the agent an AWS Lambda function as a tool that requests the portal pages over HTTPS with stored credentials and returns each order status from the HTML.
Give the agent an AWS Lambda function as a tool that calls the supplier's order status API with stored credentials and returns each order status from the JSON.
Give the agent headless Chrome browsers that run in containers on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate, so it drives them with Playwright to sign in and read each status.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Give the agent the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser tool, so it drives a managed browser session with Playwright to sign in and read each order status.
AgentCore Browser gives an agent a browser that AWS runs. The agent can open websites, fill in forms, click buttons and read content that the page builds while it loads. This is how an agent works with a web application that has no API. Libraries such as Playwright control the browser session. Each session runs isolated from other sessions, and the service scales by itself, so the team runs and patches no servers or containers.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.7: "Develop model extension frameworks to enhance FM capabilities"

Sources:

  • Interact with web applications using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser
  • Introducing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool

INCORRECT: Give the agent an AWS Lambda function as a tool that requests the portal pages over HTTPS with stored credentials and returns each order status from the HTML.
A function that downloads a page and reads its HTML works well for simple pages where the server sends the full content. Here, the portal builds its pages with JavaScript in the browser, after a user signs in and clicks. A plain HTTPS request returns the page before that code runs, and stored credentials do not change this. The order status is not in the HTML that the function reads.

INCORRECT: Give the agent an AWS Lambda function as a tool that calls the supplier's order status API with stored credentials and returns each order status from the JSON.
A Lambda function that calls a partner's API is a common and reliable tool when the partner offers an API. The function returns exact data that the agent can use. Here, the supplier offers no API, so there is nothing for this function to call.

INCORRECT: Give the agent headless Chrome browsers that run in containers on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate, so it drives them with Playwright to sign in and read each status.
A headless browser in a container can sign in and click through pages just like a user, so it can read the portal. This fits a team that wants full control of its browsers. Here, the team must build the container images, patch the browser and its operating system, and scale the containers. The team will not run or patch its own servers or containers for this task.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
An online retailer uses a model on Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API to write a summary for each catalog item. The prompt template asks the model to end each summary with a line that reads [END]. Model invocation logs show that after this line, the model often adds a long notes section that the website never shows.
Output tokens make up most of the cost. Summaries vary from two sentences to several paragraphs, and the website must never show a cut summary.
Which change should the team make to lower the cost?
questions.promptText:
An online retailer uses a model on Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API to write a summary for each catalog item. The prompt template asks the model to end each summary with a line that reads [END]. Model invocation logs show that after this line, the model often adds a long notes section that the website never shows.
Output tokens make up most of the cost. Summaries vary from two sentences to several paragraphs, and the website must never show a cut summary.
Which change should the team make to lower the cost?

options.text: Add [END] to the stopSequences list of each Converse request, so the model stops generating right after it writes the end line.
Set maxTokens in each Converse request to the output token count of the longest summary that the model invocation logs show.
After each call, have the AWS Lambda function delete the notes section after the [END] line before it stores the summary for the website.
After each call, have a smaller model delete the notes section after the [END] line before the function stores the summary for the website.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add [END] to the stopSequences list of each Converse request, so the model stops generating right after it writes the end line.
A stop sequence is a sequence of characters that makes the model stop generating. When the model generates a stop sequence from the request, it stops right after that sequence. The template already makes the model end each summary with [END], so this line can serve as the stop sequence. The model then stops at the end of every summary, long or short, and never writes the notes section. Amazon Bedrock charges for the output tokens that the model generates, so the cost of the notes goes away, and each summary still arrives complete.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.1: "Develop token efficiency systems to reduce FM costs while maintaining effectiveness"
Example: "response limiting"

Sources:

  • Influence response generation with inference parameters
  • InferenceConfiguration
  • GENCOST03-BP02 Control model response length

INCORRECT: Set maxTokens in each Converse request to the output token count of the longest summary that the model invocation logs show.
maxTokens caps the number of tokens that the model may generate in one response. A cap fits outputs whose length stays about the same from request to request. Here summaries vary from two sentences to several paragraphs. A cap at the longest summary still leaves room for a long notes section after every short summary. A new summary that is longer than any in the logs would also be cut, and the website must never show a cut summary.

INCORRECT: After each call, have the AWS Lambda function delete the notes section after the [END] line before it stores the summary for the website.
Removing text in a Lambda function is a simple way to clean a response before the application stores or shows it. It fits a team that only needs to control what users see. Here the model has already generated the notes before the function runs, and Amazon Bedrock charges for those output tokens. The website looks right, but the cost stays the same.

INCORRECT: After each call, have a smaller model delete the notes section after the [END] line before the function stores the summary for the website.
A second, smaller model can clean or shorten text when the cleaning rules are hard to write in code. Here the main model has already generated the notes, and Amazon Bedrock charges for them. The second call adds its own input and output tokens, so the total cost goes up, not down.

questions.promptText:
A retail company wants to build a customer support chatbot using Amazon Bedrock that answers product questions by retrieving information from its product catalog stored in Amazon S3 (10,000 product documents in PDF format). The chatbot must generate natural language responses based on retrieved product information, not just return search results. Customers describe what they need in their own words and rarely know product names. The vectors must stay in the company's existing Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector search collection, and Claude models on Amazon Bedrock write the responses.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the S3 bucket as its data source and the existing collection as its vector store, and have the chatbot call the RetrieveAndGenerate API.
Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the S3 bucket as its data source and the existing collection as its vector store, and have the chatbot call Retrieve, then Converse.
Write Lambda functions that chunk the PDFs, embed the chunks with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and index them in the existing collection, and have the chatbot search it and call Converse.
Extract each product's text into an Amazon DynamoDB table keyed by product name, and have the chatbot look up the named product and send its text to a Claude model.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the S3 bucket as its data source and the existing collection as its vector store, and have the chatbot call the RetrieveAndGenerate API.
A knowledge base reads the PDFs from the S3 bucket, splits them into chunks, creates the embeddings and stores them in the vector store that the team chooses. The existing OpenSearch Serverless collection is a supported vector store, so the vectors stay where the rules say. RetrieveAndGenerate does the rest in one call: it searches the knowledge base with the customer's question, and a Claude model writes the answer from the retrieved chunks. The response also cites its sources. The team writes no code for chunking, embedding, searching or building the prompt.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.5.3: "Deploy and configure vector search solutions to enable semantic search capabilities for FM augmentation"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with managed vector store functionality"

Sources:

  • RetrieveAndGenerate
  • Prerequisites for using a vector store you created for a knowledge base

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the S3 bucket as its data source and the existing collection as its vector store, and have the chatbot call Retrieve, then Converse.
This setup stores the data in the right place. Retrieve returns the matching chunks only, with no answer. The chatbot then needs its own code to build a prompt from the chunks and the question and to call the model with Converse. That fits a team that wants full control of the prompt or of the model call. Here, RetrieveAndGenerate does both steps in one call, so this design adds code that the team does not need.

INCORRECT: Write Lambda functions that chunk the PDFs, embed the chunks with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and index them in the existing collection, and have the chatbot search it and call Converse.
A pipeline that the team builds itself gives full control of chunking, indexing and search, for example for custom ranking. The team must write and maintain the code for each step: reading the PDFs, splitting them, creating embeddings, updating the index when a document changes, searching and building the prompt. A knowledge base does all of this as a managed feature, so this design needs far more development work.

INCORRECT: Extract each product's text into an Amazon DynamoDB table keyed by product name, and have the chatbot look up the named product and send its text to a Claude model.
A lookup by key is fast and exact when users know the item they ask about, for example an order number. Here, customers describe what they need in their own words and rarely know product names. A lookup by product name finds nothing for most questions. The chatbot needs semantic search, which matches the meaning of a question to the meaning of the documents.

The developer must detect responses that either hallucinate facts not present in the source passages or are irrelevant to the user's query.
During a trial, the guardrail must check each response before the user sees it, and the team must see the scores of each response that falls below a threshold. No response may be blocked during the trial.
Which guardrail configuration correctly implements these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A developer is configuring Amazon Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding checks for a RAG-based medical information service. Each request holds one user question and the source passages that a knowledge base retrieved for it, with no conversation history. The developer must detect responses that either hallucinate facts not present in the source passages or are irrelevant to the user's query.
During a trial, the guardrail must check each response before the user sees it, and the team must see the scores of each response that falls below a threshold. No response may be blocked during the trial.
Which guardrail configuration correctly implements these requirements?

options.text: Add GROUNDING and RELEVANCE filters with the action NONE, and turn on the guardrail trace in each Converse request to read the detection details.
Add GROUNDING and RELEVANCE filters with the action BLOCK, and turn on the guardrail trace in each Converse request to read the detection details.
Add a GROUNDING filter only, with the action NONE, and turn on the guardrail trace in each Converse request to read the detection details.
Add a GROUNDING filter only, with the action BLOCK, and turn on the guardrail trace in each Converse request to read the detection details.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add GROUNDING and RELEVANCE filters with the action NONE, and turn on the guardrail trace in each Converse request to read the detection details.
A contextual grounding check compares a model response with a grounding source and the user's query. The GROUNDING filter scores whether the response is supported by the source passages, and the RELEVANCE filter scores whether the response answers the query. Each request here holds one question and its retrieved passages, which is the question answering use case that the check supports. With the action NONE, the guardrail takes no action on a response that falls below a threshold, but it returns the detection details in the trace. The developer turns on the guardrail trace in each Converse request, marks the passages and the question with the grounding source and query qualifiers, and logs the scores of each response that the check flags. The guardrail checks every response before the user sees it, and no response is blocked during the trial.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.3: "Develop accuracy verification systems to reduce hallucinations in FM responses"

Sources:

  • Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses
  • GuardrailContextualGroundingFilterConfig
  • Include a guardrail with the Converse API

INCORRECT: Add GROUNDING and RELEVANCE filters with the action BLOCK, and turn on the guardrail trace in each Converse request to read the detection details.
The action BLOCK replaces a response that falls below a threshold with the guardrail's blocked message. It is the right setting once a team is ready to stop unsupported answers, and responses that pass the check still reach users. Here no response may be blocked during the trial. A response with a low score would be replaced, so the trial would change what users receive.

INCORRECT: Add a GROUNDING filter only, with the action NONE, and turn on the guardrail trace in each Converse request to read the detection details.
A GROUNDING filter alone fits a service where the only risk is a response that adds facts the source does not contain, such as a summary of one document. Here the developer must also detect responses that are irrelevant to the user's query. Only the RELEVANCE filter scores that. A response that is true to the passages but answers a different question would pass with no record.

INCORRECT: Add a GROUNDING filter only, with the action BLOCK, and turn on the guardrail trace in each Converse request to read the detection details.
A GROUNDING filter with the action BLOCK fits a service that must stop answers with facts that are not in the source, such as summaries of one document that go straight to readers. This design misses two requirements here. No response may be blocked during the trial, and the action BLOCK replaces a response that scores below the threshold. The team must also detect responses that are irrelevant to the user's query, and a GROUNDING filter alone does not score that.

questions.domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
questions.promptHtml:
An online store uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to write a personalized description for each shopper on every product page. The application calls the model on demand in one AWS Region. During flash sales, traffic rises to many times the normal level, and many calls fail with ThrottlingException or take several seconds.

Every product page must load within 2 seconds. During a spike, a generic description is acceptable for a short time, but a slow or failed page is not. The company wants to keep personalized descriptions for as many shoppers as possible, without paying for model capacity that stays unused on normal days.

Which TWO actions should the company take?

Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
An online store uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to write a personalized description for each shopper on every product page. The application calls the model on demand in one AWS Region. During flash sales, traffic rises to many times the normal level, and many calls fail with ThrottlingException or take several seconds.
Every product page must load within 2 seconds. During a spike, a generic description is acceptable for a short time, but a slow or failed page is not. The company wants to keep personalized descriptions for as many shoppers as possible, without paying for model capacity that stays unused on normal days.
Which TWO actions should the company take?
Select TWO.

options.text: Call the model through a cross-Region inference profile, so Amazon Bedrock can process each request in one of several AWS Regions in that profile.
Show a generic description, written in advance and stored in Amazon DynamoDB, when a call returns ThrottlingException or is too slow for the page load limit.
Create a Provisioned Throughput for the model in the current AWS Region, with enough model units for the busiest sale, and send all calls to it.
Raise the maximum attempts in the AWS SDK retry settings, so calls that return ThrottlingException try again with exponential backoff before the SDK returns the error.
Route the description calls through Amazon API Gateway with a rate limit at the normal traffic level, so fewer calls reach Amazon Bedrock during a spike.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Call the model through a cross-Region inference profile, so Amazon Bedrock can process each request in one of several AWS Regions in that profile.
A cross-Region inference profile names a model and the AWS Regions to which Amazon Bedrock can route requests for that model. Through the profile, Amazon Bedrock uses compute across these Regions, so a flash sale no longer depends on the capacity of one Region. More calls succeed during a spike, and more shoppers keep their personalized descriptions. The application still calls the model on demand and reserves no capacity in advance. There is no extra routing cost, and the price follows the Region that the application calls from. On normal days, the company pays nothing for unused model capacity.

CORRECT: Show a generic description, written in advance and stored in Amazon DynamoDB, when a call returns ThrottlingException or is too slow for the page load limit.
Graceful degradation means that an application keeps its core function when a service it calls fails, even if the application shows simpler data for a while. Here the core function is a product page that loads within 2 seconds. When Amazon Bedrock returns ThrottlingException, or a call has not answered in time for that limit, the application stops waiting. The application then reads the generic description of the product from Amazon DynamoDB, and the page loads on time. The company accepts a generic description during a spike, so this short loss of personalization is allowed. A slow or failed page is not allowed.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.3: "Create resilient FM systems to ensure reliable operations"
Example: "fallback mechanisms for graceful degradation"

Sources:

  • Route model inference requests across AWS Regions with cross-Region inference

  • REL05-BP01 Implement graceful degradation to transform applicable hard dependencies into soft dependencies

INCORRECT: Create a Provisioned Throughput for the model in the current AWS Region, with enough model units for the busiest sale, and send all calls to it.
Provisioned Throughput gives a model a higher level of throughput at a fixed cost. The company chooses a number of model units, and Amazon Bedrock bills them every hour until the company deletes the Provisioned Throughput. This fits steady, predictable traffic that needs high throughput every day. Here the capacity is sized for the busiest sale and serves all calls, so the company pays for that peak capacity on normal days too. The company does not want to pay for model capacity that stays unused.

INCORRECT: Raise the maximum attempts in the AWS SDK retry settings, so calls that return ThrottlingException try again with exponential backoff before the SDK returns the error.
The AWS SDK retries throttled calls with exponential backoff, and it adds a random part to each wait. On average, each retry waits longer than the one before. When a call reaches the maximum number of attempts, the SDK stops and returns the error. More attempts help work where a delay does no harm, such as a nightly job that writes descriptions for new products. On a product page, the shopper waits while each retry runs. During a flash sale, many calls are throttled again and again, so the extra waits make many pages take longer than 2 seconds. The retries also send more calls to Amazon Bedrock while it is already busy.

INCORRECT: Route the description calls through Amazon API Gateway with a rate limit at the normal traffic level, so fewer calls reach Amazon Bedrock during a spike.
Amazon API Gateway can limit the rate of requests to an API, which protects the API from too many requests. This fits when one client must not take the capacity that other clients need. When requests go over the limit, API Gateway throttles them, and the client receives a 429 Too Many Requests error. With the limit at the normal traffic level, many calls during a flash sale end with this error, and those product pages fail to load. The application could show the generic description for these calls instead. Even then, the limit stops calls that Amazon Bedrock could still answer, so fewer shoppers see a personalized description. The company wants personalized descriptions for as many shoppers as possible.

A financial services company uses Amazon Bedrock to generate investment analysis reports. The prompt engineering team frequently updates prompts to improve output quality, but recent production incidents showed that prompt changes caused incorrect financial calculations.
The company requires a solution that enables prompt versioning with the ability to rollback to previous versions, tracks which prompt version generated each report for audit compliance, sends alerts when prompt performance degrades (measured by downstream validation failures), and maintains a complete audit trail of all prompt changes for regulatory reviews.
Which solution meets ALL these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A financial services company uses Amazon Bedrock to generate investment analysis reports. The prompt engineering team frequently updates prompts to improve output quality, but recent production incidents showed that prompt changes caused incorrect financial calculations.
The company requires a solution that enables prompt versioning with the ability to rollback to previous versions, tracks which prompt version generated each report for audit compliance, sends alerts when prompt performance degrades (measured by downstream validation failures), and maintains a complete audit trail of all prompt changes for regulatory reviews.
Which solution meets ALL these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Bedrock Prompt Management, creating a numbered version for each production release. Invoke Bedrock with the prompt version ARN and log that ARN with every report to CloudWatch Logs. Create a CloudTrail trail for prompt changes. Use CloudWatch metric filters and alarms on validation failure logs to send SNS alerts, and query with CloudWatch Logs Insights.

Use Bedrock Prompt Management to create and version prompts, tagging each version with its number. Configure CloudWatch Logs to capture Bedrock InvokeModel requests with prompt details. Create a Lambda function that parses those logs, detects validation failures, and publishes alerts to SNS. Store prompt change history in DynamoDB for regulatory audit reports.

Store prompts as text files in S3 with versioning enabled. Build a Lambda-based versioning system that reads prompts from S3, tracks versions in DynamoDB, and passes them to the Bedrock InvokeModel API. Trigger Lambda through S3 Event Notifications to log prompt changes to CloudWatch. Use CloudWatch Synthetics to test prompt quality and alert via SNS.

Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to manage prompts with versioning enabled. Create a Step Functions workflow that retrieves the prompt version, invokes Bedrock, and logs the version and output to CloudWatch Logs. Track prompt updates with Parameter Store change notifications through EventBridge. Alarm on custom metrics that the workflow publishes when validation fails.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Use Bedrock Prompt Management, creating a numbered version for each production release. Invoke Bedrock with the prompt version ARN and log that ARN with every report to CloudWatch Logs. Create a CloudTrail trail for prompt changes. Use CloudWatch metric filters and alarms on validation failure logs to send SNS alerts, and query with CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management keeps one working draft of each prompt, and the team creates a version when a prompt is ready for production. Each version is a static snapshot, and versions are numbered from 1, so a released version never changes when someone edits the draft. The application calls Converse or InvokeModel with the ARN of one prompt version as the model ID, so a rollback means pointing the application at the ARN of the earlier version. The application writes that ARN to CloudWatch Logs with each report, which ties every report to the exact prompt that produced it. CloudTrail records prompt changes as management events, but its event history covers only the past 90 days, so a trail delivers the events to Amazon S3 for regulatory reviews. CloudWatch metric filters turn the validation failure lines in the logs into metrics, and alarms on those metrics send alerts through Amazon SNS with no custom code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.3: "Implement comprehensive prompt management and governance systems to ensure consistency and oversight of FM operations"

Sources:

  • Test a prompt using Prompt management

  • CreatePromptVersion

  • Monitor Amazon Bedrock API calls using CloudTrail

INCORRECT: Use Bedrock Prompt Management to create and version prompts, tagging each version with its number. Configure CloudWatch Logs to capture Bedrock InvokeModel requests with prompt details. Create a Lambda function that parses those logs, detects validation failures, and publishes alerts to SNS. Store prompt change history in DynamoDB for regulatory audit reports.
This option uses Prompt Management for versions, which is the right choice, but it adds custom parts. A Lambda function that reads the logs to find validation failures does the job of CloudWatch metric filters and alarms, which turn log patterns into metrics and send alerts through Amazon SNS with no code. A DynamoDB table of prompt changes repeats what CloudTrail already records as management events, with the caller and the time. The table needs write logic, a schema and retention rules that someone must build and maintain. The question asks for the LEAST operational overhead, so this custom code is extra work.

INCORRECT: Store prompts as text files in S3 with versioning enabled. Build a Lambda-based versioning system that reads prompts from S3, tracks versions in DynamoDB, and passes them to the Bedrock InvokeModel API. Trigger Lambda through S3 Event Notifications to log prompt changes to CloudWatch. Use CloudWatch Synthetics to test prompt quality and alert via SNS.
Prompt files in Amazon S3 with versioning keep each older copy of a file. This fits a team that keeps its prompt templates as files in a repository. Here the team would build its own code for version tracking, rollback and retrieval, which Prompt Management already provides, and Amazon Bedrock cannot run a prompt from S3 by an ARN. CloudWatch Synthetics does not fit either. Its canaries are scripts that run on a schedule, mostly to check the availability and latency of endpoints and APIs. A canary could check a test report against an expected value, but the team would have to write and maintain that script too, and it tests on a schedule, not the reports that the application really produces.

INCORRECT: Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to manage prompts with versioning enabled. Create a Step Functions workflow that retrieves the prompt version, invokes Bedrock, and logs the version and output to CloudWatch Logs. Track prompt updates with Parameter Store change notifications through EventBridge. Alarm on custom metrics that the workflow publishes when validation fails.
Parameter Store creates a new version of a parameter each time its value changes, so it can hold prompt text with a version history. It fits general settings that an application reads at run time. It has no prompt features such as variables and variants, and Amazon Bedrock cannot run a stored parameter by its ARN, so the application must read the text and build each request itself. A Step Functions workflow around every model call adds a workflow to build and run for one read and one call. Custom metrics from the workflow are more code, while metric filters read the failure lines from the logs with no code.

Add a steering file that lists the current AgentCore parameters and loads in every chat, so Kiro writes each call from that list.
Set up a hook that runs when Kiro saves a source file and runs the team's integration tests, so each wrong call fails a test after the save.
Create a spec for each Lambda function, so Kiro writes requirements, a design and a task list before it writes any AgentCore call.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add the AWS Documentation MCP server to the workspace MCP configuration of Kiro, so Kiro can search and read AWS documentation while it writes each call.
MCP lets Kiro talk to external servers that give it tools and resources. Kiro reads its MCP servers from a configuration file, and the file in the workspace applies only to that project. The AWS Documentation MCP server gives Kiro tools to search and read AWS documentation directly within Kiro. Before Kiro writes an AgentCore call, it can read the current API page, so it uses parameter names that the API accepts today. Nobody has to keep notes up to date, because Kiro reads the source pages each time. The server runs as a local process that Kiro starts on the developer's computer, so the team runs no new AWS resources.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.4: "Enhance developer productivity to accelerate development workflows for GenAI applications"
Example: "code suggestions for API assistance"

Sources:

  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Kiro documentation)
  • Configuration (Kiro documentation)
  • Steering (Kiro documentation)

INCORRECT: Add a steering file that lists the current AgentCore parameters and loads in every chat, so Kiro writes each call from that list.
A steering file is a markdown file that gives Kiro lasting knowledge about the project, and by default Kiro loads it into every interaction. It is the right tool for team rules that seldom change, such as naming patterns. Here the team already tried a file of parameter notes that Kiro loads in every chat, and the notes were out of date within weeks. A steering file with a longer list goes out of date in the same way.

INCORRECT: Set up a hook that runs when Kiro saves a source file and runs the team's integration tests, so each wrong call fails a test after the save.
A hook runs an action when an event happens, such as when Kiro saves a file. A hook that runs tests after each change catches broken code soon after Kiro writes it, which helps a team whose tests run only by hand. Here the team's checks already catch each wrong call, but only after Kiro has written it. Running the tests sooner still leaves a wrong call in the code, and Kiro must write each call correctly from the start.

INCORRECT: Create a spec for each Lambda function, so Kiro writes requirements, a design and a task list before it writes any AgentCore call.
A spec turns a request into requirements, a design and a task list before Kiro writes code. It helps when Kiro misreads what a feature must do. Here Kiro already builds the right logic in each function, and only the parameter names in the AgentCore calls are wrong. A plan for each function does not tell Kiro which parameters the API accepts today.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Subscribe to the model in Amazon Bedrock Marketplace, deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint on the chosen instance type, and call Converse with the endpoint ARN as the model ID.
Amazon Bedrock Marketplace offers popular, emerging and specialized models, including proprietary models and models built for finance. The team subscribes to the model and deploys it to an endpoint that SageMaker AI manages, and it chooses the number of instances and the instance type. The app then sends Converse requests through the Amazon Bedrock APIs, with the endpoint ARN as the model ID, so it uses the same API as the other apps. Not every Marketplace model supports Converse, and the provider states that this model does. The team deploys the model as the provider offers it, so it never needs the weights.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.2.1: "Deploy FMs based on specific application needs and performance requirements"

  • Amazon Bedrock Marketplace
  • Amazon Bedrock Marketplace brings over 100 models to Amazon Bedrock
  • Use Custom model import to import a customized open-source model into Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Deploy the model from SageMaker JumpStart to a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on an instance type that the team picks, and call the endpoint with the InvokeEndpoint API from the new app.
SageMaker JumpStart deploys a model to a SageMaker AI endpoint on an instance type that the team picks, and an app then calls the endpoint with the InvokeEndpoint API. This fits teams that call SageMaker AI endpoints directly in their code. Here the new app must use the Converse API, as the other apps do. The import job reads the model files, in the Hugging Face weights format, from Amazon S3, and the team then calls the model on demand. This fits a company that holds the weights of its own fine-tuned open model. Here the provider does not share the weights, so the team has no model files to import.

INCORRECT: Create Provisioned Throughput for the model in Amazon Bedrock, and call the provisioned model with the Converse API and its model ARN, as the other apps do.
Provisioned Throughput gives a model in Amazon Bedrock a higher level of throughput at a fixed cost, billed by the hour. It fits a steady, heavy load on a model that Amazon Bedrock itself serves. Here Amazon Bedrock does not offer this model as a serverless model, so there is no Amazon Bedrock model to provision.

questions.promptText:
A research institution manages a digital archive of mixed-format documents in Amazon S3: typed reports (text PDFs), data tables embedded in PDFs, and charts saved as JPEG and PNG images. The institution is creating a new Amazon Bedrock knowledge base for its researchers. The institution manages this knowledge base itself, so it is not a managed knowledge base, and the archive bucket is its S3 data source.
The solution must extract structured data from tables, process the charts, and prepare all content for semantic search. The institution requires an automated pipeline that processes new uploads with minimal manual intervention and handles the variety of formats without custom code or parsing prompts.
Which knowledge base configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Set Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as the parser of the knowledge base's S3 data source, and give the knowledge base an S3 location for the images and figures it extracts.
Set Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as the parser of the knowledge base's S3 data source, and give the knowledge base no extra S3 location, because the parser turns each file into text.
Set a foundation model as the parser of the knowledge base's S3 data source, and write a parsing prompt that tells the model how to read tables, charts and image files.
Add an AWS Lambda function that runs on each S3 upload, calls the Amazon Bedrock Data Automation API, and writes the extracted text to a prefix that the knowledge base syncs.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as the parser of the knowledge base's S3 data source, and give the knowledge base an S3 location for the images and figures it extracts.
Amazon Bedrock Data Automation is a managed parser that processes multimodal data with no prompt to write. It parses figures, charts and tables in PDF files, and it also parses JPEG and PNG image files. The default parser reads only the text in text files, so it does not process the charts saved as images. Data Automation stores the figures, tables and images that it extracts in the S3 location that the team gives the knowledge base. Each sync of the data source then parses new uploads with the same parser, so no file type needs its own code. This parser setting works on a knowledge base that the institution manages itself, because a managed knowledge base accepts only its own smart parsing.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.3.2: "Create data processing workflows to handle complex data types including text, image, audio, and tabular data with specialized processing requirements for FM consumption"
Example: "advanced multimodal pipeline architectures"

Sources:

  • Parsing options for your data source
  • ParsingConfiguration
  • Prerequisites for multimodal knowledge bases

INCORRECT: Set Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as the parser of the knowledge base's S3 data source, and give the knowledge base no extra S3 location, because the parser turns each file into text.
Data Automation converts content to text, so an S3 location for multimodal content is optional when text parsing is enough. This setting fits an archive of PDF files where the text and the tables are all the team needs. Here the archive also holds charts saved as JPEG and PNG images. Without an S3 location for multimodal content, the parser offers only text parsing, so those image files are not processed.

INCORRECT: Set a foundation model as the parser of the knowledge base's S3 data source, and write a parsing prompt that tells the model how to read tables, charts and image files.
A foundation model parser also processes multimodal data, and it lets a team change the prompt that tells the model what to extract. This fits a team that needs its own extraction rules for its documents. Here the institution wants no parsing prompts. Data Automation needs no prompt at all, so writing and maintaining a parsing prompt is work that the requirements rule out.

INCORRECT: Add an AWS Lambda function that runs on each S3 upload, calls the Amazon Bedrock Data Automation API, and writes the extracted text to a prefix that the knowledge base syncs.
Calling Data Automation from a Lambda function on each upload is a real pattern when a team also needs the extracted output in other systems, or wants its own steps around it. Here the institution wants no custom code. The function, its error handling and the extra prefix are code and storage that the team must build and run, while the knowledge base can use the same service as its parser.

A customer support system uses Amazon Bedrock to answer product questions through multi-turn conversations. The workflow must: (1) retrieve relevant product documentation from a knowledge base, (2) generate an initial response using a Claude model, (3) only if the response mentions out-of-stock items, query an inventory API to get current availability, (4) generate a final response incorporating inventory data.
The application already stores each conversation's history and sends it with each turn. It must make one call per turn and receive the final answer in that call's response. An existing AWS Lambda function calls the inventory API, and the team will write no other code.
Which design meets the requirements for each turn?

A customer support system uses Amazon Bedrock to answer product questions through multi-turn conversations. The workflow must: (1) retrieve relevant product documentation from a knowledge base, (2) generate an initial response using a Claude model, (3) only if the response mentions out-of-stock items, query an inventory API to get current availability, (4) generate a final response incorporating inventory data.
The application already stores each conversation's history and sends it with each turn. It must make one call per turn and receive the final answer in that call's response. An existing AWS Lambda function calls the inventory API, and the team will write no other code.
Which design meets the requirements for each turn?

options.text: Build a flow in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows with a Knowledge base node, Prompt nodes, the inventory Lambda function node, and a Condition node that checks whether a classifier Prompt node returned "YES".

Build a flow in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows with a Knowledge base node, Prompt nodes, and the inventory Lambda function node, which receives the initial response on every turn before the final Prompt node runs.
Write a new Lambda function that retrieves from the knowledge base, calls the model with the Converse API, calls the inventory function when needed, and returns the final answer.
Build an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow with Amazon Bedrock tasks, a Choice state and the inventory Lambda function, and have the application start one execution for each turn.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Build a flow in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows with a Knowledge base node, Prompt nodes, the inventory Lambda function node, and a Condition node that checks whether a classifier Prompt node returned "YES".
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows links nodes into one workflow, and the application runs the whole flow with one InvokeFlow call. The application passes the question and the stored history in the flow input. A Knowledge base node retrieves the documentation, and a Prompt node writes the initial response. A second Prompt node reads that response and returns only YES or NO for whether it mentions an out-of-stock item. A Condition node can compare strings only as equal or not equal, so it checks whether that output equals "YES". Only that branch runs the Lambda function node, which calls the existing inventory function, and a last Prompt node writes the final answer. The flow returns the answer in the response, and the team writes no new code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.6: "Design complex prompt systems to handle sophisticated tasks with FMs"
Example: "conditional branching based on model responses"

Sources:

  • Node types for your flow

  • Choosing workflow type in Step Functions

  • Invoke and customize Amazon Bedrock models with Step Functions

INCORRECT: Build a flow in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows with a Knowledge base node, Prompt nodes, and the inventory Lambda function node, which receives the initial response on every turn before the final Prompt node runs.
A flow that calls the inventory function on every turn is simpler, and it fits when every answer needs current stock data. Here the workflow may query the inventory API only when the initial response mentions out-of-stock items. With no Condition node, every turn calls the API, including turns about product features that have nothing to do with stock.

INCORRECT: Write a new Lambda function that retrieves from the knowledge base, calls the model with the Converse API, calls the inventory function when needed, and returns the final answer.
One Lambda function that calls each service in turn is a common way to build a chain of model calls, and it gives a team full control of each step. It fits a team that is ready to write and maintain that code. Here the team will write no new code, and the only Lambda function in the design is the existing inventory function. This option adds a new function with its own retrieval, model calls, branching and error handling.

INCORRECT: Build an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow with Amazon Bedrock tasks, a Choice state and the inventory Lambda function, and have the application start one execution for each turn.
Step Functions Standard workflows fit long, durable processes, such as an approval that waits for days. A Choice state can branch on the model's output, and the workflow can call Amazon Bedrock with the optimized InvokeModel integration and run the inventory function. But the call that starts an execution returns only the execution ARN and its start time, not the result. The application would need more calls to get the final answer, and it must receive that answer in the response to its one call.

questions.promptHtml:
A support assistant searches product manuals. A custom pipeline in an AWS Lambda function passes the text of each manual to Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings in Amazon Bedrock in one request, with the text truncation mode END, and stores one vector for each manual in Amazon OpenSearch Service.
Questions about any part of a short manual work. For long manuals, questions about the first pages work, but questions about the last sections find nothing. In the pipeline's log, each response for a long manual includes an extra field that holds a character position. Responses for short manuals do not.
Which change makes every section of every manual searchable?
questions.promptText:
A support assistant searches product manuals. A custom pipeline in an AWS Lambda function passes the text of each manual to Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings in Amazon Bedrock in one request, with the text truncation mode END, and stores one vector for each manual in Amazon OpenSearch Service.
Questions about any part of a short manual work. For long manuals, questions about the first pages work, but questions about the last sections find nothing. In the pipeline's log, each response for a long manual includes an extra field that holds a character position. Responses for short manuals do not.
Which change makes every section of every manual searchable?

options.text: Split each manual into chunks below the model's input limit, and store one vector for each chunk, so the model reads every part of each manual.
Set the text truncation mode to NONE, so each request for a manual that is over the model's input limit fails instead of being cut.
Set the text truncation mode to START, so the model drops the start of a manual that is over its input limit and keeps the end.
Raise the embedding dimension to the largest size that the model offers, so each vector holds more detail from the later sections of a long manual.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Split each manual into chunks below the model's input limit, and store one vector for each chunk, so the model reads every part of each manual.
An embedding model reads only a limited number of tokens in one request. With Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, the text truncation mode decides what happens to text past that limit: START or END drops part of the text, and NONE makes the request fail. When the model cuts the text, the response includes truncatedCharLength, the character position where the text was cut. That is the extra field in the log. Questions about the first pages of long manuals still work, so the cut removed the end of each long manual, and its last sections never reached the vector. Chunks that stay below the limit give every part of each manual its own vector. After the change, the team checks that no response carries truncatedCharLength.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.1: "Resolve content handling issues to ensure that necessary information is processed completely in FM interactions"
Example: "truncation-related error analysis"

Sources:

  • Complete embeddings request and response schema (Amazon Nova User Guide)
  • Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings: State-of-the-art embedding model for agentic RAG and semantic search

INCORRECT: Set the text truncation mode to NONE, so each request for a manual that is over the model's input limit fails instead of being cut.
The truncation mode NONE makes a request fail when the text is over the model's limit. It is a good choice when a team wants to know at once that an input is too long, instead of storing a vector of part of a text. Here it turns each cut manual into a failed request. The long manuals would then have no vector at all, so even their first pages would stop being searchable.

INCORRECT: Set the text truncation mode to START, so the model drops the start of a manual that is over its input limit and keeps the end.
The truncation mode START drops the start of a text that is over the limit and keeps the end. It fits text where the last part matters most, such as a long message thread where the newest messages come last. Here every section must be searchable. The last sections would start to work, but questions about the first pages of long manuals, which work today, would then find nothing.

INCORRECT: Raise the embedding dimension to the largest size that the model offers, so each vector holds more detail from the later sections of a long manual.
The model offers several output dimensions, and a team picks a larger one when search quality matters more than the cost of storage. Here short manuals are found at every section with the current size, so the vectors are detailed enough. The problem is text that never reaches the model. A larger vector of the first part of a manual still holds nothing from its last sections.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A developer has deployed an AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and also uses AgentCore Memory and AgentCore Gateway. The default AgentCore metrics appear in CloudWatch, but the CloudWatch generative AI observability dashboard shows no spans or traces.
The agent code runs with OpenTelemetry instrumentation, and tracing is on for the agent runtime and the memory. The application logs of all three resources reach CloudWatch Logs. The team uses only CloudWatch for observability.
Which step makes the spans and traces appear in the dashboard?
questions.promptText:
A developer has deployed an AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and also uses AgentCore Memory and AgentCore Gateway. The default AgentCore metrics appear in CloudWatch, but the CloudWatch generative AI observability dashboard shows no spans or traces.
The agent code runs with OpenTelemetry instrumentation, and tracing is on for the agent runtime and the memory. The application logs of all three resources reach CloudWatch Logs. The team uses only CloudWatch for observability.
Which step makes the spans and traces appear in the dashboard?

options.text: Turn on CloudWatch Transaction Search as a one-time setup, so CloudWatch ingests the spans as structured logs and can show the traces.
Add the ADOT SDK to the agent's dependencies and run the agent with opentelemetry-instrument, so the agent code emits its own spans.
Add log delivery with the APPLICATION_LOGS log type to the memory and the gateway, so CloudWatch Logs receives their records.
Set DISABLE_ADOT_OBSERVABILITY to true in the agent runtime, so the agent sends its telemetry to the platform that the team configures.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on CloudWatch Transaction Search as a one-time setup, so CloudWatch ingests the spans as structured logs and can show the traces.
AgentCore provides metrics by default for every resource type, which is why the metrics already appear. Spans and traces need more. To view them, the account needs a one-time setup that turns on CloudWatch Transaction Search, which ingests spans as structured logs. Here the agent code already sends spans, tracing is on for the runtime and the memory, and the gateway produces its spans by default. The dashboard stays empty only because Transaction Search is off. After the developer turns it on, the dashboard can show the spans and traces.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.1: "Create holistic observability systems to provide complete visibility into FM application performance"
Example: "FM interaction tracing"

Sources:

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore generated observability data

  • Add observability to your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore resources

  • AgentCore generated runtime observability data

INCORRECT: Add the ADOT SDK to the agent's dependencies and run the agent with opentelemetry-instrument, so the agent code emits its own spans.
The ADOT SDK, run with opentelemetry-instrument, is how an agent on AgentCore Runtime sends spans and traces from its own code. A developer adds it when the agent code is not instrumented yet. Here the agent code already runs with OpenTelemetry instrumentation. Adding it again changes nothing, because the dashboard cannot show any span until Transaction Search is on.

INCORRECT: Add log delivery with the APPLICATION_LOGS log type to the memory and the gateway, so CloudWatch Logs receives their records.
Log delivery with the APPLICATION_LOGS log type sends the application logs of a memory or a gateway to a destination such as CloudWatch Logs. It is the step to take when those logs are missing. Here the logs of all three resources already reach CloudWatch Logs. The missing data is spans and traces, and log delivery is a separate setting from tracing.

INCORRECT: Set DISABLE_ADOT_OBSERVABILITY to true in the agent runtime, so the agent sends its telemetry to the platform that the team configures.
Setting DISABLE_ADOT_OBSERVABILITY to true removes the runtime's default ADOT settings, so a team can send its agent's telemetry to another observability platform. Here the team uses only CloudWatch. This setting would turn off the default settings that send the agent's data to CloudWatch, so it would remove data from the dashboard and add no spans.
